cards.title: Describe a person who has chosen a career in the medical field (doctor, nurse, vet)
points: How you feel about his/her career choice.
cards.note: Người trong bài: em trai 17 tuổi muốn làm bác sĩ (chi tiết giả định; bạn thay bằng người thật nếu muốn).

notes.v: wants to be a doctor (studying for medical school)
grandmother ill, doctor helped, wants to help people
proud, a bit worried (long, hard study)

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my younger brother, Khoi. He's seventeen and still at high school, but he has chosen to become a doctor, so he's preparing for the entrance exam to medical university.

He isn't a doctor yet, but he studies biology, chemistry and maths very hard every day. His dream is to work in a hospital and treat patients.

He chose this career because of our grandmother. When she was ill a few years ago, a kind doctor took care of her very well. My brother saw how happy our family was, and he decided he wanted to help people like that.

I think he has many good qualities. He's hard-working, caring and patient. He is also calm when something goes wrong, which is important for a doctor.

I feel very proud of him. I think it's a great choice, but I'm also a bit worried because studying medicine takes many years and is very stressful. Anyway, I will always support him.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my younger brother, Khoi, who's seventeen and has set his heart on becoming a doctor. He's currently preparing for the entrance exam to a medical university.

Strictly speaking, he isn't in the profession yet, but he's already putting in long hours on biology, chemistry and maths. His ambition is to work in a hospital and treat patients.

What inspired him was our grandmother's illness a few years ago. A caring doctor looked after her so well that our whole family felt reassured, and that experience made my brother determined to make a difference in other people's lives.

As for his qualities, he's hard-working, compassionate and remarkably patient. What I admire most is that he stays calm under pressure, which is essential for a doctor.

I'm extremely proud of his choice. It's a noble career, although I do worry a little, since medical training is long and demanding. Still, I'm fully behind him, and I believe he'll make an excellent doctor one day.

Whenever I see him revising late at night, I'm reminded how much determination it takes. I often bring him tea and test him on vocabulary, and I'd love to be the first person he calls when he finally becomes a doctor.

p3.q: Why do some people choose to work in the medical field?
p3.a6: Some people want to help others, like my brother. Others choose it because doctors have a stable job and a good income.
p3.a7: Some are motivated by a desire to help people, as my brother is, while others are drawn by job security and a respectable income.

p3.q: How does working in a medical profession impact a person's life?
p3.a6: They are often very busy and have night shifts, so they have less time for family. But they feel proud because they save lives.
p3.a7: It can be tough on their personal lives because of long hours and night shifts, but the sense of purpose from saving lives is hugely rewarding.

p3.q: Do you think medical professionals are valued in society?
p3.a6: I think so, especially after COVID-19. People respected them more. But sometimes they still get little understanding when things go wrong.
p3.a7: Largely, yes, particularly since the pandemic, when their sacrifices were widely recognised, although they can still face unfair criticism when things go wrong.

p3.q: Which is more important: doctors or nurses?
p3.a6: I think both are equally important. Doctors make the treatment plan, and nurses take care of patients every day.
p3.a7: Both are equally vital. Doctors diagnose and plan treatment, while nurses provide round-the-clock care.

p3.q: Can a hospital function effectively without nurses? / Differences between doctors and nurses?
p3.a6: No, it can't. Nurses give medicine, check patients and support doctors. Doctors diagnose diseases and decide on treatment, so their work is different.
p3.a7: Not at all. Nurses administer medication, monitor patients and support doctors, whose role is mainly diagnosis and treatment decisions, so the two jobs complement each other.

p3.q: How can technology influence medical professions in the future?
p3.a6: AI can help doctors read X-rays and find diseases faster. Patients can also have online consultations, so it saves time.
p3.a7: AI can help detect diseases from scans more quickly, and telemedicine will let patients consult doctors remotely, saving time for both sides.

p3.q: What qualities are essential for success in medicine? / Is it difficult to become a doctor?
p3.a6: They need patience, knowledge and good communication. It's very difficult because students study for many years and the exams are hard.
p3.a7: Patience, solid knowledge, empathy and communication skills. Becoming a doctor is highly demanding, with years of study and fierce competition.

p3.q: Is the medical field more stressful than other jobs? / Are they paid enough?
p3.a6: Yes, because a small mistake can affect someone's life. In my opinion, in Vietnam, many doctors and nurses are not paid enough for the hard work.
p3.a7: Yes, because errors can have life-or-death consequences. And I'd argue many healthcare workers in Vietnam are underpaid relative to their workload.

p3.q: Is it necessary to learn first aid? / Does studying biology make students healthier?
p3.a6: Yes, first aid can save lives in emergencies, so everyone should learn it. Biology helps students understand their body, so they may take better care of their health.
p3.a7: Absolutely, it can be life-saving in emergencies. Biology also raises health awareness, so students may adopt healthier habits.

p3.q: Are young people interested in becoming doctors?
p3.a6: Some are, but many prefer IT or business because medical study is long and difficult.
p3.a7: Some are, but many gravitate towards IT or business, as medical training is long and gruelling.

cards.title: Describe a person you know who loves to grow plants
points: How you feel about this person.
cards.note: Người trong bài: mẹ bạn, trồng rau thơm trên sân thượng (chi tiết giả định).

notes.v: roof terrace, pots and foam boxes

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my mother, who loves growing plants. She's in her fifties and she spends a lot of her free time on it.

She mostly grows herbs, like mint, basil and coriander, and some chilli. She also has a few flowers, such as roses, because she likes the colours.

She grows them on the roof terrace of our house. We don't have a garden, so she uses pots and old foam boxes. Every morning she waters the plants and checks them carefully.

She enjoys it for two reasons. First, she thinks it's relaxing and it makes her feel happy. Second, she likes using fresh vegetables for cooking, because they are clean and safe for the family.

I really admire my mother. She's patient and hard-working, and she never gives up even when the plants die. I also feel grateful because we can enjoy her delicious meals with fresh herbs every day.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my mother, who's passionate about growing plants. She's in her fifties and devotes much of her spare time to it.

She mainly grows herbs, such as mint, basil and coriander, along with a few chilli plants. She also keeps some flowers, roses in particular, because she loves their colours.

Since we don't have a garden, she's turned our roof terrace into a miniature green space, using pots and old foam boxes. Every morning, she waters the plants and examines the leaves for any signs of pests.

As for why she enjoys it, firstly, she finds it incredibly therapeutic, a way to unwind after a day of housework. Secondly, she likes having fresh, pesticide-free vegetables for cooking, which gives her peace of mind about the family's health.

I deeply admire her. She's patient and persistent, and she never gives up even when some plants die. I'm also grateful, as her home-cooked meals taste so much better with herbs picked just minutes earlier.

She often gives herbs to our neighbours too, which has turned our little roof into a source of joy for the whole lane. Seeing her smile while she picks leaves for dinner is honestly one of my favourite everyday moments.

p3.q: Are there many people growing their own vegetables now? / Do people in your country like it?
p3.a6: Yes, more and more. People in Hanoi worry about food safety, so they grow vegetables on balconies and roofs.
p3.a7: Increasingly so. Out of concern for food safety, many Hanoians now grow vegetables on balconies and rooftops.

p3.q: Do you think it's good to let kids learn how to plant?
p3.a6: Yes, it teaches them to be patient and responsible, and they learn where food comes from.
p3.a7: Definitely. It teaches patience and responsibility and shows children where their food actually comes from.

p3.q: What do you think of the job of a farmer? / Does farming matter?
p3.a6: It's hard work, but very important, because farmers give us food. I think they should earn more.
p3.a7: It's back-breaking work, yet indispensable, since farmers feed the nation. They deserve better incomes.

p3.q: Differences between traditional and modern agriculture? / Is food produced differently from the past?
p3.a6: In the past, farmers used buffaloes and did everything by hand. Now they use machines and technology, so they produce more food faster.
p3.a7: Traditionally, farmers relied on buffaloes and manual labour, whereas modern farming uses machinery and technology to produce larger quantities more efficiently.

p3.q: What happened to farmers' income during the pandemic?
p3.a6: Many farmers lost income because transport was stopped and they couldn't sell their products. Some began to sell online.
p3.a7: Many suffered because lockdowns disrupted transport and markets, though some adapted by selling their produce online.

p3.q: How do people grow plants in cities? / Benefits of growing plants at home?
p3.a6: They use pots, small boxes or vertical gardens on balconies. Plants make the air cleaner and the home more beautiful.
p3.a7: They use pots, planter boxes or vertical gardens on balconies. Plants purify the air and make a home feel more welcoming.

p3.q: Is gardening easier now than in the past? / Is planting easy or difficult?
p3.a6: It's easier now because we can learn from YouTube and buy tools and seeds online. But it still takes time and patience.
p3.a7: Easier, thanks to online tutorials and ready-made supplies, but it still demands time and patience.

p3.q: Why do some people enjoy gardening? / Is it popular among young people?
p3.a6: It helps them relax and escape stress. Young people are busy, but some like small plants such as cactus because they are easy to take care of.
p3.a7: It's a great stress-reliever. Young people are busy, but low-maintenance plants like cacti are quite popular with them.

p3.q: How can plants improve people's quality of life?
p3.a6: Plants make the air cleaner and the house cooler. Looking at green plants also makes people feel calm and happy.
p3.a7: Plants purify the air, keep a home cooler and the greenery has a calming effect, which boosts both physical and mental wellbeing.

p3.q: Do you have a favourite type of plant to grow?
p3.a6: I like mint and basil, because they smell good and I can use them in cooking. They are also easy to grow.
p3.a7: Mint and basil, since they smell wonderful, are handy for cooking and are very easy to look after.

p3.q: What preparations do you need for planting?
p3.a6: You need seeds or small plants, soil, pots, water and a place with sunlight. You also need some basic knowledge about each plant.
p3.a7: Seeds or seedlings, good soil, pots or boxes, a sunny spot, a watering routine and some basic knowledge of each plant's needs.

p3.q: What do you gain after solving problems in planting?
p3.a6: You feel proud and happy, and you learn from your mistakes. For example, my mother learned how to deal with insects without chemicals.
p3.a7: A real sense of achievement and valuable lessons; for example, my mother learned to fight pests without chemicals.

cards.title: Describe a type of favourite food that you ate at a special event
points: When and where you ate it
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: bánh chưng / mâm cỗ Tết ở nhà bà ở Thanh Hóa.
cards.a6:
I want to talk about banh chung, which is a traditional sticky rice cake. It's made from sticky rice, pork and green beans, and it's wrapped in green leaves.

I ate it during Tet, the Lunar New Year, at my grandmother's house in Thanh Hoa, last February.

Tet is the most important event of the year for Vietnamese people. At that time, all my relatives come back to the village. The day before Tet, we sit together around the fire, wrap the cakes and boil them all night. We chat and tell stories.

I ate the cake with my parents, my brother, my uncles, aunts and cousins. We sat around a big table and ate it with pickled onions.

It was special to me because it wasn't only delicious food. It was a tradition, and it made me feel close to my family. I only see many of my relatives once a year, so I will always remember this meal.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about banh chung, a traditional square sticky-rice cake filled with pork and mung beans and wrapped in green leaves.

I enjoyed it during Tet, the Lunar New Year, at my grandmother's house in Thanh Hoa last February.

Tet is the biggest festival in Vietnam, and it's when all my relatives return to the village. The day before, we gather around a fire to wrap the cakes, which then simmer through the night. We chat, tell stories and keep each other company while the cakes cook.

I ate it with my parents, my brother, my uncles, aunts and cousins. We sat around a huge table, enjoying the cake with pickled onions, which cut through the richness perfectly.

What made it so special was the experience around it. It's a tradition that has been handed down through generations, and the cake symbolises gratitude and family unity. Since I only see many of my relatives once a year, that meal is one of the warmest memories I have.

Even now, the smell of the leaves boiling brings back the sound of my grandmother's laughter and the crackling of the fire. Every Tet I promise myself that I'll learn to wrap banh chung properly, so that the tradition can continue with me.

p3.q: What kind of food is generally popular in Vietnam? / Do Vietnamese people grow their own food?
p3.a6: Rice, pho, noodles and spring rolls are popular. In the countryside, many people grow their own vegetables and raise chickens, but in the city, it's less common.
p3.a7: Rice, pho, noodles and spring rolls are staples. In rural areas, many families grow their own produce and raise poultry, though this is less common in cities.

p3.q: Why do some people prefer growing food themselves? / Will more people do so?
p3.a6: They want clean and safe food, and they like the hobby. I think more people will do it in the future because of food safety worries.
p3.a7: They want safe, pesticide-free food and enjoy the hobby. I expect the trend to grow as food safety concerns rise.

p3.q: Why do people like big meals at festivals? / Why is food important on special occasions?
p3.a6: Because it's a chance for the family to meet. Food shows respect to ancestors and brings people together.
p3.a7: Because festivals are a chance for families to reunite, and food is a way to honour ancestors and bring people together.

p3.q: What do people eat during festivals or family celebrations?
p3.a6: At Tet, we eat banh chung, boiled chicken and spring rolls. At mid-autumn, we eat mooncakes. At weddings, there are many dishes.
p3.a7: At Tet, banh chung, boiled chicken and spring rolls; at Mid-Autumn, mooncakes; and at weddings, an elaborate multi-course banquet.

p3.q: Do young people prefer traditional food or fast food? / How have eating habits changed?
p3.a6: Many young people like fast food because it's quick and cheap. In the past, people ate at home more; now they eat out and order food online.
p3.a7: Many prefer fast food for its speed and price. Compared to the past, people eat out and order delivery far more often than they cook at home.

p3.q: Is it bad to look at phones during a meal? / Does eating together strengthen family relationships?
p3.a6: Yes, I think it's impolite and we don't talk to each other. Eating together is a good time to share and listen, so it makes the family closer.
p3.a7: I think it's rude, as it undermines conversation. Sharing a meal is a precious opportunity to talk and listen, which strengthens family bonds.

p3.q: Better to cook at home or eat out on special occasions? / Do people cook as much as before? Why are people unwilling to cook?
p3.a6: Cooking at home is warmer and cheaper, but restaurants are more convenient. People cook less now because they are busy, tired after work and food delivery is easy.
p3.a7: Home cooking feels warmer and is cheaper, while restaurants are more convenient. People cook less nowadays since they're busy and delivery apps make eating out effortless.

p3.q: What is special about the way this food is made?
p3.a6: It takes a long time. We need to prepare the ingredients, wrap carefully and boil for about ten hours.
p3.a7: It's labour-intensive: you prepare the ingredients, wrap each cake carefully and boil it for around ten hours.

p3.q: Do most people prefer vegetables bought from the supermarket or grown at home?
p3.a6: Most city people buy from supermarkets because it's convenient. But many prefer home-grown vegetables because they are fresher and safer.
p3.a7: Most urban people buy from supermarkets for convenience, though many would prefer home-grown vegetables for freshness and safety.

p3.q: What plants can people grow in cities?
p3.a6: Herbs, lettuce, tomatoes, chilli and small flowers. They can grow them in pots on balconies.
p3.a7: Herbs, lettuce, tomatoes, chilli and small flowers, all of which grow well in pots on balconies.

p3.q: Are there any difficulties when people grow plants in cities?
p3.a6: Yes. There is little space and sunlight, and the air is polluted. People are also busy, so they forget to water the plants.
p3.a7: Yes: limited space and sunlight, polluted air and busy schedules that make people neglect watering.

cards.title: Describe a difficult decision that you made and had a good result
points: Why it was a good decision.
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: quyết định chuyển từ công việc cũ sang làm Tester, hoặc đăng ký khóa học Selenium/IELTS. Ở đây: chọn học ngành IT thay vì ngành bố mẹ muốn.

notes.v: change career: from manual to automation learning / choose IT
afraid of failure, salary, parents' worry
new skills, better job, more confident

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a difficult decision I made two years ago. I decided to study for an automation testing course in the evening, after work.

At that time, I was working as a manual tester. The job was stable, and I was tired after work. To study at night, I had to give up my free time and some of my weekends.

It was difficult because I was afraid that I couldn't learn programming. I also worried about being too tired, and my parents wanted me to rest more.

But I made up my mind and joined a course. I studied for six months. At first, it was hard, but gradually I understood and could write simple scripts.

The result was good. I could do my work faster and my manager gave me more important tasks. My salary also increased a bit.

I think it was a good decision because I learned new skills and became more confident. It also encouraged me to improve my English now.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a tough decision I made two years ago: signing up for an evening automation testing course while holding down my full-time job.

At that point, I was a manual tester with a comfortable, stable routine. Taking the course meant sacrificing my evenings and some weekends after already long working days.

What made it difficult was self-doubt. I wasn't sure I could pick up programming, and I worried about burning out. My parents were also concerned about me overworking.

Nevertheless, I made up my mind and enrolled. The first few weeks were quite a struggle, but little by little things clicked, and by the end of six months I could write simple scripts.

The outcome was very positive. I worked more efficiently, my manager entrusted me with more important tasks, and I even got a small pay rise.

I'd say it was a great decision because it broadened my skill set and boosted my confidence. More importantly, it taught me that stepping out of my comfort zone pays off, which is partly why I'm now working on my English.

Looking back, I'm glad I trusted myself instead of staying in my comfort zone. That decision opened the door to the career goals I have today, and I'd recommend the same to anyone who is hesitating.

p3.q: Do advertisements influence consumers' decisions?
p3.a6: Yes, a lot. Ads make products look good, so people want to buy them, especially when famous people appear in the ads.
p3.a7: Very much so. Ads make products appealing, particularly when celebrities endorse them, which sways purchasing decisions.

p3.q: Who do young people ask for advice? / Who do people usually ask for important decisions?
p3.a6: Young people often ask friends and parents. For important decisions, people ask family members or people with experience.
p3.a7: Typically friends and parents. For major decisions, people turn to family or those with relevant experience.

p3.q: Is it necessary for kids to make decisions by themselves?
p3.a6: Yes, with small things first. This teaches them to be independent and responsible.
p3.a7: Yes, starting with small matters, as it fosters independence and a sense of responsibility.

p3.q: Can some people make decisions without advice? / Do you prefer deciding alone or with advice?
p3.a6: Some confident people can, but I prefer to ask for advice, because other people see things that I don't.
p3.a7: Some confident people can, but I like to hear other opinions, as others often notice things I overlook.

p3.q: Are young people easily influenced by others?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so, because they lack experience and they want to follow friends and social media trends.
p3.a7: Yes, because they lack experience and are keen to fit in with friends and online trends.

p3.q: What decisions do young people have to make? / Do they decide differently from older people?
p3.a6: They decide about their major, jobs, and moving out. Young people are more willing to take risks. Older people are more careful.
p3.a7: Choices about their degree, career and living arrangements. Young people tend to take more risks, while older people are more cautious.

p3.q: Why is it difficult for some people to make important decisions?
p3.a6: They are afraid of making a mistake or losing something. Some people also have too many options.
p3.a7: They fear making the wrong choice and facing the consequences, and having too many options can be paralysing.

p3.q: Should people always think carefully? / Do difficult decisions help people grow?
p3.a6: For big decisions, yes. But sometimes we can't wait too long. Difficult decisions help us learn and become stronger.
p3.a7: For major ones, yes, though over-thinking can cost us opportunities. Tough decisions certainly help us mature and build resilience.

cards.title: Describe a special cake you received
points: What it looked and tasted like
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: bánh sinh nhật bạn bè bất ngờ tặng ở văn phòng (bạn thay chi tiết thật).

notes.v: my birthday last year, evening at office
pink flowers, my name, soft, sweet-sour
surprise, first birthday party at work

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a birthday cake that I received last year from my colleagues.

It was a small mango cake with soft cream and fresh mango on top. On the cake, there was my name, written in pink cream, and a few pink flowers around it.

My team gave it to me on my birthday last year. I received it at the office in the evening. That day, I thought they forgot my birthday, because nobody said anything in the morning. Then, before we went home, they turned off the lights, sang "Happy Birthday" and brought the cake.

It tasted very good. It was soft, a little sweet and a little sour from the mango. We shared the cake and took many photos.

It was special to me because I didn't expect it. It was the first time my colleagues made a birthday party for me, so I felt happy and I knew that I'm a part of the team.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a birthday cake my colleagues surprised me with last year.

It was a small mango mousse cake, topped with fresh mango slices and my name piped in pink cream, with a few sugar flowers around the edge. It looked almost too pretty to eat.

I received it at the office on my birthday, in the evening. All day long, nobody had mentioned it, so I assumed everyone had forgotten. Then, just before we left, the lights went out, and my team walked in singing "Happy Birthday" with the cake.

As for the taste, it was light, creamy and pleasantly sweet with a hint of tartness from the mango. We shared it, chatted and took loads of photos.

It was special because it was completely unexpected. It was the first time colleagues had organised a birthday surprise for me, and it made me feel valued and genuinely part of the team, which I still remember warmly.

I even kept the little candle as a souvenir. Every time I see it on my desk, I'm reminded that small, thoughtful gestures can make an ordinary day unforgettable.

vocab.m: đẹp đến mức không nỡ ăn

p3.q: Differences between special food in Vietnam and other countries? / Is there food eaten on special occasions?
p3.a6: In Vietnam, special food is often traditional and made at home, like banh chung at Tet and mooncakes at Mid-Autumn. In western countries, people eat turkey at Christmas.
p3.a7: In Vietnam, festive dishes such as banh chung and mooncakes are often home-made and tied to tradition, whereas in the West, people have turkey at Christmas, for instance.

p3.q: Why do some people spend a lot on meals on special days?
p3.a6: They want to make the day memorable, and they want to show love and respect to people. Some also want to show off.
p3.a7: They want to make the occasion memorable and show appreciation to loved ones, and some simply want to impress others.

p3.q: Is it good to communicate when eating with family?
p3.a6: Yes, a meal is the best time to share our day. It makes the family closer. Without talking, we may feel distant.
p3.a7: Yes, mealtimes are ideal for sharing our day, and talking keeps family bonds strong.

p3.q: Do people cook at home as often as before? / Why are people unwilling to cook?
p3.a6: No, they don't. They are busy, tired after work and it's easy to order food by app. Some young people also can't cook.
p3.a7: Not as often. Busy schedules, fatigue and the convenience of delivery apps all play a part, and some young people never learned to cook.

p3.q: What do you think of people using phones during a meal?
p3.a6: For birthdays, I think a cake is nicer than money because it shows more thought. I like to give small surprises to my friends.
p3.a7: For birthdays, a cake feels more thoughtful than cash, and I enjoy giving friends small surprises.

cards.title: Describe a friend from childhood who you remember very well
points: how you got to know each other
and explain why you remember this friend so well
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: Quan, hàng xóm cùng xóm, chơi từ nhỏ.

notes.v: lived next door, same primary school
happy childhood, moved away in grade 9

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my childhood friend, Quan. I remember him very well.

I knew him because he lived next door to my house. We were the same age, and we went to the same primary school, so we became friends when we were about six.

We did many things together. After school, we played football in the yard, flew kites in the field and caught small fish in the pond. Sometimes we played video games at his house, but his mother only let us play for one hour.

He was a funny and kind boy. He was also brave. For example, when a big dog ran to us, he stood in front of me. He also shared his snacks with me.

I remember him so well because my childhood with him was very happy. In grade 9, his family moved to another city, and we slowly lost contact. I still miss him sometimes.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Quan, a childhood friend I remember vividly.

We met because he lived right next door. We were the same age and attended the same primary school, so we became inseparable from about the age of six.

We did pretty much everything together. After school, we'd kick a ball around in the yard, fly kites in the fields or try to catch tiny fish in the pond. Occasionally we played video games at his house, though his mother strictly limited us to an hour.

As a person, he was hilarious and big-hearted, and surprisingly brave. I recall a big dog once running at us and him stepping in front of me. He was also generous, always splitting his snacks with me.

The reason I remember him so clearly is that he's tied to my happiest memories of childhood. When his family moved to another city in grade 9, we gradually drifted apart. I still think of him fondly and wonder what he's doing now.

Sometimes I scroll through old photos of us in school uniform and can't help smiling. I'd love to find him on social media one day and catch up over a coffee, just like old times.

p3.q: Do you still keep in touch with childhood friends? Why or why not?
p3.a6: Not really. We live far from each other and we're busy. I only meet one or two of them on Tet.
p3.a7: Not much, I'm afraid. Distance and busy lives get in the way, so I only see one or two of them at Tet.

p3.q: How important is childhood friendship? / Why are childhood friendships special? / Do kids need close friends?
p3.a6: It's very important because children learn to share and to talk with others. These friendships are pure because there's no competition.
p3.a7: Very important, as children learn to share, cooperate and express themselves. These bonds are special because they're pure and free of competition or self-interest.

p3.q: What do you think of communicating via social media? / Will it replace face-to-face communication?
p3.a6: It's quick and convenient and I can talk to friends anywhere. But I don't think it will replace face-to-face talking, because we can't feel emotions fully online.
p3.a7: It's fast and convenient, but I doubt it will replace face-to-face contact, since you can't fully convey emotions through a screen.

p3.q: Difference between younger and older friends?
p3.a6: Older friends give more advice and experience. Younger friends are more energetic and have fresh ideas.
p3.a7: Older friends offer guidance and experience, while younger ones bring energy and fresh perspectives.

p3.q: Has technology changed friendships?
p3.a6: Yes. People can keep in touch more easily and make friends online. But some friendships become less deep because people only chat on the phone.
p3.a7: Definitely. It's easier to stay in touch and make friends online, though some friendships become shallower when they stay purely virtual.

p3.q: Is it easy to maintain friendships as people get older? / Do children make friends more easily?
p3.a6: No, it is harder because adults have work and family. Children make friends more easily because they're open and simple.
p3.a7: It's harder, as adults juggle work and family. Children make friends more readily because they're open-minded and uncalculating.

p3.q: What qualities are important in friendship? / How do friendships influence development?
p3.a6: Honesty, trust and kindness are important. Good friends encourage us to study and learn good habits.
p3.a7: Honesty, trust and loyalty. Good friends motivate us and shape our habits and values.

cards.title: Describe a time you changed your opinion
points: and explain how you felt about changing your mind
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: từng nghĩ học tiếng Anh không quan trọng với IT Tester, rồi đổi ý.

notes.v: work in Vietnamese, tools have Vietnamese guide
new project with foreign client, couldn't read docs/talk

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a time I changed my opinion about learning English.

In the past, I thought English was not important for a tester like me. I thought I only needed technical skills. My colleagues and I spoke Vietnamese at work, and I could use translation tools to read documents.

That opinion changed last year, when my company got a new project with a foreign client. I had to read English documents and join meetings with the client. I couldn't understand many things, and I couldn't answer when they asked me a question. My translation tool also made mistakes.

After that, I realised that English is very important for my career. Good English helps me to understand the work better, to communicate and to get a better job.

I felt embarrassed at first. But later I felt motivated, and I started studying for IELTS. I'm glad I changed my mind.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the time I changed my mind about the importance of English.

I used to believe English wasn't essential for a tester like me. I figured technical skills were all that mattered; after all, my colleagues and I spoke Vietnamese at work, and I could always run documents through a translation tool.

That belief was shattered last year, when my company took on a project for a foreign client. I had to read English specifications and join calls with the client. I struggled to follow the conversation, and when I was asked a question, I froze. The translation tool wasn't much help either, as it often missed technical nuances.

That experience made me realise that English is a key to career progression. It lets you understand your work thoroughly, communicate with confidence and open up better opportunities.

I felt rather embarrassed at first, but that quickly turned into motivation. I started studying for IELTS, and I'm really glad I changed my mind, as it has set me on a much better path.

What I learned is that it's perfectly fine to change your mind when you have new evidence. Now I try to keep an open mind and listen before I judge, which has helped me both at work and in my daily life.

p3.q: At what age do children begin to have their own opinions?
p3.a6: I think from about 3 or 4 years old, they can say "I like" or "I don't like". Their opinions become stronger at school age.
p3.a7: From around the age of three or four, when they start expressing likes and dislikes, with more developed views emerging at school age.

p3.q: Who influences children's opinions most: parents or friends?
p3.a6: For young children, parents are more important. For teenagers, friends are more influential because they spend a lot of time together.
p3.a7: Parents for young children, but friends take over as the major influence during the teenage years.

p3.q: Should teachers ask for children's opinions in lessons?
p3.a6: Yes, it helps students to think and to be more confident. In Vietnam, students are often too shy, so teachers should encourage them.
p3.a7: Yes, it encourages critical thinking and confidence. In Vietnam, students tend to be shy, so teachers should actively draw them out.

p3.q: When should people not give their real opinions?
p3.a6: When the truth hurts someone, or in a formal situation like with a boss. We should be polite and choose our words carefully.
p3.a7: When the truth would hurt someone unnecessarily, or in sensitive situations such as with a manager. Tact is important.

p3.q: Does culture affect the way people express their opinions?
p3.a6: Yes. In Vietnam, people often avoid direct disagreement and want to keep harmony, but in some western countries, people speak directly.
p3.a7: Very much. In Vietnam, people tend to avoid direct confrontation to preserve harmony, whereas in many Western cultures, directness is valued.

p3.q: Does social media influence opinions? / Is it hard to tell fact from opinion?
p3.a6: Yes, a lot. People read fast and believe what they see. Fake news makes it hard to distinguish facts from opinions.
p3.a7: Enormously. People often accept what they read at face value, and the spread of fake news makes it hard to separate fact from opinion.

p3.q: Why do people change their opinions? / Is it easy to admit being wrong?
p3.a6: When they get new information or experience. It isn't easy to admit being wrong because people feel embarrassed and want to keep their face.
p3.a7: When they gain new information or experience. Admitting error is hard, as it bruises the ego and, in our culture, people worry about losing face.

p3.q: Do older people change opinions less? / Should people always stick to their opinions?
p3.a6: Yes, older people are more fixed. But we shouldn't always stick to our opinion. We need to listen to other viewpoints and be flexible.
p3.a7: Generally, yes, as they're more set in their ways. But rigidly sticking to one's opinion isn't wise; listening to other viewpoints is a sign of maturity.

p3.q: Who do most young people discuss their opinions with?
p3.a6: Mostly with friends, because they feel free and equal. For serious matters, they talk with parents or a trusted older person.
p3.a7: Mostly friends, with whom they feel at ease; for serious matters, parents or a trusted mentor.

p3.q: Does society need more people who aren't afraid of expressing opinions?
p3.a6: Yes. When people share different ideas, society can find better solutions. But they should be respectful and not hurt others.
p3.a7: Yes, since diverse ideas lead to better solutions, provided people express them respectfully.

p3.q: Can other people influence our opinions? How?
p3.a6: Yes. Family, friends, teachers and the media can change our opinions by sharing information and experience. Sometimes we change just to follow the group.
p3.a7: Yes. Family, friends, teachers and the media shape our views through information and example, and sometimes we conform simply to fit in.

p3.q: Is it important to listen to different viewpoints?
p3.a6: Yes, very. It helps us see problems from many sides and avoid mistakes. It also shows respect.
p3.a7: Very. It lets us see issues from several angles, helps us avoid mistakes and shows respect.

cards.title: Describe a time when you had to make an important decision
points: and explain why it was important
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: chọn ngành IT khi nộp nguyện vọng đại học (khác Topic 4 là học khóa tự động hóa).

notes.v: which major to apply for university
asked teachers, parents, searched jobs online, compared

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about the decision of choosing my university major.

I made this decision in grade 12, about eight years ago. I had to choose a major for my university application.

It was an important decision because it affected my career and my whole future. If I chose the wrong major, I would study for four years and could not enjoy my job.

To make the decision, first I wrote down my favourite subjects. I liked maths and computers. Then I looked for information about jobs online and asked my teachers, my cousin who worked in IT and my parents. My parents wanted me to choose a stable job, and they supported IT because it has many jobs. I also compared several universities.

Finally, I chose Information Technology. I felt a little worried before the exam, but I'm happy with the result. I got into university, graduated and found a job easily. I think I made the right decision.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the decision I made about my university major.

It was in grade 12, around eight years ago, when I had to submit my university application and pick a field of study.

It was a pivotal decision because it would shape my career path and my future. Had I picked the wrong major, I'd have spent four years studying something I didn't enjoy.

To make up my mind, I began by listing the subjects I was good at and enjoyed, which were maths and computers. Then I researched job prospects online and sought advice from my teachers, my parents and a cousin who worked in IT. My parents wanted me to have a secure job and they backed IT, which offers plenty of opportunities. I also compared a number of universities.

In the end, I chose Information Technology. I was anxious before the entrance exam, but it turned out well. I got in, graduated and found a job fairly quickly. Looking back, I'm very satisfied with the decision, and I believe it was the right call.

I still remember the night before I submitted the form: I read the list of universities again and again. Even though I was scared, taking responsibility for my own future made me feel more mature.

p3.q: Do children sometimes have to make important decisions? / Who can they turn to?
p3.a6: Yes, a little, for example choosing a school or a club. They can ask parents, teachers or older siblings.
p3.a7: Yes, to some extent, such as choosing a school or extracurricular activity. They can turn to parents, teachers or older siblings.

p3.q: Important decisions teenagers make after graduation?
p3.a6: They have to choose a university, a major, or find a job. Some also decide to study abroad.
p3.a7: Whether to go to university, which major to choose, or whether to start working, and some consider studying abroad.

p3.q: Do advertisements influence decisions when shopping? / Is the influence good?
p3.a6: Yes, they do. Ads give information about products, which is good. But they can also make people buy things they don't need.
p3.a7: Yes. Ads provide useful information, which is a plus, but they can also encourage impulse buying of things people don't need.

p3.q: How do people usually make important decisions?
p3.a6: They collect information, compare the pros and cons and ask for advice. Some also follow their feelings.
p3.a7: They gather information, weigh the pros and cons and seek advice, though some go with their gut feeling.

p3.q: Why is decision-making difficult for some? / Do men and women decide differently?
p3.a6: They're afraid of failing. I think men may decide faster, and women think more carefully, but it depends on the person.
p3.a7: The fear of failure. People say men decide faster while women deliberate more, but I think it varies from person to person.

p3.q: Better to decide alone or ask for advice?
p3.a6: I think it's better to ask for advice for big decisions, but the final choice should be ours.
p3.a7: For big decisions, seeking advice is wise, but the final choice should be ours.

p3.q: Can technology help people decide? / How can experience improve decision-making?
p3.a6: Yes, we can search for information and read reviews on the internet. Experience helps us avoid old mistakes and understand risks.
p3.a7: Yes, online research, reviews and even AI tools help. Experience teaches us from past mistakes and helps us assess risks.

cards.title: Describe a wild animal you would like to learn more about
points: what you already know about it
and explain why you would like to learn more about it
cards.note: Lựa chọn giả định: loài voi (elephant), dễ có từ vựng và ý.

notes.v: Africa, Asia; in Vietnam: Dak Lak forests
biggest land animal, herbivore, intelligent, herds, long trunk

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about the elephant, a wild animal that I'd like to learn more about.

Elephants live in Africa and in Asia. In Vietnam, there are still some wild elephants in the forests of Dak Lak province, but there are only a few of them now.

I already know some things about elephants. They are the biggest land animals in the world. They eat only plants, and they live in groups called herds, led by an older female. They have a long trunk to drink, eat and smell. I also know they are intelligent and have good memories.

I want to learn more about them for two reasons. First, they are endangered because people cut down forests and hunt them for ivory. I want to know how we can protect them. Second, I read that elephants show feelings, for example they are sad when a family member dies, and I find this very interesting.

I really admire elephants, and I feel sorry for them. I hope I can see them in the wild someday.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the elephant, a wild animal I've always wanted to know more about.

Elephants inhabit parts of Africa and Asia. In Vietnam, a small number still survive in the forests of Dak Lak province, although their numbers have dropped dramatically.

I already know a few things about them. They're the largest land animals on Earth, they're herbivores and they live in tight-knit herds led by the oldest female. They use their long trunks for drinking, feeding and smelling, and they're famously intelligent, with excellent memories.

There are two reasons I'd like to learn more. Firstly, they're endangered due to deforestation and poaching for ivory, and I'd like to understand how we can protect them. Secondly, I've read that they show emotions, such as mourning a deceased family member, which I find fascinating.

I have enormous admiration for elephants, and I also feel sympathy for them, given the threats they face. I truly hope to see them in their natural habitat one day.

I often watch documentaries about elephant rescue centres, and I'd even like to volunteer at one someday. If more people understood how intelligent and gentle these animals are, I think they would do more to protect them.

p3.q: Are people more interested in animals now than in the past?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. People now keep pets, watch animal videos and join protection campaigns. Social media also makes people care about animals more.
p3.a7: Yes. Pet ownership, animal videos and conservation campaigns are everywhere, and social media has heightened awareness.

p3.q: Difference between how animals were used for work in the past and now? / How did animals help people in the past?
p3.a6: In the past, people used buffaloes for farming and horses for transport. Now machines do these jobs, so animals are used more for company or by the police.
p3.a7: In the past, buffaloes ploughed fields and horses provided transport. Now machines have taken over, and animals mostly serve as companions or in roles like police work.

p3.q: How do animals help us today?
p3.a6: Dogs help the police and blind people. Pets give us company and reduce stress. Some animals are also used in medical research.
p3.a7: Sniffer dogs assist the police, guide dogs help the blind, pets offer emotional support, and animals contribute to medical research.

p3.q: Why should wild animals be protected? / Are animals important?
p3.a6: Because every animal is part of nature. If some animals disappear, the food chain is broken and humans are affected too.
p3.a7: Because each species plays a role in the ecosystem; if one disappears, the food chain is disrupted, and eventually humans suffer too.

p3.q: What should we do to protect endangered animals?
p3.a6: We should stop forest cutting and make strict laws against hunting. We should also educate people and not buy products from wild animals.
p3.a7: Stop deforestation, enforce strict anti-poaching laws, educate the public and refuse to buy wildlife products.

p3.q: Why do children's stories and movies feature animals? / Do children love animals more than old people?
p3.a6: Animals are cute and easy for children to understand. Stories also teach lessons through animals. Children usually love animals more because they are curious and innocent.
p3.a7: Animals are endearing and make moral lessons easy to grasp. Children tend to love them more, as they're curious and innocent, whereas older people are often more reserved.

cards.title: Describe an interesting building that you would like to visit
points: and explain why you would like to visit it
cards.note: Lựa chọn giả định: Đại Nội Huế (Imperial City of Hue) hoặc bạn đổi thành Burj Khalifa.

notes.v: red gates, old palaces, moat, tiles, gardens

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about the Imperial City in Hue, which I have wanted to visit for a long time.

It's located in Hue, a city in central Vietnam, next to the Perfume River. It was the capital of Vietnam during the Nguyen dynasty.

From the pictures I've seen, the place looks very big and beautiful. It has high walls, a deep river around it and many gates. Inside, there are palaces with red columns and yellow roofs, with old decorations and green gardens. It looks quiet and traditional.

I'm interested in it because I like history, and my father often told me stories about the kings of Vietnam. It's also a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

I would like to visit because I want to see it with my own eyes. I'd like to walk inside the palaces, take photos and learn more about the life of the kings. I also hope to try Hue food, like bun bo Hue, during that trip.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the Imperial City in Hue, a place that has been on my travel wish list for years.

It's situated in Hue, in central Vietnam, on the banks of the Perfume River, and it served as the capital under the Nguyen dynasty.

From photos I've seen, it's an imposing complex with towering walls, a moat and numerous gates. Inside are palaces with red columns and golden-yellow roofs, adorned with intricate decorations and surrounded by peaceful gardens. It exudes a calm, ancient atmosphere.

What draws me to it is my passion for history. My father, a history lover, used to tell me stories about Vietnamese emperors, and that sparked my curiosity. It's also a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

I'd love to visit because photos can't capture the sheer scale and atmosphere. I'd like to wander through the palaces, take photographs and learn about how the royal family lived. And, of course, I'd happily taste authentic bun bo Hue while I'm there.

I'd plan to go in spring, when the weather is mild, and perhaps hire a guide so that I could really understand the stories behind each gate and hall. I think that walking through it would make my history lessons come alive.

p3.q: Why do some people build houses by themselves?
p3.a6: They can design the house as they like and it may be cheaper. In the countryside, many people build houses for their large family.
p3.a7: They can tailor the design to their own needs and often save money. In rural areas, many families build their own homes to accommodate several generations.

p3.q: What factors do you consider when choosing a house or apartment? / What do people consider when renting or buying?
p3.a6: The price, location, size and safety. People also think about transport, schools and hospitals nearby. For renting, the monthly rent is important.
p3.a7: Price, location, size and security, as well as proximity to schools, hospitals and public transport. When renting, affordability of monthly rent matters most.

p3.q: Do a city's buildings affect its atmosphere?
p3.a6: Yes. Hanoi's old French buildings give the city a romantic and calm feeling, but modern high-rise buildings in other cities make it feel busy and modern.
p3.a7: Definitely. Hanoi's French colonial buildings give it a romantic, nostalgic feel, whereas glass skyscrapers lend other cities a dynamic, modern vibe.

p3.q: Should old buildings be preserved?
p3.a6: Yes, they show our history and culture, and they attract tourists. If we destroy them, we can't bring them back.
p3.a7: Yes, they embody our heritage and attract tourists, and once demolished, they're irreplaceable.

p3.q: How do people in Vietnam feel about old buildings?
p3.a6: Many people respect them, but some think old buildings are unsafe and want to replace them with modern ones, especially in big cities where land is expensive.
p3.a7: Opinions are divided. Many cherish them, while others regard them as unsafe or outdated, particularly where land prices are high.

cards.title: Describe a person who is good at learning languages
points: and explain why you think he/she is good at it
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: bạn Trang, đồng nghiệp/ bạn cũ, nói tiếng Anh và tiếng Hàn.

notes.v: English, Korean, a bit of Japanese
apps, K-dramas, speaks every day, notebook

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my friend, Trang. She was my classmate at university, and now she works as a translator.

She can speak three languages. Her English and Korean are very good, and she can speak a little Japanese.

She learns languages in a smart way. She uses apps to learn new words every day. She watches Korean dramas and English videos without subtitles. She also writes new words in a notebook and reviews them. The most important thing is that she is not afraid of speaking. She talks to foreigners and makes mistakes, but she doesn't feel shy.

I think she's good at learning languages because she is hard-working and she studies every day, even when she's tired. She also has a good memory and a good ear for pronunciation.

I really admire her. She is a good example for me. When I see her progress, I feel motivated to study English harder.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my friend Trang, a former university classmate who now works as a translator.

She speaks three languages. Her English and Korean are excellent, and she can hold a basic conversation in Japanese.

She goes about learning languages very cleverly. She uses apps to pick up new vocabulary daily, watches Korean dramas and English videos without subtitles, and jots down new words in a notebook to revise. Above all, she isn't afraid of speaking; she chats with foreigners and happily makes mistakes without feeling self-conscious.

I'd say she's so good at it because of her consistency. She studies every single day, even when she's exhausted. She also has an excellent memory and a good ear for pronunciation.

I genuinely admire her. She's a role model for me, and watching her progress motivates me to take my own English more seriously and put in more effort.

She once told me that the secret is to enjoy the language rather than treat it as homework. I've started copying her habit of learning five new words a day, and I can already see the difference in my confidence.

p3.q: Why are some people better at learning languages than others?
p3.a6: Some have a good memory or a good ear. But more important is the method and how much they practise. Motivation is also important.
p3.a7: Natural aptitude plays a part, such as a good memory and ear, but practice, effective methods and motivation matter even more.

p3.q: Is it easier for children to learn languages?
p3.a6: Yes, children learn faster because they are not afraid of making mistakes and their brains are flexible. But adults can learn well if they have good methods.
p3.a7: Generally, yes. Their brains are more adaptable and they aren't afraid of mistakes, although adults with good strategies can progress well too.

p3.q: What is the best way to learn a foreign language?
p3.a6: I think the best way is to use it every day: listen, speak, read and write. Watching films and talking with other people also helps.
p3.a7: Immersion and daily practice: listening, speaking, reading and writing regularly, plus watching films and chatting with others.

p3.q: Why do people learn foreign languages?
p3.a6: For work and study abroad. Some people learn for travelling or just for interest. In my case, English helps me find a better job.
p3.a7: For career opportunities, studying abroad, travelling or personal interest. In my case, English will open doors at work.

p3.q: Can technology help language learning?
p3.a6: Yes. There are apps, online dictionaries and videos. We can also practise speaking with AI and get correction immediately.
p3.a7: Absolutely. Apps, online dictionaries and videos are great, and AI tools even let us practise speaking and get instant feedback.

p3.q: Should schools teach more foreign languages?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. In the globalisation era, it's good to know more than one language. But schools should focus on speaking more, not only grammar.
p3.a7: Yes, in a globalised world, multilingualism is an asset, but schools should emphasise speaking rather than just grammar.

cards.title: Describe a piece of advertisement which is about a famous person
points: what product or service it was for
who the famous person was and what he/she did in it
and explain why you remember this advertisement
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: quảng cáo kem chống nắng/ sữa rửa mặt có ca sĩ nổi tiếng (tên ca sĩ do bạn thay bằng người thật; mình để "a famous Vietnamese singer").

notes.v: washed face, smiled, sang a short jingle, showed clear skin
catchy song, I bought the product

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about an advertisement for a face wash that I saw some months ago.

I saw it on YouTube while I was watching a video. Later I also saw it on Facebook many times.

The famous person in the ad was a Vietnamese singer. He is very popular among young people and has a great voice.

In the ad, he was in a bright bathroom. He washed his face with the product and then he looked at the camera and smiled. His skin looked clean and fresh. After that, he sang a short, catchy song about the brand.

I remember this ad for two reasons. First, the song was very easy to remember, and I sang it for several days. Second, I like skincare, so I was interested in the product. In fact, I bought it after watching the ad, and it was quite good for my skin. I think it was a successful advertisement.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a face wash advertisement featuring a famous singer, which I came across a few months ago.

I first saw it on YouTube, in the middle of a video, and after that it kept popping up on my Facebook feed.

The celebrity was a well-known Vietnamese singer who's hugely popular among young people for his smooth voice.

In the ad, he stood in a bright, minimalist bathroom and washed his face with the product. Then he looked straight into the camera with a warm smile, showing off his clear, fresh-looking skin, before singing a short, catchy jingle about the brand.

There are two reasons it stuck in my mind. First, the jingle was so catchy that I found myself humming it for days. Second, as someone who's keen on skincare, the product caught my eye. In fact, I ended up buying it, and it suited my skin well. For me, that's the sign of a really effective advertisement.

What impressed me most was how naturally the brand was woven into the story, so it didn't feel like a hard sell at all. As a tester who pays attention to details, I appreciated how polished and consistent the whole video was.

p3.q: Why do companies use celebrities in advertisements?
p3.a6: Because celebrities have many fans, so they get attention quickly. People trust products that their idol uses.
p3.a7: Celebrities command huge followings, so they grab attention instantly, and fans tend to trust the products their idols endorse.

p3.q: Do celebrity advertisements influence consumers?
p3.a6: Yes, especially young people. I bought the face wash after seeing the ad. But some people know that celebrities are paid, so they don't trust them.
p3.a7: Yes, particularly young people; I bought that face wash myself. However, savvy consumers know celebrities are paid, so they stay sceptical.

p3.q: Are advertisements more creative nowadays?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. Ads now are short videos with funny stories or music, and they use social media and AI. In the past, ads were simple.
p3.a7: Yes, they've become far more inventive, with short, humorous videos, music and AI visuals, whereas ads used to be fairly plain.

p3.q: What makes an advertisement effective?
p3.a6: A good ad is short, clear and easy to remember. It needs a good idea, nice music and it must show how the product helps people.
p3.a7: Brevity, a clear message and a memorable hook, such as a catchy tune or a clever idea, and it has to show what the product can do for the viewer.

p3.q: Do children get influenced by ads easily?
p3.a6: Yes, because they cannot tell the difference between real and ads. They ask parents to buy toys and snacks they see on TV.
p3.a7: Yes, since they can't distinguish persuasion from information, and they keep nagging their parents for toys and snacks they've seen advertised.

p3.q: Should there be stricter control of advertising?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. Some ads have false information or are not suitable for children. The government should check them and punish them.
p3.a7: Yes. Misleading claims and inappropriate content aimed at children should be regulated more strictly, with real penalties.

cards.title: Describe a person who has not replied to your messages for a long time
points: and explain how you feel about not getting a reply
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: Nam, bạn đại học cũ (bạn thay tên/chi tiết thật).

notes.v: invite to reunion / ask how he is
busy new job, changed phone, forgot, moved city

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my friend, Nam. He was my close friend at university, but he hasn't replied to my messages for a long time.

I sent him a message on Zalo about two months ago. I asked how he was and invited him to a reunion party with our old classmates. I saw that he had read the message, but he didn't answer.

I think there are a few reasons. First, he may be very busy because he started a new job in Ho Chi Minh City. Second, he may have forgotten to answer, because it's easy to do that when you have many messages. Maybe he doesn't want to go to the party, too.

I feel a bit sad about this situation, because we were close. But I also understand that people change and have different lives after graduating. I will send him one more message, and if he answers, I'll be happy. If not, I'll respect that.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my friend Nam, a close friend from university who hasn't replied to my messages for quite some time.

About two months ago, I sent him a message on Zalo, asking how he was and inviting him to a reunion with our old classmates. The app showed he'd seen it, but he never wrote back.

I can think of a few explanations. For one thing, he's probably swamped, since he started a new job in Ho Chi Minh City. For another, he may have meant to reply but it slipped his mind, which easily happens when you're flooded with messages. It's also possible he simply isn't keen on the reunion.

I feel a little sad, to be honest, since we used to be really close. At the same time, I understand that people's lives take different directions after graduation. I'm planning to send one gentle follow-up. If he replies, great; if not, I'll accept it and let things be.

This situation has taught me to value the friends who do keep in touch, and to reply promptly myself so that nobody feels ignored. A short message like "I'm busy, talk soon" would have meant a lot.

p3.q: Why do people sometimes ignore messages? / Is it rude not to reply?
p3.a6: They're busy, forget, or don't know what to say. Sometimes they don't want to talk. I think it's rude if the message is important, but if it's a casual one, it's OK.
p3.a7: They may be busy, forgetful or unsure what to say, or simply don't want to engage. Ignoring an important message is rude, but being slow with casual ones is forgivable.

p3.q: Is online communication better than face-to-face?
p3.a6: Online is faster and more convenient, but face-to-face is better for important and emotional topics because we can see faces and voices.
p3.a7: Online is quicker and handier, but face-to-face wins for serious or emotional matters, as body language and tone are lost in text.

p3.q: Do young people communicate differently from older people?
p3.a6: Yes. Young people use short messages, emojis and social media. Older people prefer phone calls or meeting in person.
p3.a7: Yes. Young people favour short texts, emojis and social media, while older people prefer calls or meeting in person.

p3.q: How has technology changed communication?
p3.a6: We can talk to anyone anywhere, immediately and for free, even with video. But people have less real conversation.
p3.a7: We can reach anyone instantly and cheaply, even by video, though it has arguably reduced the quality of real conversation.

p3.q: Can texting damage relationships?
p3.a6: Yes, because messages can be misunderstood without a tone of voice. Also, if someone doesn't reply, it may make the other person upset.
p3.a7: Yes, text lacks tone, so misunderstandings are common, and unanswered messages can breed resentment.

cards.title: Describe a story you knew that involves an animal (in a movie or a book)
points: and explain why you remember it
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: "Rùa và Thỏ" (The Tortoise and the Hare) – truyện ngụ ngôn mọi người biết, dễ kể.

notes.v: race, hare fast, sleeps, tortoise slow but steady, wins
primary school, in a textbook / told by mum

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a story called "The Tortoise and the Hare". It's a famous fable.

The animals in the story are a tortoise and a hare. The hare is very fast, but he's proud. The tortoise is slow, but he is patient.

In the story, the hare laughs at the tortoise because he's so slow. The tortoise says he wants to race. They begin, and the hare runs very fast. He is far ahead, so he thinks he can win easily. He stops under a tree and falls asleep. Meanwhile, the tortoise keeps walking slowly and never stops. When the hare wakes up, the tortoise is already close to the finish line. The hare runs, but it's too late, and the tortoise wins.

I first knew this story in primary school. My mother told it to me at bedtime, and later I read it in my textbook.

I remember it because the lesson is simple, but very useful: patient and hard work are better than being proud and lazy.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about "The Tortoise and the Hare", a classic fable that I've known since childhood.

The two animals are, of course, a tortoise and a hare. The hare is lightning-fast but arrogant, whereas the tortoise is slow but patient and determined.

The story begins with the hare mocking the tortoise for being so slow. Unfazed, the tortoise challenges him to a race. The hare sprints off and soon leaves the tortoise far behind. Confident of victory, he decides to take a nap under a tree. Meanwhile, the tortoise plods on without stopping. By the time the hare wakes up, the tortoise is nearly at the finish line. The hare dashes forward, but it's too late, and the tortoise wins.

I first came across it in primary school, when my mother told it to me at bedtime, and then I read it again in a textbook.

I remember it so well because its message is simple yet powerful: slow and steady wins the race, and arrogance and laziness lead to failure. It's a lesson I still apply to my studying today.

Whenever I feel like giving up on my English studies, I remember the tortoise and tell myself that a little progress each day will get me there. I'm planning to tell the same story to my little cousin, so that she can learn the same lesson.

vocab.p: slow and steady wins the race

p3.q: Why do children enjoy stories about animals? / Why are animals often used in stories?
p3.a6: Animals are cute and funny, and children find them easy to understand. Writers also use animals to teach lessons in a simple way.
p3.a7: Animals are endearing and relatable to children, and authors use them to convey moral lessons in an accessible, non-preachy way.

p3.q: What can people learn from animal stories?
p3.a6: They learn values such as honesty, hard work and kindness. They also learn to respect animals and nature.
p3.a7: Values such as honesty, perseverance and kindness, as well as respect for animals and nature.

p3.q: Do films influence how people view animals?
p3.a6: Yes. For example, after a film about a dog, many people want to keep one. But films can show animals in the wrong way, like making sharks look dangerous.
p3.a7: Yes. A heart-warming dog film can spark a wave of adoption, though films can also create false impressions, such as portraying sharks as villains.

p3.q: Should children learn about animals at school?
p3.a6: Yes, it helps them to love nature and protect it. Visiting a zoo or a farm is a good way to learn.
p3.a7: Yes, it fosters respect for nature, and field trips to zoos or farms make learning memorable.

p3.q: Do people care more about animal welfare nowadays?
p3.a6: Zoos can help protect endangered animals, but the animals need a large and clean space. Otherwise, they are not happy.
p3.a7: Well-run zoos help conserve endangered species, but animals must have adequate space and good conditions.

cards.title: Describe a person you know who successfully achieved something difficult
points: and explain how you feel about his/her achievement
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: anh đồng nghiệp tự học và đạt chứng chỉ ISTQB/ hoặc bạn Minh giảm 20kg. Ở đây: anh Tuan, đồng nghiệp, đỗ chứng chỉ ISTQB Advanced.

notes.v: busy, family with 2 kids, hard content, low pass rate
studied 1 hour at 5 am, mock exams, study group

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about Mr Tuan, my senior colleague at work. He's about forty and he's an experienced tester.

Last year, he passed the ISTQB Advanced exam, which is a very difficult testing certificate.

It was difficult for three reasons. First, the exam has a lot of knowledge and difficult questions, and many people fail. Second, he was very busy with his job. Third, he has two small children, so he didn't have much free time.

He achieved it by a very good plan. Every morning, he got up at five and studied for an hour before his children woke up. He also did many practice tests and joined an online study group. He studied like this for eight months.

I admire Mr Tuan very much. He shows me that if you are patient and keep trying, you can do difficult things. He also inspires me to study English every day.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Mr Tuan, a senior colleague of mine in his early forties and a very experienced tester.

Last year, he passed the ISTQB Advanced certification, which is notoriously tough.

It was a real feat for three reasons. The syllabus is vast and the questions are tricky, so many candidates fail. He was also swamped at work, and on top of that, he has two young children, which left him very little free time.

The way he did it was through discipline and a clear plan. He got up at five every morning to study for an hour before his kids woke up. He also took plenty of mock exams and joined an online study group to exchange tips. He kept that up for eight months.

I really admire him. He's proof that persistence pays off, even when you have a hectic schedule, and he motivates me to keep going with my own English studies every day.

On the day the results came out, the whole team clapped and he shyly invited us all for coffee. Seeing someone so ordinary achieve something extraordinary reminded me that success is mostly about daily habits.

vocab.m: kiên trì sẽ được đền đáp

p3.q: Why do some people succeed while others give up?
p3.a6: Successful people have clear goals and they keep trying even if they fail. Others give up when it becomes hard or they lose motivation.
p3.a7: Those who succeed have clear goals and persevere through setbacks, while others lose motivation when things get tough.

p3.q: Is determination important for success?
p3.a6: Yes, very important. Talent helps, but without determination, we can't finish difficult things.
p3.a7: Absolutely. Talent helps, but without determination, we rarely see difficult goals through.

p3.q: Should parents teach children not to give up easily?
p3.a6: Yes, they should. Parents can encourage them and praise their effort, not only the result. But they shouldn't put too much pressure on children.
p3.a7: Yes, by praising effort rather than just results, though without piling on pressure.

p3.q: Can failure help people become successful?
p3.a6: Yes. When we fail, we learn from mistakes and become stronger. Many successful people failed many times before.
p3.a7: Yes. Failure teaches us what doesn't work and builds resilience; many successful people failed repeatedly first.

p3.q: What motivates people to achieve difficult goals?
p3.a6: Money, family and a desire to improve themselves. Support and encouragement from friends also help.
p3.a7: Financial rewards, family, self-improvement and the encouragement of others.

p3.q: Do successful people always work harder?
p3.a6: Not always. Many work hard, but some also have luck or good connections. Working smart is also important.
p3.a7: Not necessarily. Hard work matters, but luck, connections and working smartly play a role too.

cards.title: Describe a place you have been to and felt bored
points: when you went there and who you went with
and explain why you felt bored
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: một bảo tàng/ khu triển lãm khi đi cùng đoàn công ty.

notes.v: too much text, no activity, crowded, hot, no guide

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a museum I visited last year, where I felt very bored.

It was a history museum in Hanoi. I went there on a Sunday morning with some colleagues, because one of them said it was interesting.

I felt bored for several reasons. First, the museum had many old objects behind glass, with long descriptions in small letters, and we had to read everything. There was no guide and no activity. Second, it was a hot day and the room was crowded and noisy. Third, I'm not very interested in military history, so I couldn't understand much.

After about thirty minutes, my friends and I were tired. We looked at our phones and walked quickly through the other rooms. Then we left to have a coffee.

I felt a little disappointed, because I wasted a morning. But it was also a good lesson: I should check a place before I go.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a history museum in Hanoi that I visited last year and found surprisingly dull.

I went on a Sunday morning with a few colleagues, because someone had recommended it as a must-see.

There were several reasons it bored me. Firstly, it was just row after row of old artefacts behind glass, accompanied by lengthy descriptions in tiny print. There was no guide, and nothing interactive to hold our attention. Secondly, it was a sweltering day, and the halls were crowded and stuffy. Thirdly, military history isn't really my thing, so I struggled to connect with the exhibits.

After about half an hour, we were all fidgeting, checking our phones and rushing through the remaining rooms. Eventually, we gave up and went for coffee instead.

I felt slightly let down, as I'd sacrificed a precious weekend morning. On the bright side, it taught me to read reviews and check what's on offer before heading somewhere.

I might go back someday with a guide or with someone who loves history, because I think the right company can completely change how you see a place. Until then, I'd rather spend my weekend mornings at a lakeside café.

p3.q: Why do some people get bored easily? / On what occasions do people feel bored?
p3.a6: Some people need new things all the time, and they have a short attention span. People feel bored when they wait, do repeated work or listen to something they don't understand.
p3.a7: Some crave constant stimulation and have short attention spans. Boredom strikes during long waits, repetitive tasks or when we can't follow what's going on.

p3.q: What kinds of places do young people enjoy visiting?
p3.a6: They like cafes, shopping malls, cinemas and fun places like theme parks. They also like places that are good for taking photos.
p3.a7: Cafés, shopping malls, cinemas and theme parks, plus photogenic spots they can share on social media.

p3.q: Do people have different ideas of what is interesting?
p3.a6: Yes. Some like history, others like nature or shopping. It depends on personality, age and experience.
p3.a7: Certainly. Some love history, others prefer nature or shopping, depending on personality, age and experience.

p3.q: How can tourist attractions become more appealing?
p3.a6: They can add activities, use technology such as virtual reality and have good guides. They should also keep the place clean and have fair prices.
p3.a7: By adding interactive activities, using tech like virtual reality, offering engaging guides, and keeping places clean and reasonably priced.

p3.q: Is it important to try new experiences?
p3.a6: Yes, it helps us learn and gives us more confidence. It also makes life less boring.
p3.a7: Yes, it broadens our horizons, builds confidence and keeps life from becoming monotonous.

p3.q: Do people have less patience than before?
p3.a6: I think so. Now we have fast internet and short videos, so people don't like waiting and get bored quickly.
p3.a7: I think so. With instant internet and short videos, people have grown used to instant gratification and find waiting hard.

p3.q: Why do students find lessons boring? / Why do some people find playing on phones boring?
p3.a6: If teachers only talk and students can't join, it's boring. Some people find phones boring when they play the same game or scroll for too long.
p3.a7: When teachers just lecture and students can't participate, it's dull. Phones turn boring when you repeat the same game or scroll endlessly.

p3.q: How to avoid feeling bored?
p3.a6: Find a hobby, exercise, meet friends or learn something new. Planning activities also helps.
p3.a7: Take up hobbies, exercise, socialise or learn new skills, and plan activities in advance.

cards.title: Describe a place you went to on holiday that you would recommend
points: when and with whom you went there
and explain why you would recommend it to others
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: Đà Nẵng (Mỹ Khê, Bà Nà, Hội An) cùng bạn bè.

notes.v: swim at My Khe, Ba Na Hills, Golden Bridge, seafood, Hoi An night
clean, safe, cheap, friendly, many things to do

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about Da Nang, a coastal city in central Vietnam, which I'd recommend to everyone.

I went there two years ago in summer, for four days, with three close friends from university.

We did many things. In the morning, we swam at My Khe beach, and the water was clean and warm. We went to Ba Na Hills and took photos on the Golden Bridge. In the evenings, we ate fresh seafood and drank coffee by the Han River. One day, we also visited the ancient town of Hoi An and walked among the colourful lanterns at night.

I'd recommend this place for several reasons. The city is clean, safe and quiet, and people are friendly. The food is delicious and not expensive. Also, there are many things to do for different people, such as beaches, mountains and culture.

I'm sure that everyone will have a good time there, so I hope to go back again one day.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Da Nang, a coastal city in central Vietnam that I'd wholeheartedly recommend.

I went there two summers ago for four days with three close friends from university.

We packed quite a lot into the trip. In the mornings, we swam at My Khe beach, where the water was clear and warm. We visited Ba Na Hills and took photos on the famous Golden Bridge. In the evenings, we feasted on fresh seafood and sipped coffee by the Han River. We also spent a day in the ancient town of Hoi An, strolling beneath hundreds of glowing lanterns at night.

There are several reasons I'd recommend it. The city is remarkably clean, safe and peaceful, and the locals are warm and welcoming. The food is delicious and reasonably priced. Plus, it caters to all tastes, with beaches, mountains and rich culture all within reach.

I'm confident that anyone would have a wonderful time there, and I'm already dreaming of going back.
