My advice to anyone going is to stay near the beach and rent a motorbike for a day to explore the coast. It's the kind of trip that leaves you refreshed and full of stories to tell.

p3.q: Why do people enjoy travelling? / What are the benefits?
p3.a6: They can relax, see new places and learn about other cultures. Travelling also helps people forget work stress and make memories with family and friends.
p3.a7: It lets people unwind, discover new places and cultures, escape work stress and create lasting memories.

p3.q: What makes a place attractive to tourists?
p3.a6: Beautiful scenery, local culture, good food and safe environment. Convenient transport and fair prices are also important.
p3.a7: Stunning scenery, rich culture, great food and safety, along with convenient transport and reasonable prices.

p3.q: Alone or with others?
p3.a6: Most people prefer travelling with others, because it's safer and they can share costs and memories. Some like to travel alone to be free.
p3.a7: Most prefer company, as it's safer, cheaper and more fun, although solo travellers enjoy the freedom.

p3.q: How has tourism changed in recent years?
p3.a6: More people use apps and social media to book hotels and plan trips. After the pandemic, people want more private and outdoor trips.
p3.a7: Booking and planning have gone online through apps and social media, and post-pandemic, people favour private, outdoor experiences.

p3.q: Can tourism have negative effects on local communities?
p3.a6: Yes. Too many tourists cause rubbish, noise and higher prices, and sometimes they damage local culture and nature.
p3.a7: Yes, overcrowding leads to litter, noise and inflated prices, and can erode local culture and damage the environment.

p3.q: Where do people prefer to travel? / Why is it difficult for young people to choose a destination?
p3.a6: They like the sea and mountains. Young people find it hard because there are too many options, and they have a limited budget.
p3.a7: Beaches and mountains are favourites. Young people struggle because there are so many options and budgets are tight.

p3.q: How do people decide on their travel dates?
p3.a6: They usually choose public holidays or when they have leave from work. They also consider the weather and the price.
p3.a7: Usually around public holidays or annual leave, taking weather and prices into account.

cards.title: Describe an interesting video you watched on social media
points: where and when you watched it
and explain why you think it was interesting
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: video TikTok về thợ làm gốm/ hoặc video hướng dẫn chăm da. Ở đây: video một người nấu ăn đường phố ở Hà Nội.

notes.v: street food seller makes egg coffee / skincare tips

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a video I watched on TikTok last month.

The video was about an old man in Hanoi who makes egg coffee in a small shop in the Old Quarter. It was about two minutes long.

I watched it on the bus on my way home from work, in the evening. TikTok suggested it to me.

In the video, he showed how to make egg coffee. He beat the egg yolk with sugar for a long time, then put it on strong, hot coffee. It looked soft and golden. He also talked about how his father started this shop many years ago.

I found it interesting for several reasons. First, his hands moved very skillfully. Second, the video had beautiful pictures and calm music. Third, I learned something about the history of the drink.

After watching, I felt relaxed after a long day, and I also wanted to drink egg coffee immediately. I went to that shop the next weekend with my friend.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a TikTok video I watched last month, which I found really captivating.

It featured an elderly man in Hanoi's Old Quarter making egg coffee in his tiny shop, and it was only about two minutes long.

I watched it on the bus home from work one evening; TikTok's algorithm had recommended it to me.

In the clip, he demonstrated how he makes the drink, whisking egg yolks with sugar for ages until they became silky, then pouring the golden cream over strong, hot coffee. Between steps, he told the story of how his father opened the shop decades ago.

There were several reasons I found it fascinating. His hands moved with such practised skill. The footage was beautifully shot with soothing background music. And I picked up some history about the drink too.

Afterwards I felt really relaxed after a tiring day, and also craving egg coffee. Naturally, I visited the shop the following weekend with a friend.

I saved the video and sent it to my mother, who remembered drinking egg coffee in that very street when she was young. It struck me how a two-minute clip could connect us across generations.

p3.q: Why do people spend so much time watching videos online?
p3.a6: Videos are short and entertaining, and we can watch them anywhere. The algorithm also shows videos we like, so it's difficult to stop.
p3.a7: They're short, entertaining and available anywhere, and algorithms feed us exactly what we like, making it hard to stop.

p3.q: What types of videos are popular nowadays?
p3.a6: Short funny videos, music videos, cooking videos, travel videos and live-streams. Many young people also watch tutorials.
p3.a7: Short comedy clips, music videos, cooking and travel vlogs, livestreams and how-to tutorials.

p3.q: Do social media videos influence opinions?
p3.a6: Yes, very much. People often believe what they see in videos, so videos can change opinions about products or politics. Sometimes fake videos also spread.
p3.a7: Very much so. People tend to trust what they see, so videos can sway views on products or issues, and misleading ones spread easily.

p3.q: Are online videos educational?
p3.a6: Yes, many are. We can learn languages, cooking and skills for free. But not all are accurate, so we should check information.
p3.a7: Many are, as you can learn languages, cooking or professional skills for free, but accuracy varies, so it's wise to verify.

p3.q: Does social media have more advantages than disadvantages?
p3.a6: I think the advantages are a bit more. We get information and connect with friends. But it wastes time and affects mental health.
p3.a7: On balance, perhaps slightly more advantages, such as information and connection, but it also wastes time and can harm mental health.

p3.q: Should children's use of social media be controlled?
p3.a6: Yes, definitely. Children can see bad content and spend too much time. Parents should limit time and use child safety apps.
p3.a7: Definitely. Children may encounter harmful content and become addicted, so parents should set time limits and use parental controls.

cards.title: Describe a time that you had to change your plan
points: why you had to change it
and explain how you felt about the change
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: chuyến đi Sa Pa bị hủy vì mưa bão/ sạt lở, đổi sang ở Hà Nội.

notes.v: 3-day trip to Sa Pa with friends
storm, landslide, road closed, train cancelled
stayed in Hanoi: Ba Vi / museums / hot pot

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a time that I had to change my plan for a trip.

My original plan was to go to Sa Pa for three days with some friends last September. We booked a hotel, train tickets and a guide. We were very excited because I had never been there.

But two days before the trip, there was a big storm in the north. There was a landslide on the road, and the train company cancelled our tickets. It wasn't safe to go.

So we changed our plan. We stayed in Hanoi and went to Ba Vi National Park for one day, then spent the other days visiting a museum, drinking coffee and eating hot pot.

The new plan worked quite well. It was relaxing and cheaper, and we had a good time together. But I was a bit disappointed at first because I really wanted to see Sa Pa. I hope I can go there later this year.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the time I had to scrap a long-awaited trip.

My original plan was a three-day trip to Sa Pa with a group of friends last September. We'd booked the hotel, train tickets and a local guide, and I was thrilled, as I'd never been there.

Two days before departure, however, a massive storm hit the north. A landslide blocked the road and the railway company cancelled our tickets. Going would have been unsafe.

We therefore had to improvise. We stayed in Hanoi, spent a day at Ba Vi National Park, then used the remaining days to visit a museum, hop between cafés and enjoy hot pot.

Surprisingly, the alternative worked out rather well. It was relaxing, cheaper, and we bonded over it. I did feel crushed at first, because I'd been so looking forward to Sa Pa, but in the end I made peace with it, and I'm planning to try again later this year.

The experience taught me to always have a plan B, and to enjoy what is in front of me instead of dwelling on what I lost. It also made me appreciate that good company matters more than the destination.

p3.q: Why do people sometimes change their plans?
p3.a6: Because of bad weather, sickness, money or work. Sometimes something better appears, so they change.
p3.a7: Due to bad weather, illness, finances or work commitments, or because a better option comes up.

p3.q: Is it important to be flexible in life?
p3.a6: Yes, very important. Life is unpredictable, so flexible people can adapt and feel less stress.
p3.a7: Absolutely. Life is unpredictable, and flexible people adapt more easily and stress less.

p3.q: Do young people change plans more often than older people?
p3.a6: I think so. Young people are more spontaneous and have fewer responsibilities. Older people prefer fixed schedules because they have a family and work.
p3.a7: I'd say so. Young people are more spontaneous with fewer responsibilities, while older people tend to stick to schedules because of family and work.

p3.q: How do people feel when plans suddenly change?
p3.a6: At first, they feel annoyed or disappointed or anxious, but after that they usually accept it.
p3.a7: Typically frustrated or anxious at first, though most people accept it with time.

p3.q: Can changing plans lead to better results?
p3.a6: Yes, sometimes. My Sa Pa plan was cancelled, but our Hanoi trip was relaxing and cheaper. New plans can bring new chances.
p3.a7: Yes, sometimes. Our Hanoi substitute turned out cheaper and more relaxing than the original. Changes can open unexpected doors.

p3.q: How can people deal with unexpected changes?
p3.a6: They should stay calm, think about the situation and make a backup plan. Talking to friends or family also helps.
p3.a7: By staying calm, assessing the situation, preparing backup plans and talking things through with others.

cards.title: Describe a problem of technology you have encountered (computer or cell phone)
points: when it happened and what device it was
and explain how you felt about the problem
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: laptop bị treo / mất dữ liệu trước deadline (hợp với nghề IT).

notes.v: laptop froze, blue screen, almost lost report
restart, recover from cloud backup, asked colleague, cleaned disk

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a problem with my laptop that happened last year.

I was working on an important test report, and the deadline was the next morning. It was about 9 p.m. when suddenly my laptop froze, and then the screen turned blue. I tried to restart it many times, but it didn't work.

I was very worried because I hadn't saved the last two hours of my work. I tried to stay calm. First, I called my colleague who is good with computers. He told me to turn off the laptop, wait for a few minutes and start it in safe mode. Then it worked. After that, I found an auto-saved version of my report in the cloud and recovered most of my work.

I finished the report at midnight. I felt panicked at first and very relieved at the end.

After that, I learned an important lesson: I should save my work often and make a backup.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a nasty laptop problem I ran into last year.

I was finalising an important test report due the next morning. Around 9 p.m., my laptop suddenly froze and then displayed the dreaded blue screen. No matter how many times I restarted it, nothing worked.

I was in a total panic, because I hadn't saved the last two hours of work. I forced myself to stay calm and phoned a colleague who's a hardware whiz. He advised me to power the laptop off, wait a few minutes, then boot into safe mode, which did the trick. Then I located an auto-saved version of my report in the cloud and recovered most of it.

I finished the report just after midnight. I went from sheer panic to enormous relief.

It was a real wake-up call. Since then, I save my work frequently, turn on automatic cloud backup and never leave critical tasks to the last minute.

Ironically, as a tester I spend my days hunting for other people's bugs, yet I had ignored the basics of protecting my own data. I now share this story with newer colleagues to remind them to save their work.

vocab.m: khởi động chế độ an toàn

p3.q: What technological problems do people often face?
p3.a6: Slow internet, a phone with no battery, software errors, viruses and forgetting passwords. Sometimes people lose data.
p3.a7: Slow internet, drained batteries, software glitches, viruses, forgotten passwords and occasionally data loss.

p3.q: Do older people have more difficulty using technology?
p3.a6: Yes, usually. They didn't grow up with it, and apps change quickly. But some older people learn well if someone teaches them patiently.
p3.a7: Generally, yes, as they didn't grow up with it and apps change quickly, although many learn well with patient guidance.

p3.q: How has technology made lives easier?
p3.a6: We can work, study, shop and pay online, so it saves time. We can also contact people everywhere.
p3.a7: We can work, study, shop and pay online, saving huge amounts of time, and stay in touch with people anywhere.

p3.q: Do people depend too much on technology?
p3.a6: I think so. Many people can't live without their phones, and some can't do simple calculations or remember a route now. If the internet stops, they feel lost.
p3.a7: I think so. Many can't function without their phones, and basic skills like navigation or mental arithmetic are fading. An outage leaves them helpless.

p3.q: What should people do when technology fails?
p3.a6: They should stay calm and try simple solutions, like restart the device. If it doesn't work, they should ask for help or go to a repair shop. Backup is also important.
p3.a7: Stay calm, try basic fixes like restarting, search for solutions or consult an expert, and always keep backups.

p3.q: Will technology become more reliable in the future?
p3.a6: I think so. Companies are improving, and AI can find errors faster. But no technology is perfect, so problems will still happen.
p3.a7: Probably, as AI helps detect faults sooner, but nothing is flawless, so occasional failures are inevitable.

cards.title: Describe a piece of local news that people are interested in
points: and explain why people are interested in it
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: tin Hà Nội mở thêm tuyến metro / tuyến xe bus điện mới (hợp người đi bus).

notes.v: new metro / electric bus line opened in Hanoi

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a piece of local news about a new electric bus route in Hanoi that opened recently.

I read the news on a news app and saw a lot of posts about it on Facebook. I also saw the news on the TV screen of my bus.

Many people in Hanoi were interested in it, especially students, office workers and people who commute every day, like me. Many of them shared the news with their friends.

People were interested for several reasons. Traffic in Hanoi is very bad and the air is polluted, so people hope public transport can help. The electric buses are clean and quiet. The ticket is also cheap, and the bus has Wi-Fi and air conditioning.

I felt very happy about this news. I take the bus every day, so a new route may save my time and make my trip more comfortable. I also think it's good for the environment.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a piece of local news that has generated a lot of buzz: the launch of a new electric bus route in Hanoi.

I first read about it on a news app, then saw plenty of Facebook posts about it, and I even spotted it on the TV screen on my bus.

The people most interested were commuters, students and office workers, people like myself who rely on public transport every day. Many of them shared the news with friends.

There are several reasons for the interest. Hanoi suffers from severe congestion and air pollution, so people are pinning their hopes on public transport. The electric buses are clean and quiet, the tickets are affordable, and they come with air conditioning and Wi-Fi.

I was genuinely delighted, since as a daily bus rider, a new route could cut my travel time and make my commute much more comfortable. I also think it's a positive step for the environment.

I'm already planning to try the new route on the weekend just to see how it compares with my current journey. If the service is reliable, I'd happily switch and perhaps persuade a few colleagues to do the same.

p3.q: How do people usually get local news nowadays?
p3.a6: Mostly from social media, like Facebook and Zalo, and from news apps. Older people still watch TV.
p3.a7: Mainly through Facebook, Zalo and news apps, while older people still rely on television.

p3.q: Is local news more important than international news? / Do people pay more attention to local or national news?
p3.a6: I think local news is more important for daily life, like traffic or weather. People pay more attention to local news because it affects them directly.
p3.a7: For everyday life, local news matters more as it affects us directly, so people tend to follow it more closely.

p3.q: Why are some news stories more popular?
p3.a6: If news is surprising, emotional or related to people's lives, it spreads fast. Some news has a strong title or video.
p3.a7: Stories that are surprising, emotional or relevant to people's lives spread fast, especially with catchy headlines or video.

p3.q: Does social media affect the way people receive news?
p3.a6: Yes. News is faster, but it's also shorter and less deep. People read only the headline and share without checking.
p3.a7: Yes. News arrives faster but more superficially; many people read only headlines and share without checking.

p3.q: Can news influence public opinion?
p3.a6: Yes, a lot. News can change how people think about an issue. If the news is wrong, it can also cause problems.
p3.a7: Absolutely. News shapes how people perceive issues, and inaccurate reporting can cause real harm.

p3.q: Is all news reliable nowadays?
p3.a6: No. There's a lot of fake news, especially on social media. We should read from trusted sources and check other websites.
p3.a7: No, fake news is rampant, especially on social media. We should stick to trusted sources and cross-check.

p3.q: Do many people talk about local news? / Who cares more, young or old?
p3.a6: Yes, people talk about it in daily conversation. Older people care more because they have more time and they care about their neighbourhood. Young people prefer entertainment news.
p3.a7: Yes, it's a common conversation topic. Older people tend to care more, having more time and community ties, while young people lean toward entertainment news.

cards.title: Describe a live sport match you have ever watched
points: when and where you watched it
and explain how you felt while watching it
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: xem bóng đá đội tuyển Việt Nam ở sân Mỹ Đình cùng bạn bè.

notes.v: tense, goal in 2nd half, 1–0 win, crowd screaming

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a football match that I watched live three years ago, between Vietnam and Thailand.

I watched it at My Dinh National Stadium in Hanoi, on a Tuesday evening. I went with three of my friends. It was my first time watching a live match in a stadium, so I was very excited.

The stadium was full of fans in red shirts, and they were singing and waving flags. In the first half, there were no goals, and both teams played hard. In the second half, Vietnam scored a goal from a corner, and the whole stadium jumped up and screamed. Then Thailand tried hard to score, but our goalkeeper made some great saves. Finally, Vietnam won 1–0.

I felt very excited and proud. I shouted so loudly that I lost my voice the next day. The atmosphere was amazing, and I will never forget it.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a live football match I watched three years ago: Vietnam versus Thailand.

It took place at My Dinh National Stadium in Hanoi on a Tuesday evening, and I went with three friends. It was my first time at a live match, so I was buzzing with anticipation.

The stands were a sea of red shirts, with fans chanting and waving flags. The first half was goalless, with both sides playing intensely. Then, in the second half, Vietnam scored from a corner, and the whole stadium erupted. Thailand pushed hard for an equaliser, but our goalkeeper pulled off a few fantastic saves, and we held on to win 1–0.

I felt a mix of thrill and pride. I screamed so much that I lost my voice the next day. The electric atmosphere is something no TV broadcast could ever match, and it's a memory I'll cherish for life.

After the final whistle, we walked out with thousands of strangers, high-fiving and singing all the way to the bus stop. I still replay that goal in my head whenever I hear the crowd's roar on TV.

p3.q: Why do many people enjoy watching sports? / Why do some become passionate fans?
p3.a6: Sports are exciting and unpredictable. People can also feel part of a group when they support a team. Some fans have supported a team since childhood.
p3.a7: Sport is thrilling and unpredictable, and supporting a team gives people a sense of belonging, often rooted in childhood loyalty.

p3.q: Is live better than watching on TV?
p3.a6: I think live is better, because the atmosphere is amazing and you can feel the emotion. But TV has slow-motion replays and is more comfortable and cheaper.
p3.a7: For the atmosphere, yes, you can't replicate it. TV has the advantage of replays, comfort and cost.

p3.q: How can sports events benefit a city or country?
p3.a6: They attract tourists and bring money for hotels and restaurants. They also make the city famous and make people proud.
p3.a7: They draw tourists, boost local businesses, raise the city's profile and instil national pride.

p3.q: Do international sports events bring people together?
p3.a6: Yes, they do. After the Vietnam team won, people celebrated together in the streets, even strangers. Different countries also meet in a friendly way.
p3.a7: Yes. When Vietnam wins, even strangers celebrate together in the streets, and international events foster friendly contact between nations.

p3.q: Should children be encouraged to play sports regularly? / What sports suit children in Vietnam?
p3.a6: Yes, sport makes children healthy and teaches teamwork. Football, badminton, swimming and table tennis are suitable and not expensive.
p3.a7: Yes, it builds health and teamwork. Football, badminton, swimming and table tennis are affordable and suitable for Vietnamese kids.

p3.q: What are the advantages of watching sports online?
p3.a6: It's cheap or free, convenient and we can watch from anywhere. We can also watch again later or choose different cameras.
p3.a7: It's cheap or free, convenient from anywhere, and you can rewatch highlights at any time.

cards.title: Describe a person you know about who runs a successful business
points: and explain why you think his/her business is successful
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: chú ruột, chủ xưởng đồ gỗ (hoặc người nổi tiếng, bạn tự chọn).

notes.v: quality, honest, customer care, online sales

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my uncle, who runs a successful furniture business.

He's about fifty years old. He owns a workshop and a shop near Hanoi, where he makes and sells wooden tables, beds and cabinets.

I know about him because he's my father's younger brother. In the summer holidays, I sometimes helped him in the shop, so I saw how he works.

I think his business is successful for several reasons. First, his products have good quality and last for a long time. Second, he is honest and always keeps his promise, so customers trust him and come back. Third, he cares about customers and answers their questions quickly. In recent years, he also started selling online on Facebook and Shopee, so he has more customers.

I think people can learn from him that honesty and hard work are the base of success, and we should change with the times.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my uncle, who runs a thriving furniture business.

He's in his fifties and owns a workshop and showroom on the outskirts of Hanoi, where he makes and sells wooden tables, beds and wardrobes.

I know about him because he's my father's younger brother, and I used to help out in his shop during summer holidays, so I got to see his work ethic first-hand.

There are three main reasons behind his success. First, his furniture is durable and well-crafted. Second, he's scrupulously honest and always keeps his word, which has earned him loyal customers and plenty of word-of-mouth referrals. Third, he's very attentive to customers, replying to queries promptly. In recent years, he's also moved with the times by selling through Facebook and Shopee, which has widened his customer base.

I think people can learn from him that integrity and hard work are the foundations of success, and that adapting to change is essential if you want to stay ahead.

He once told me that he started with just two workers and a rented yard, and that every failure taught him something. That story encourages me to be patient in my own career and never to fear starting small.

p3.q: What qualities make a successful businessperson?
p3.a6: Hard work, honesty, a clear plan and good communication. They should also be brave and flexible.
p3.a7: Diligence, integrity, a clear vision and strong communication, plus courage and adaptability.

p3.q: Is starting a business risky? / Why do some businesses fail?
p3.a6: Yes, it's risky. You need money and there is a lot of competition. Many businesses fail because they have no plan, not enough money or they don't understand customers.
p3.a7: Yes, it demands capital and competition is fierce. Many fail due to poor planning, cash-flow problems or failing to understand customers' needs.

p3.q: Is it better to work for a company or run your own business?
p3.a6: It depends. Working for a company is stable and safe. Running a business can bring more money and freedom, but it's stressful.
p3.a7: It depends. A company offers stability, whereas your own business offers freedom and higher potential earnings, but with greater stress and risk.

p3.q: Do young people prefer entrepreneurship?
p3.a6: Many young people want to start their own business because they want freedom and they see success stories online. But many are afraid of risk, so they prefer a stable job.
p3.a7: Many are attracted by the freedom and online success stories, but a lot still prefer job security because of the risks.

p3.q: How important is customer service?
p3.a6: Very important. Good service makes customers happy so they come back and tell others. Bad service can destroy a business.
p3.a7: Crucial. Good service builds loyalty and referrals, while poor service can ruin a business's reputation.

p3.q: Do you approve of the business model of small shops?
p3.a6: Yes, I do. Small shops are flexible and close to local people, and they create jobs. But they find it hard to compete with big supermarkets and online shopping.
p3.a7: Yes. They're flexible, personable and create local jobs, although they struggle to compete with supermarkets and e-commerce.

cards.title: Describe a tall building in your town that you like or dislike
points: what it is used for and what it looks like
and explain why you like or dislike it
cards.note: Lựa chọn giả định: Landmark 81 / Keangnam (Hà Nội). Bài này chọn Lotte Center Hanoi (thích).

notes.v: offices, hotel, shopping mall, observation deck
glass, modern, crown-shaped top, lights at night
view, convenient, symbol of modern Hanoi

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about Lotte Center Hanoi, a tall building that I like.

It's located in Ba Dinh district in Hanoi, near the Lieu Giai street. It's about one hour from my house by bus.

The building is used for many purposes. It has offices, a hotel and a big shopping mall with a food court. On the top floor, there's an observation deck where visitors can see all of Hanoi.

It looks very modern. It's made of glass, and the top is shaped like a crown. At night, it has beautiful lights, so you can see it from far away.

I like this building for several reasons. First, from the observation deck, I can see the city at night, and it's amazing. Second, it's convenient because I can shop, eat and see a film in one place. Third, I think it's a symbol of modern Hanoi.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Lotte Center Hanoi, a skyscraper that I'm rather fond of.

It's located in Ba Dinh district, close to Lieu Giai Street, about an hour from my home by bus.

It's a mixed-use building. It houses offices, a hotel and a huge shopping mall with a food court, while the top floor features an observation deck with panoramic views of the city.

In terms of appearance, it's sleek and modern, with a glass façade and a crown-like top. At night, it's illuminated with elegant lights, so it stands out from miles away.

There are several reasons I like it. Firstly, the night view of Hanoi from the observation deck is breathtaking. Secondly, it's incredibly convenient, since I can shop, dine and catch a film all under one roof. Finally, I see it as a symbol of Hanoi's modernisation, showing how far the city has come.

Whenever I have visitors from out of town, I take them there as a first stop, because the view of the city lights from above never fails to impress. It reminds me why I'm proud of living in Hanoi.

p3.q: What will buildings be like in the future?
p3.a6: They will be taller, smarter and greener. They may use solar energy, have robots and use less electricity.
p3.a7: Taller, smarter and greener, with solar power, automation and energy-saving designs.

p3.q: Bungalow or tall building? / Why do many Vietnamese live in high-rise buildings? / Future preference?
p3.a6: In cities, many people live in apartments because land is expensive and they are near work. In the future, I think apartments will be more popular, but many people still want houses with a garden.
p3.a7: In cities, land is scarce and costly and apartments are close to workplaces, so high-rises are increasingly popular, though many still dream of a house with a garden.

p3.q: Why are taller buildings being built? / Do they make cities attractive?
p3.a6: The population is growing and the land is limited, so building up saves space. Tall buildings can make the city look modern, but too many can make it feel crowded.
p3.a7: With growing populations and limited land, building upwards saves space. They give a city a modern skyline, though too many feel oppressive.

p3.q: Advantages and disadvantages of tall buildings?
p3.a6: They have good views, they are safe and have services like a gym and a pool. But the lifts are crowded, there is less privacy and, if there is a fire, it's dangerous.
p3.a7: Great views, security and amenities; on the downside, crowded lifts, less privacy and fire risks.

p3.q: Modern or old buildings better? / Preserve old buildings?
p3.a6: Modern buildings are more convenient and safe, but old buildings have history. I think we should keep the old ones that are important and repair them, not replace them.
p3.a7: Modern buildings are more functional and safe, but old ones carry history, so we should preserve the significant ones and restore them rather than demolish.

p3.q: Have you ever lived in a high-rise?
p3.a6: No, I live in a house with my parents. But I had a friend and I visited his apartment on the 20th floor, and the view was great.
p3.a7: No, I've always lived in a house, but I've visited a friend on the 20th floor, and the view was fantastic.

p3.q: How does climate affect architectural design? / Why do some people design their own homes?
p3.a6: In hot, rainy countries like Vietnam, buildings need big windows, strong roofs and good drainage. In cold countries, they need good heating. People design their own homes to get what they want, and sometimes it's cheaper.
p3.a7: In hot, humid Vietnam, buildings need ventilation, sturdy roofs and drainage, whereas cold countries focus on insulation. Some design their homes to get exactly what they want.

cards.title: Describe a person you know who encourages people to protect the environment or nature
points: what he/she does to encourage people
and explain how you feel about this person
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: chị Linh, đồng nghiệp, sống xanh, không dùng đồ nhựa.

notes.v: same team, sit next to me
reusable bottle/bag, sorts rubbish, cycles, recycles
posts, small challenge "plastic-free week", gives gifts

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my colleague, Linh. She's about thirty years old and she works in the same team as me.

I know her because she sits next to me at the office. We have lunch together every day.

She does many things to protect the environment. She never uses plastic bags or plastic bottles. She brings her own water bottle and a cloth bag. She sorts rubbish at home and recycles paper. She also rides a bike to work when the weather is good.

She also encourages other people. She organised a "plastic-free week" at the office, and many colleagues joined. She posts tips on Facebook, and she gave us small gifts like cloth bags.

I admire her because she doesn't only talk but acts. She makes small changes every day, and her ideas are practical and easy to follow. Because of her, I also started to use my own bottle and bring my own bag.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my colleague Linh, who's in her early thirties and sits right next to me in the office. We have lunch together every day, so I know her well.

She goes to great lengths to protect the environment. She refuses single-use plastic, carrying her own water bottle and cloth bag everywhere. She sorts her household waste, recycles paper and cycles to work whenever the weather allows.

What's more, she encourages others without being preachy. She organised a "plastic-free week" at our office that many colleagues joined, shares practical tips on Facebook and even hands out small cloth bags as gifts.

I admire her because she practises what she preaches. Her suggestions are realistic and easy to adopt, rather than extreme. She's actually influenced me: I now bring my own bottle and bag, and I've started refusing plastic straws.

Last month, she even organised a small clean-up around West Lake on a Sunday, and a dozen colleagues turned up with gloves and bags. Her enthusiasm is contagious, and it shows me that one person really can start a positive chain reaction.

p3.q: How can parents help children learn about nature?
p3.a6: They can take children to parks, farms or the countryside. They can also grow plants with children and teach them not to throw rubbish.
p3.a7: By taking them to parks and the countryside, growing plants together and setting an example, such as never littering.

p3.q: Should children spend more time learning about nature at school?
p3.a6: I agree. Children learn better from real experience than from books. Schools can organise field trips and tree-planting activities.
p3.a7: I agree. Hands-on experience beats textbooks, so schools should organise field trips and tree-planting days.

p3.q: Is it easy for city children to enjoy nature?
p3.a6: No, it's not easy. Cities have little green space and the air is polluted. Children spend a lot of time on screens. But parents can take them to parks or on weekend trips.
p3.a7: Not really. Green space is scarce and children are glued to screens, though parks and weekend trips can help.

p3.q: What can people do to protect nature?
p3.a6: Save water and electricity, reduce plastic, sort rubbish, use public transport and plant trees.
p3.a7: Conserve water and energy, cut down on plastic, sort waste, use public transport and plant trees.

p3.q: Is there a need for new laws to protect nature?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. Some laws exist, but they're not strict enough. For example, we need heavier fines for factories that pollute and for illegal hunting.
p3.a7: Yes. Existing laws aren't always enforced strictly enough, so we need heavier fines for polluters and illegal poachers.

p3.q: Are punishments or rewards more effective?
p3.a6: I think both are needed. Fines make people afraid and stop bad behaviour, while rewards, such as tax reductions for green companies, encourage people to do good things voluntarily.
p3.a7: A combination. Fines deter harmful behaviour, while rewards such as tax breaks motivate people to go green voluntarily.

cards.title: Describe a time when you had to pay more than you expected for something
points: why you had to pay more than you expected
and explain how you felt about it
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: sửa điện thoại, màn hình hỏng, báo giá thêm.

notes.v: last winter, phone shop in Hanoi
also battery damaged, original screen expensive
annoyed, but OK, lesson: ask price first

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a time I paid more than I expected for repairing my phone.

It happened last winter. I dropped my phone and the screen broke. I took it to a small phone repair shop near my company in Hanoi.

The shop owner said it cost about one million VND to change the screen. I agreed and waited. But after one hour, he told me that the battery was also damaged and it was dangerous to keep using it. He also said the original screen cost more than the cheap one. So I paid 1.7 million VND, around 700,000 VND more than I expected.

I felt annoyed because I didn't ask about all the prices at the beginning. But I also needed my phone for work, so I accepted. In the end, the phone worked well and the battery lasted longer.

After this experience, I learned that I should ask for a full price before repairing and compare shops.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the time I ended up paying much more than I'd budgeted for a phone repair.

It happened last winter. I dropped my phone and cracked the screen, so I took it to a small repair shop near my office in Hanoi.

The owner quoted around one million dong for a new screen, and I agreed. An hour later, though, he informed me that the battery was also damaged and unsafe to keep using, and that the original screen I'd chosen cost more than a generic one. In the end, I paid 1.7 million dong, about 700,000 more than expected.

I was irritated, mainly because I hadn't asked for a full breakdown of costs upfront. However, I needed the phone for work, so I swallowed my pride and paid. To be fair, it worked perfectly afterwards and the battery lasted far longer.

It was a valuable lesson: always ask for an itemised quote before agreeing to a repair, and compare a few shops first.

Since then, I've also bought a protective case and screen cover, so I don't have to go through the same hassle again. In the end, a small mistake turned into a lesson about managing money and asking questions early.

p3.q: What do young people like to spend money on?
p3.a6: They spend money on clothes, phones, eating out, coffee, travel and entertainment like concerts and games.
p3.a7: Fashion, gadgets, eating out, coffee, travel and entertainment such as concerts and games.

p3.q: Why do some people spend money on things they don't need?
p3.a6: Because of advertising and sales. Some people want to follow trends or show off, or they feel happy when they shop. Online shopping makes it too easy.
p3.a7: Advertising and discounts tempt them, and some want to keep up with trends or impress others. Online shopping makes impulse buying effortless.

p3.q: How important is saving money for the future?
p3.a6: Very important. We might have an emergency, like illness or losing our job. Saving also helps us buy a house or retire.
p3.a7: Vital. It protects us against emergencies such as illness or job loss and helps us fund major goals like a house or retirement.

p3.q: How important is it to teach children about giving money to support people in need?
p3.a6: I think it's important. Children learn to be kind and to share. We can teach them to give a small amount or donate old clothes.
p3.a7: Very important. It cultivates kindness and empathy, and we can start small, for example donating pocket money or old clothes.

p3.q: Do you think young people save enough money?
p3.a6: Not really. Many young people spend most of their income and use credit cards or "buy now, pay later" services.
p3.a7: Not really. Many spend most of their income and lean on credit cards or "buy now, pay later" schemes.

p3.q: Is it a good idea to compare prices before buying?
p3.a6: Yes, definitely. We can use apps or websites to compare shops, and it helps us save money and avoid surprises like mine.
p3.a7: Absolutely. Price-comparison apps and websites help us save money and avoid nasty surprises like mine.

cards.title: Describe a person who you think is good at planning things
points: what kind of things he/she plans
and explain why you think he/she is good at planning
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: chị quản lý dự án (project manager) trong công ty.

notes.v: project schedules, team outings, her own day
lists, priorities, deadlines, backup plan, calm

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about Ms Hoa, who is the project manager in my company. She's about thirty-five years old.

I know her because she's my manager. I've worked with her for two years.

She plans many things. At work, she plans the schedule of our projects and divides tasks for team members. She also plans team trips and parties every year, and she always manages everything well. Even her daily schedule is clear.

I think she's good at planning for several reasons. She makes a to-do list every morning and puts important tasks first. She always thinks about problems that may happen, so she makes a backup plan. She also stays calm when the plan changes.

I respect her a lot, and I learn many things from her. After working with her, I also make a daily plan, so I feel less stressed.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Ms Hoa, the project manager at my company, who's in her mid-thirties.

I know her because she's my direct supervisor, and I've worked under her for about two years.

She plans all sorts of things. At work, she maps out project schedules and allocates tasks to the team. She also organises our annual team trips and parties, and everything always runs like clockwork. Even her personal day is meticulously structured.

I'd say she's a brilliant planner for several reasons. She writes a to-do list every morning and prioritises the most urgent tasks. She anticipates potential problems and always has a contingency plan. And she doesn't panic when plans change; she simply adjusts.

I have enormous respect for her, and I've learned a lot from her. Since working with her, I've also started planning my day in advance, and I feel far less stressed as a result.

What I admire most is how she keeps everyone informed, so nobody is left guessing about deadlines. Her calm leadership has shown me that good planning isn't about control; it's about caring for the team and making work easier for everyone.

p3.q: What types of plans do people make with friends and family?
p3.a6: They plan trips, parties, meals and weekend activities. For family, they also plan big things like buying a house.
p3.a7: Trips, parties, meals and weekend outings, and with family, bigger plans such as buying a home.

p3.q: Is it important to plan special events like weddings?
p3.a6: Yes, very. A wedding has many things to prepare and is expensive. Without a plan, there will be mistakes and stress.
p3.a7: Very much. Weddings involve countless details and big costs, so without planning, things can easily go wrong.

p3.q: Why don't some people like to plan their social life in advance?
p3.a6: They like freedom and want to do whatever they feel like at the moment. Others are afraid that the plan may change and they'll be disappointed.
p3.a7: They value spontaneity and don't want to feel tied down, or they dislike the disappointment when plans fall through.

p3.q: Advantages for young people of planning their careers?
p3.a6: They know what skills to learn and they save time. They are more confident and can avoid choosing the wrong job.
p3.a7: They know which skills to develop, save time, avoid wrong turns and feel more confident about their direction.

p3.q: Should young people ask for career advice from teachers or family?
p3.a6: Yes, they can learn from their experience. But young people should make their own final decision.
p3.a7: Yes, they bring valuable experience, though the final decision should rest with the young person.

p3.q: Is a successful career only possible if carefully planned?
p3.a6: I disagree. A plan is helpful, but luck and chances also matter. Some people become successful by trying different things and changing direction.
p3.a7: I disagree. Planning helps, but luck, opportunities and adaptability matter too; many people succeed by exploring and changing course.

cards.title: Describe an ambition you have had for a long time
points: what you have done to achieve it
and explain why it is important to you
cards.note: Tham vọng giả định: trở thành Automation QA Lead và đạt IELTS 6.5 (khớp mục tiêu của bạn).

notes.v: become QA lead, work in international team

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my long-term ambition: I want to become a QA lead and work in an international team.

I first had this ambition about three years ago, when I started my first job as a tester. I saw my manager lead the team and talk to foreign clients, and I thought it was a great job.

Since then, I've done several things. I studied an automation testing course and learned programming. I'm also preparing for the ISTQB certificate. Besides, I'm studying English every day because I need to speak English with foreign customers. My target is IELTS 6.5.

It's difficult to achieve this ambition. I have to study after work, and my English is not good yet. There are also many people competing for these jobs.

But this ambition is very important to me because it gives me a clear direction. If I achieve it, I'll have a better career, a higher income and I can support my family.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a long-held ambition of mine: to become a QA lead and work in an international team.

It took root about three years ago, in my first job as a tester. I watched my manager lead the team and communicate with overseas clients, and I thought, "That's where I want to be."

Since then, I've taken several steps. I completed an automation testing course and learned to code, and I'm now preparing for the ISTQB certificate. On top of that, I'm studying English every day, with IELTS 6.5 as my target, as I'll need to communicate fluently with foreign customers.

It's certainly challenging. I have to study after a full day's work, my English still needs a lot of improvement, and the competition for these roles is stiff.

Nevertheless, this ambition matters enormously to me, as it gives my life direction and purpose. Achieving it would mean a better career, a higher income and the means to support my family.

Every time I feel tired after work, I picture myself in a meeting room talking confidently with an international team, and that image pushes me to open my notebook again. I know the road is long, but I believe each small step counts.

p3.q: Why is it important for people to have ambitions?
p3.a6: Ambition gives people a goal and motivation. Without it, people may feel lost and don't try to improve.
p3.a7: Ambition provides direction and motivation; without it, people may drift and stop growing.

p3.q: Do young people have different ambitions from older people?
p3.a6: Yes. Young people want to be famous, make a lot of money or have an exciting career. Older people care more about a stable life and family.
p3.a7: Yes. Young people tend to aim for fame, wealth or exciting careers, while older people prioritise stability and family.

p3.q: Can ambition help people become successful?
p3.a6: Yes, because ambitious people work harder and don't give up easily. But ambition must go together with a plan and action.
p3.a7: Yes, ambitious people work harder and persevere, though ambition must be paired with planning and action.

p3.q: What can stop people from achieving ambitions?
p3.a6: Lack of money, time, support or confidence. Fear of failure and laziness also stop them. Sometimes family problems or health problems are also obstacles.
p3.a7: Lack of money, time or support, low confidence, fear of failure, laziness, and sometimes family or health problems.

p3.q: Should parents influence their children's ambitions?
p3.a6: Parents can give advice, because they have experience. But they shouldn't force children, because children will be unhappy.
p3.a7: They can offer guidance, as they have experience, but they shouldn't impose their wishes, as it leads to unhappiness.

p3.q: Is it easier to achieve ambitions nowadays?
p3.a6: In some ways, yes. We can learn online and find information easily. But competition is bigger and life is more expensive, so it's not easy.
p3.a7: In some respects, yes, since online learning and information are accessible, but competition is fiercer and living costs are higher.

cards.title: Describe a home that you like to visit but would not want to live in
points: and explain why you would not want to live there
cards.note: Nhà giả định: nhà bà ngoại ở quê Thanh Hóa.

notes.v: old house, big yard, garden, well, tile roof, porch
far from work, few shops, mosquito, poor internet, lonely

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my grandmother's house, which I love to visit, but wouldn't live in.

It's in a village in Thanh Hoa province, about 150 kilometres from Hanoi.

It's an old, one-storey house with a tile roof and a big wooden door. There is a large yard in the front and a garden with banana trees and vegetables. Next to the house, there is a small pond. Inside, the house is simple but clean and cool.

I like visiting it for several reasons. The air is fresh, and everything is quiet and peaceful. My grandmother cooks delicious food for us, and I can relax with all my family there. It's a place where I can forget my work stress.

However, I wouldn't want to live there. It's far from my workplace, and there are only a few shops and no hospitals nearby. The internet is also slow, and at night there are many mosquitoes. I think I would feel lonely there.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my grandmother's house, which I love visiting but couldn't imagine living in.

It's in a village in Thanh Hoa province, roughly 150 kilometres from Hanoi.

It's an old single-storey house with a tiled roof and a heavy wooden door. In front, there's a spacious yard and a garden with banana trees and vegetables, and next to it a small pond. The interior is simple but spotless and pleasantly cool.

I enjoy visiting for several reasons. The air is fresh and the surroundings are wonderfully peaceful. My grandmother cooks mouth-watering meals, and the whole family gets together there. It's the perfect place to switch off from work stress.

Having said that, I wouldn't want to live there. It's too far from my workplace, the nearest shops are quite distant and there's no hospital nearby. The internet is sluggish, and the mosquitoes at night are relentless. I'd also feel isolated, as there's so little going on.

So for me, it's a place to visit rather than to live, a retreat that I look forward to every Tet and every summer. I come back to Hanoi refreshed, and I appreciate both lifestyles more because of the contrast.

p3.q: What makes a home comfortable to live in?
p3.a6: A clean and quiet place, enough light and fresh air, and good furniture. It should also be safe and near shops and work.
p3.a7: Cleanliness, quietness, good light and ventilation, comfortable furniture, safety, and convenient access to shops and work.

p3.q: Do housing preferences change as people get older?
p3.a6: Yes. Young people like apartments in the city centre, near work and entertainment. Older people prefer quiet places near parks and hospitals.
p3.a7: Yes. Young people prefer central apartments near work and nightlife, whereas older people favour quiet areas near parks and hospitals.

p3.q: House or apartment?
p3.a6: A house has more space and privacy, and it's good for a big family. An apartment is safer and more convenient and has services. I prefer a house, but an apartment is more realistic in Hanoi.
p3.a7: Houses offer space and privacy, apartments offer security and amenities. I'd prefer a house, but in Hanoi an apartment is more realistic.

p3.q: What factors do people consider? / How important is location?
p3.a6: Price, size, safety and especially location. Location is very important because it affects travel time, schools and daily life.
p3.a7: Price, size and safety, with location arguably the most crucial, as it determines commuting time, schools and daily convenience.

p3.q: Do modern homes differ from homes in the past?
p3.a6: Yes. Modern homes are smaller, with smart devices and modern kitchens. In the past, houses were bigger with gardens and had several generations living together.
p3.a7: Yes. Modern homes tend to be smaller, with smart devices and modern kitchens, while older houses had gardens and housed several generations together.

cards.title: Describe a place you'd like to visit in your free time
points: and explain why you would like to visit it in your free time
cards.note: Lựa chọn giả định: Phú Quốc (hoặc Ninh Bình). Bài này: Hội An/ Phú Quốc → chọn Phú Quốc.

notes.v: swim, snorkel, cable car, night market, seafood

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about Phu Quoc, an island in the south of Vietnam that I would like to visit in my free time.

There are many things to do there. I could swim in the clear blue sea and try snorkelling to see colourful fish. I could take the longest sea cable car in the world and visit the night market to eat fresh seafood. I also want to watch the sunset on the beach.

I'd like to go with my close friends or my family, because it's more fun and we can share the cost.

I want to visit this place for several reasons. The beaches are said to be very beautiful and clean. I have never been there, and I want to have a long relaxing holiday after a lot of work.

When I'm there, I think I'll feel very relaxed and free from stress. I'd feel happy and also very energetic when I go back to work.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Phu Quoc, an island in southern Vietnam that's high on my wish list for a free-time getaway.

There's so much to do there. I could swim in the crystal-clear sea, go snorkelling among colourful fish, ride the world's longest over-sea cable car and graze on fresh seafood at the night market. And of course, I'd love to watch the sunset from the beach.

I'd go with my close friends or family, since it's more enjoyable in company and we could split the cost.

There are two main reasons I'm drawn to it. Its beaches are reputed to be pristine and stunning, and I've never been, so I'm curious. I also badly need a proper break after long stretches of work.

I imagine I'd feel utterly relaxed, completely free from stress and recharged. I'd probably return to work refreshed and far more productive.

I've already started saving a little money each month for this trip, and I check flight prices from time to time. Having something to look forward to makes my busy weeks feel lighter.

p3.q: Why do some people prefer to travel in their own country rather than going abroad?
p3.a6: It's cheaper and easier. There's no need for a visa or a passport, and they speak the same language. They also want to explore their own country.
p3.a7: It's cheaper and simpler, with no visa hassle or language barrier, and many want to discover their own country first.

p3.q: Some people don't like to travel abroad. Why?
p3.a6: They worry about the cost, language problems and safety. Some people don't like different food or culture, and some are afraid of flying.
p3.a7: They worry about cost, language barriers and safety, and some dislike unfamiliar food, culture or flying.

p3.q: Why do people choose to travel or live abroad?
p3.a6: I think so, because the transport is better and more beautiful places are being developed, and prices are more suitable for most people.
p3.a7: Likely, thanks to improving transport and newly developed destinations at affordable prices.

cards.title: Describe an occasion when you got up extremely early
points: why you got up so early
what you did after you got up
and explain how you felt about getting up that early
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: dậy 3:30 sáng để đi Sa Pa/ ra sân bay đi du lịch. Ở đây: dậy 4 giờ sáng để ra sân bay đi Đà Nẵng.

notes.v: taxi to Noi Bai airport, check-in, coffee

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about the day I got up extremely early, at 3:30 in the morning.

It happened in the summer, two years ago. I had a flight to Da Nang with my friends at 6 a.m., so I had to be at Noi Bai airport at 4:30.

After I got up, I washed my face quickly, checked my luggage again and called a taxi. I picked up my friends on the way. At the airport, we did the check-in, then we had a coffee while waiting to board.

It was quite difficult for me. I'm not a morning person, and I only slept for three hours because I was too excited the night before. When the alarm rang, I felt very tired and I wanted to sleep more.

However, I was happy because we were going on a holiday. I felt sleepy on the plane, but when I saw the sea in Da Nang, I forgot my tiredness. I think it was worth it.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the morning I dragged myself out of bed at 3:30 a.m.

It was two summers ago. My friends and I had a 6 a.m. flight to Da Nang, which meant being at Noi Bai airport by 4:30.

Once I was up, I splashed some water on my face, double-checked my luggage and ordered a taxi, picking up my friends on the way. At the airport, we checked in and grabbed a coffee while waiting to board.

It was pretty tough for me. I'm definitely not a morning person, and I'd only managed three hours' sleep because I was too excited the night before. When the alarm rang, I felt exhausted and desperately wanted to stay in bed.

Even so, I was thrilled, as we were heading off on holiday. I dozed off on the plane, but the moment I saw the blue sea of Da Nang, my tiredness vanished. It was absolutely worth the effort.

That morning showed me that waking up early isn't so bad when you have something exciting waiting for you. Ever since, I try to rise a bit earlier on weekdays to study English before work.

p3.q: Why do people get up early?
p3.a6: Some need to go to work or school early, or catch a flight. Others get up early to exercise or have more quiet time for themselves.
p3.a7: Some have to commute or catch a flight, while others rise early to exercise or enjoy some quiet time to themselves.

p3.q: Is it good to arrive early? Are there situations when it isn't?
p3.a6: Usually it's good, because we feel calm and we don't worry about traffic. But sometimes it's not good, for example arriving early to a party when the host is not ready.
p3.a7: Generally yes, as it reduces stress and leaves room for delays, but arriving early at someone's home when the host is still preparing can be awkward.

p3.q: Why do some people stay up late?
p3.a6: They work or study at night, or they watch videos or play games. Some people think they are more creative at night.
p3.a7: Because of work or study, or entertainment like videos and games, and some feel more creative at night.

p3.q: Is it easy to get up early?
p3.a6: It's not easy for most people, especially in winter. But if we go to bed early and have a goal for the morning, it's easier.
p3.a7: Not for most, particularly in winter, though going to bed early and having something to look forward to helps.

p3.q: Do young and older people have different sleeping habits?
p3.a6: Yes. Older people go to bed early and wake up early. Young people sleep late and use phones at night.
p3.a7: Yes. Older people turn in early and rise early, while young people stay up late, often on their phones.

p3.q: Is it healthier to wake up early?
p3.a6: I think so, if you also sleep enough. Early risers have time to exercise and eat breakfast. But sleeping enough hours is more important than the time.
p3.a7: Generally, provided you still get enough sleep, as early risers have time for exercise and breakfast; total sleep matters more than timing.

p3.q: What jobs require waking up very early?
p3.a6: Bakers, market sellers, farmers, street cleaners, pilots and delivery drivers.
p3.a7: Bakers, market vendors, farmers, street cleaners, airline crew and delivery drivers.

p3.q: How can people develop good sleeping habits?
p3.a6: Go to bed and wake up at the same time, avoid the phone before bed, and don't drink coffee in the evening. A quiet, dark room also helps.
p3.a7: Keep regular sleep and wake times, avoid screens and coffee in the evening, and make the bedroom dark and quiet.

p3.q: Do modern lifestyles affect sleep?
p3.a6: Yes. People work long hours, use phones at night and have stress, so many of them don't sleep well.
p3.a7: Definitely. Long working hours, late-night screen time and stress leave many people sleep-deprived.

cards.title: Describe a new law that you want to implement in your country
points: how it could be put into practice
and explain why you think it is necessary
cards.note: Luật giả định: cấm sử dụng điện thoại khi lái xe máy / phạt nặng xả rác. Bài này: phạt nặng xả rác nơi công cộng.

notes.v: heavy fines for littering in public places
dirty streets, lakes, pollution, flooding, bad habit

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a law that I want to make in Vietnam: a law with heavy fines for littering in public places.

This law would affect everyone, including local people and tourists. Everyone must follow it when they go to the streets, parks, lakes or beaches.

I think it's necessary because many people in my country still throw rubbish on the street, in the lakes and on beaches. It makes the city dirty and ugly. Rubbish also blocks drains and causes flooding in the rain. It's also bad for people's health and for tourism.

To implement the law, we need to put more rubbish bins in public places. Officers and cameras can check the area, and people who litter would pay a fine, about 500,000 to 2 million dong. The government should also have an education campaign in schools.

I believe it will help our cities be cleaner, healthier and more beautiful, and people will have better habits.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a law I'd like to see introduced in Vietnam: substantial fines for littering in public places.

It would apply to everyone, from residents to tourists, in streets, parks, lakes and beaches.

I think it's necessary because littering is still a widespread habit. Rubbish ends up on pavements, in lakes and on beaches, making our cities look dirty and unappealing. It also clogs drains, which causes flooding in heavy rain, and it harms public health and tourism.

To enforce it, we'd need to install plenty of rubbish bins first. Then officers and surveillance cameras would monitor key areas, with offenders paying fines of between 500,000 and two million dong. Alongside this, schools should run awareness campaigns so that children grow up with good habits.

I'm convinced this would make our cities cleaner, healthier and more attractive, and gradually change people's mindset towards public spaces.

Countries like Singapore have shown that strict rules combined with education can change habits within a single generation. I truly believe Vietnam could achieve the same, and the benefits would reach every citizen.

p3.q: Does it take a long time to introduce a new law?
p3.a6: Yes, usually. A law needs to be discussed, written, voted on and then explained to the public. It can take months or even years.
p3.a7: Typically yes. A law must be drafted, debated, voted on and publicised, which can take months or even years.

p3.q: Which is better: make people obey, punish them or encourage them?
p3.a6: I think a mix is best. Punishment stops bad behaviour quickly, but encouragement and education create long-term habits.
p3.a7: A combination: punishment deters bad behaviour in the short term, while education and encouragement build lasting habits.

p3.q: What rules should students follow at school?
p3.a6: They should come on time, wear uniforms, respect teachers, not cheat in exams and keep the school clean. They shouldn't use phones in class.
p3.a7: Arrive on time, wear uniform, respect teachers, avoid cheating, keep the school clean and stay off phones in class.

p3.q: Can children learn about the law outside school?
p3.a6: Yes. They can learn from their parents, TV, books and the internet, and from daily life, like seeing traffic rules.
p3.a7: Yes, from parents, media, the internet and everyday life, such as observing traffic rules.

p3.q: How can parents teach children to obey rules?
p3.a6: Parents should be a good example, explain the reasons for the rules and be consistent. Praise is better than punishment.
p3.a7: By setting an example, explaining why rules exist, staying consistent and using praise more than punishment.

p3.q: What are the benefits of obeying rules?
p3.a6: Society is safe and orderly, and people avoid accidents and fines. It also makes people respect each other.
p3.a7: It keeps society safe and orderly, prevents accidents and fines, and fosters mutual respect.

p3.q: What behaviour is considered good behaviour?
p3.a6: Being polite, honest, helping others, queueing, keeping public places clean and respecting elders.
p3.a7: Politeness, honesty, helping others, queueing, keeping public spaces clean and respecting elders.

p3.q: Do people in your country usually obey the law?
p3.a6: Not always. In big cities, many people ignore traffic rules, like running red lights or riding on the pavement. But when there are strict fines and cameras, people obey more.
p3.a7: Not always. Traffic violations are common in big cities, though compliance improves when fines are strict and cameras are present.

cards.title: Describe a quiet place you like to go
points: and explain why you like going there
cards.note: Nơi giả định: quán cà phê sách yên tĩnh / thư viện gần Hồ Tây. Bài này: quán cà phê sách.

notes.v: read, study English, listen to music, think
rule of silence, small, few customers, soft music

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a quiet book café near West Lake in Hanoi.

I go there about twice a month, usually on Saturday morning. It takes me about one hour by bus.

I usually take a book or my laptop. I read, listen to English podcasts and study vocabulary. Sometimes I just sit and look at the lake and think about my life while drinking a cup of coffee.

It's quiet for some reasons. The café is small and in a small lane, away from the main road. It doesn't have many customers in the morning. There is also a rule: people must speak softly and keep their phones on silent. The music is soft and slow.

I like going there because Hanoi is noisy and crowded, and my job is stressful. In that place, I can relax and concentrate. I always feel peaceful and refreshed when I leave.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a quiet book café near West Lake in Hanoi, which is my favourite escape.

I go there about twice a month, usually on a Saturday morning. It takes about an hour by bus, but it's well worth the trip.

I usually bring a book or my laptop. I read, listen to English podcasts and revise vocabulary. At times, I simply sit gazing at the lake, sipping my coffee and reflecting on life.

There are several reasons it's so peaceful. The café is small and tucked away in a lane, far from the main road, and there are few customers in the mornings. There's also a house rule: guests must speak softly and keep their phones on silent. The background music is soft and gentle.

I love it there because Hanoi is so noisy and chaotic, and my job can be quite stressful. In that café, I can unwind and concentrate properly. I always leave feeling calm and refreshed.

I've even made a few quiet friends there, regular customers who nod politely and share a smile as we each get on with our own things. It's comforting to know that such a peaceful corner still exists in a busy city.

p3.q: How do people express happiness in your culture?
p3.a6: They smile, laugh and talk a lot. Vietnamese people often celebrate with food, drinks and karaoke, and they share the good news with family and friends.
p3.a7: By smiling, laughing and celebrating with food, drinks and karaoke, and by sharing good news with family and friends.

p3.q: How do people spend leisure time? How does technology affect it?
p3.a6: They have coffee with friends, go shopping or watch films. Now, technology changes it a lot. People spend more time on phones and watching videos, and less time on outdoor activities.
p3.a7: Café meet-ups, shopping, films and family time. Technology has shifted leisure towards screens, with less time for outdoor activities.

p3.q: Do only old people have time for leisure?
p3.a6: No. Retired people have more time, but young people also have leisure time on weekends. It depends on the person's lifestyle.
p3.a7: Not at all. Retirees have more free time, but young people enjoy weekends and evenings too; it depends on lifestyle.

p3.q: Why do old people prefer quiet places? What quiet places do people like?
p3.a6: They need rest and quiet is better for their health and sleep. In Vietnam, people like parks, lakes, temples, pagodas, libraries and the countryside.
p3.a7: Quiet is better for their health and sleep. Vietnamese people favour parks, lakes, pagodas, libraries and the countryside.

p3.q: Why are there more noises at home now than in the past?
p3.a6: We have more devices, like TVs, phones and washing machines, and traffic outside is louder. People also play music and watch videos loudly.
p3.a7: We own more devices, such as TVs and washing machines, traffic outside is heavier and people watch videos and play music loudly.

p3.q: Why do some people not like quiet places?
p3.a6: They feel lonely or bored when it's too quiet. Some are used to noise and activity.
p3.a7: They find silence boring or lonely, having grown used to noise and activity.

p3.q: Are there more or fewer quiet places? Can a place be completely quiet?
p3.a6: Fewer, because cities grow and there is more traffic and construction. No place is completely quiet, because even in the forest we can hear the wind and animals.
p3.a7: Fewer, due to urban growth, traffic and construction. No place is entirely silent; even forests have wind and wildlife sounds.

p3.q: Can people listen to music while doing something else?
p3.a6: Yes, when doing easy tasks like cleaning or exercising. But for studying or working on difficult tasks, music with words can distract us.
p3.a7: Yes, for simple tasks like cleaning or exercising, though music with lyrics can distract during demanding work or study.

p3.q: Benefits of quietness? Do people feel uncomfortable without noise?
p3.a6: Quiet reduces stress, helps us sleep and concentrate, and is good for children and old people. I agree that some people feel uncomfortable without noise, because they depend on music or TV.
p3.a7: Quietness lowers stress and improves sleep and focus for all ages. I agree that some feel uneasy without noise, as they've grown dependent on music or TV.

cards.title: Describe a story you read recently
points: when and where you read it
who the main character is and what happens
and explain why you found it interesting
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: truyện ngắn/ sách "Cho tôi xin một vé đi tuổi thơ"? (bạn đổi thành truyện thật). Ở đây: một truyện ngắn về chú mèo hoang trên mạng. Dùng cốt truyện tự dựng để dễ nói.

notes.v: short story about an old man and a stray cat
last month, on the bus, in an app
lonely old man, feeds stray cat, cat visits daily, he gets ill, cat stays, neighbours help

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a short story that I read last month.

I read it on my phone on the bus to work, on a reading app. It was a short story and it took only about twenty minutes.

The main character is Mr Ba, an old man who lives alone in a small house. His children live far away, so he feels lonely. One day, he sees a stray cat in front of his door, and he gives it some food. After that, the cat comes every day, and they become friends. One winter, Mr Ba gets sick and cannot get up. The cat makes a lot of noise outside, so the neighbours come and find him. They take him to the hospital, and he gets well.

I found this story interesting because it was simple and touching. It shows that kindness comes back, and that even a small animal can bring happiness and help. I felt very warm after reading it.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a short story I read last month.

I came across it in a reading app on my phone during my commute, and it took only about twenty minutes to finish.

The protagonist is Mr Ba, an elderly man who lives alone in a small house, with his children living far away, so he's rather lonely. One day, he notices a stray cat outside his door and gives it some food. From then on, the cat turns up daily, and the two become companions. One winter, Mr Ba falls ill and can't get out of bed. The cat starts yowling outside, which alerts the neighbours, who find him and rush him to hospital, and he recovers.

I found it fascinating because it was simple yet deeply touching. It shows that kindness is repaid and that even a tiny animal can bring comfort and even save a life. It left me with a warm feeling for the rest of the day.

After finishing it, I phoned my grandmother, who lives alone in the village, to ask how she was. It made me realise that a simple story can remind us to care for the people we love.

p3.q: Why do most children like listening to stories before bedtime?
p3.a6: It helps them feel safe and relaxed, and it's a special time with their parents. Stories also stimulate their imagination, so they sleep better.
p3.a7: It makes them feel safe and relaxed, gives them special time with a parent and sparks their imagination, which helps them sleep.

p3.q: Is a good storyline important for a movie?
p3.a6: Yes, very. Special effects and famous actors are attractive, but without a good story, the audience will feel bored and forget it quickly.
p3.a7: Absolutely. Effects and stars attract attention, but without a compelling plot, audiences lose interest and forget the film.

p3.q: Why do children like hearing the same bedtime story?
p3.a6: They learn new words, imagination and moral lessons like honesty and kindness.
p3.a7: New vocabulary, imagination and moral values such as honesty and kindness.

cards.title: Describe a foreign country you would like to stay in or work in for a short period of time
points: how long you would like to stay
and explain why you would like to stay or work there
cards.note: Nước giả định: Nhật Bản (ngành IT, văn hoá làm việc, 6 tháng).

notes.v: IT industry, discipline, culture, safe, clean
work as tester in a Japanese company, learn work style, travel, try food

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about Japan. I would like to work there for a short time.

I want to go there for several reasons. Japan has a very developed IT industry, and Japanese people are known for working carefully and with discipline. For a tester, that is an excellent environment to learn. I also like Japanese culture. The country is clean and safe, and the scenery is beautiful.

I would like to work in a Japanese IT company as a tester. In my free time, I'd like to travel to cities like Tokyo and Kyoto, see the cherry blossoms in spring and try Japanese food such as sushi and ramen.

I'd like to stay there for about six months, because it's long enough to learn something, but not too long to be far from my family.

I think this experience would benefit me a lot. I could improve my professional skills and my English, and learn a more careful way to work. It would also make me more independent.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Japan, where I'd love to work for a short period.

There are several reasons I'm drawn to it. Japan has a highly advanced IT industry, and the Japanese are renowned for their meticulous, disciplined approach to work, which makes it an ideal environment for a tester to learn. I'm also fascinated by the culture, and the country is famously clean, safe and scenic.

I'd like to work for a Japanese IT company as a tester. In my spare time, I'd travel around Tokyo and Kyoto, see the cherry blossoms in spring and sample authentic sushi and ramen.

I'd aim to stay for about six months, which is long enough to gain real experience but not so long that I'd be away from my family for too long.

I'm convinced this would be hugely beneficial. I'd sharpen my professional skills and language abilities, learn a more rigorous work ethic and become much more independent and open-minded.

To prepare, I've started learning a few basic Japanese phrases alongside my English, and I follow some Japanese tech channels online. Even if the plan takes years to come true, working towards it already gives me direction.

vocab.m: tinh thần làm việc nghiêm ngặt

p3.q: Why do people go to other cities/countries to travel? Why do people like travelling?
p3.a6: They want to see new places, relax and learn about other cultures. Travelling also helps people forget daily stress and make memories.
p3.a7: To discover new places and cultures, unwind and escape daily stress, and create memories.

p3.q: What jobs can people do abroad for a short period of time?
p3.a6: They can work as English teachers, waiters, tour guides, seasonal farm workers, volunteers or freelancers. Some do short IT or business projects.
p3.a7: English teaching, hospitality, tour guiding, seasonal farm work, volunteering, freelancing, or short-term IT and business projects.

p3.q: Is it good that people now have an opportunity to work abroad?
p3.a6: Yes. People can earn more money, learn new skills and see the world. But some people go to work in bad conditions, so they should research carefully.
p3.a7: Yes, it means higher earnings, new skills and exposure, though people should research carefully to avoid poor conditions or scams.

p3.q: Why might some people not want to work in another country?
p3.a6: They miss their family and food. They are afraid of language problems, high living costs and loneliness. Some feel it's not safe.
p3.a7: Homesickness, language barriers, high living costs, loneliness and safety concerns.

p3.q: Advantages of working for an international company?
p3.a6: Higher salary, better training, chances to use English and travel, and meeting people from different cultures.
p3.a7: Higher pay, better training, opportunities to use English and travel, and exposure to diverse cultures.

p3.q: What personal skills are needed?
p3.a6: Good English, communication, teamwork, flexibility and cultural understanding. They also need time management skills.
p3.a7: Strong English and communication, teamwork, adaptability, cultural awareness and time management.

p3.q: Is practical experience more useful than qualifications?
