p3.a6: I think both are important. A degree helps you get the interview, but practical experience helps you do the job well. If I must choose, I think experience is slightly more useful.
p3.a7: Both matter: qualifications open the door, but experience determines how well you perform, so if forced to choose, I'd say experience carries slightly more weight.

cards.title: Describe a shopping mall
points: what you usually do there and how often you go
and explain whether you like it or not
cards.note: Trung tâm thương mại giả định: Aeon Mall Long Biên (Hà Nội).

notes.v: big, bright, modern, 3 floors, glass, wide halls
shop, eat, cinema, kids' play area, supermarket

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about Aeon Mall Long Bien, a big shopping mall in Hanoi.

It's located in Long Bien district. It takes me about an hour from my house by bus.

It's a very big and modern building with three floors. It has a lot of glass, wide halls and bright lights, so it looks clean and comfortable.

There are many things to do there. People can buy clothes, shoes, skincare products and electronics. There's a big supermarket and a food court with many kinds of food. There is also a cinema and a children's play area. Many families come at the weekend.

I go there once or twice a month, usually on Saturday with my friends or my family.

I like this mall because it has everything in one place. It's cool in summer with air conditioning, and it has a big parking area. Also, the prices are reasonable and there are often sales, so I like it very much.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Aeon Mall Long Bien, a huge shopping centre in Hanoi.

It's in Long Bien district, about an hour from my home by bus.

It's a spacious, contemporary three-storey building with plenty of glass, wide walkways and bright lighting, which gives it a clean, airy feel.

There's something for everyone. You can shop for clothes, shoes, skincare and electronics, do your grocery shopping at the big supermarket, or eat at the food court, which offers a wide range of cuisines. There's also a cinema and a play area for children, so it's packed with families at weekends.

I visit once or twice a month, usually on Saturdays with friends or family.

What I like most is its convenience, as everything is under one roof. It's pleasantly air-conditioned in the summer heat, has ample parking, and the prices are reasonable, with frequent promotions. It's an ideal place to spend a relaxing weekend.

The only downside is that it gets very crowded on Sundays, so I try to go early in the morning or on a weekday evening. Even so, it remains my go-to place when I want to relax and treat myself a little.

p3.q: Why do people buy things they don't need?
p3.a6: Because of sales, advertising and following trends. Some people shop when they feel stressed or bored, and they feel happy for a short time.
p3.a7: Discounts, advertising and trends tempt them, and some shop to relieve stress or boredom, which gives a brief mood boost.

p3.q: Do you think people buy a lot of things they don't need?
p3.a6: They can make a list, set a budget, and wait one day before buying something expensive.
p3.a7: By writing a list, setting a budget and applying a "wait 24 hours" rule for costly items.

cards.title: Describe a person who encouraged you to protect nature
points: and explain how he/she encouraged you to protect nature
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: bố bạn (người bạn giả định đã dùng ở các file trước: bố thích lịch sử, đạp xe), hoặc cô giáo. Bài này: bố đi nhặt rác và trồng cây.

notes.v: collects rubbish in lane, plants trees, saves water, reuses
took me along, explained, example, small tasks

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my father, who encouraged me to protect nature.

He's fifty-five years old and I've known him all my life. Of course, he's my dad.

My father does many small things to protect nature. In the morning, he often picks up rubbish in the lane near our house. He plants trees in front of the house and in our neighbourhood. He also saves water, for example he uses the water from washing rice to water plants. He doesn't throw away things that can be reused.

He encouraged me in a gentle way. When I was a child, he took me with him to plant trees and clean the lane. He explained that if we protect nature, nature will protect us. He never forced me. He just did the things himself every day, so I followed.

I feel proud of my father and thankful to him. Because of him, I have the habit of sorting rubbish, saving water and not using too much plastic.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my father, who instilled in me a love and respect for nature.

He's fifty-five, and, being my dad, I've known him all my life.

He does plenty of small but meaningful things for the environment. Every morning he picks up litter in our lane, he's planted trees outside our house and around the neighbourhood, and he's very thrifty with water, for instance reusing the water from rinsing rice to water the plants. He also hates throwing away anything that can be reused.

His way of encouraging me was gentle. When I was little, he'd take me along to plant trees and clean the lane, explaining that if we look after nature, it will look after us. He never lectured or forced me; he simply led by example every day, and I naturally followed.

I'm enormously proud of him and grateful to him. Thanks to his influence, I sort my rubbish, save water and avoid unnecessary plastic.

Now, when I see a plastic bag on the street, I pick it up without thinking, exactly as he does. I hope that one day I can pass the same habit on to my own children.

p3.q: How can parents teach their children to protect nature?
p3.a6: They should be a good example, like not throwing rubbish and saving water. They can also take children to the countryside and plant trees with them.
p3.a7: By setting an example, such as not littering and saving water, and by involving children in activities like planting trees and trips to the countryside.

p3.q: Should schools teach children to get close to nature?
p3.a6: Yes. Children can have lessons outdoors, visit gardens or national parks, and join programmes for planting trees. They will love and protect nature more.
p3.a7: Yes, through outdoor lessons, visits to gardens and national parks and tree-planting projects, so that they come to love and protect nature.

p3.q: Should there be laws to protect nature?
p3.a6: Both. Governments make laws and big projects, but individuals' daily habits are also important.
p3.a7: Both: governments set laws and fund large projects, while individuals' daily habits make a real difference.

cards.title: Describe a bicycle, motorcycle or car trip you would like to go on
points: where you would like to go
and explain why you would like to go on this trip
cards.note: Chuyến đi giả định: đi xe máy từ Hà Nội lên Hà Giang (Mã Pì Lèng) với bạn bè.

notes.v: ride mountain roads, Ma Pi Leng pass, buckwheat flowers, homestay, local food

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a motorbike trip that I want to take to Ha Giang, in the north of Vietnam.

I would like to go by motorbike, because it gives us freedom. We can stop anywhere to take photos. I would rent a motorbike at Ha Giang city, and my friend would drive, because the mountain road is dangerous and I'm not very good at riding.

I would like to go with three close friends. We would go for four days and three nights.

During the trip, we'd ride along the Ma Pi Leng Pass, visit the small villages, and see the beautiful flower fields. We'd stay at local homestays, eat local food and talk with the people there. At night, we'd sit around the fire and look at the stars.

I want to take this trip because the scenery is amazing, and I want an adventure to escape my busy daily life. I think it'd also make our friendship stronger.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a motorbike trip to Ha Giang in northern Vietnam, which has been on my bucket list for ages.

I'd go by motorbike because it gives you complete freedom. You can stop wherever you like to take photos. We'd rent bikes in Ha Giang city, and as the mountain roads are treacherous and I'm not an experienced rider, I'd let my more skilled friend take the handlebars.

I'd go with three close friends for four days and three nights.

On the trip, we'd cruise along the spectacular Ma Pi Leng Pass, pass through small ethnic minority villages and admire the fields of wildflowers. We'd stay in local homestays, taste regional dishes and chat with local people, and at night we'd sit by a fire gazing at the stars.

I'm drawn to this trip because the scenery is breathtaking and I crave an adventure that takes me far from my hectic routine. I'm sure it would also strengthen the bond between us.

Of course, safety would come first, so we'd wear helmets, check the weather and avoid riding at night. I'm already collecting tips from travel blogs, and the more I read, the more excited I become.

p3.q: Which vehicle is popular in your country? Are bicycles and motorbikes popular?
p3.a6: Motorbikes are the most popular in Vietnam because they are cheap, flexible and good for narrow roads. Cars are getting more popular, but bicycles are only used by students, old people and for exercise.
p3.a7: Motorbikes dominate, being cheap, flexible and ideal for narrow streets. Cars are on the rise, while bicycles are mostly used by students, older people and for exercise.

p3.q: Does air pollution come mostly from vehicles? Do people need to change transport drastically?
p3.a6: Vehicles are one of the main reasons, along with factories and burning rubbish. I think people need to change, for example use buses, electric motorbikes and cars.
p3.a7: Vehicles are a major source, alongside factories and waste burning. A shift to public transport and electric vehicles is needed.

p3.q: How are transport systems in urban and rural areas different? How do people travel?
p3.a6: In cities, there are buses, taxis, metro and many cars. In the countryside, people mostly use motorbikes, bicycles and sometimes walk, because there is little public transport.
p3.a7: Cities have buses, taxis, ride-hailing and the metro, whereas rural areas rely on motorbikes, bicycles and walking, with scant public transport.

p3.q: What is the best thing about public transport in your area?
p3.a6: The bus is cheap and I don't need to worry about parking or traffic. I can also relax or listen to English on the bus.
p3.a7: It's cheap, I don't have to deal with parking or stress, and I can use the journey to relax or practise English.

p3.q: More people want to buy cars these days?
p3.a6: Yes. Income is higher, and people want comfort and safety. Cars are also a symbol of success. But traffic jams and parking are big problems.
p3.a7: Yes. Rising incomes and a desire for comfort and status are behind it, but congestion and parking are worsening.

p3.q: Do city planners consider the needs of pedestrians enough?
p3.a6: No, not enough. In Hanoi, many pavements are used for parking or selling, so people have to walk on the road. We need wider and safer pavements and crossings.
p3.a7: Not really. In Hanoi, pavements are often occupied by parked bikes and street stalls, forcing pedestrians onto the road.

p3.q: What impact can an inadequate transport system have on a country?
p3.a6: It causes traffic jams, accidents, pollution and wastes time. It also slows down the economy because goods are late.
p3.a7: It leads to congestion, accidents and pollution, wastes time and hampers the economy by delaying goods and workers.

cards.title: Describe a city that you have been to and enjoy visiting
points: what the city is and where it is
and explain why you enjoy visiting it
cards.note: Thành phố giả định: Huế hoặc Đà Nẵng (đã dùng); bài này: Đà Lạt.

notes.v: visit flower gardens, Xuan Huong Lake, coffee, night market, strawberries

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about Da Lat, a city that I enjoy visiting.

It's located in the Central Highlands of Vietnam, in Lam Dong province, about 1,500 metres above the sea. It takes about one hour by plane from Hanoi to Lien Khuong airport, then one hour by car.

I went there last spring, for three days, with my friends.

We did many things. We visited flower gardens, took a walk around Xuan Huong Lake and drank coffee in small cafés on the hills. In the evening, we went to the night market, ate hot grilled rice paper, and drank warm soy milk. We also picked fresh strawberries at a farm.

I enjoy visiting this city for several reasons. The weather is cool all year, which is great after the hot summer in Hanoi. The city is quiet and romantic, with many pine trees and flowers. The people are friendly and the food is cheap. It's a perfect place to relax.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Da Lat, a city I always enjoy visiting.

It's in the Central Highlands, in Lam Dong province, perched at roughly 1,500 metres above sea level. From Hanoi, it's about an hour's flight to Lien Khuong airport, followed by an hour's drive.

I last went in spring, for three days, with some friends.

We packed in plenty of activities. We wandered through flower gardens, strolled around Xuan Huong Lake and lingered in cosy hillside cafés. In the evenings, we hit the night market, tucking into grilled rice paper and sipping warm soy milk. We even picked strawberries at a local farm.

What I love about Da Lat is, firstly, the cool, spring-like climate all year round, which is a blessed relief from Hanoi's sweltering summers. Secondly, the city is serene and romantic, with pine forests and flowers everywhere. Finally, the locals are welcoming and everything is reasonably priced. It's the ideal place to unwind.

I came home with a bag of dried fruit and a few photos that I still use as my phone wallpaper. I'd happily go back every year, and I tell all my friends that Da Lat is the best remedy for a stressful year.

p3.q: Difference between living in the countryside and the city? Which do you prefer?
p3.a6: The city has more jobs, schools and entertainment, but it's crowded, noisy and polluted. The countryside is quiet, fresh and friendly, but has fewer services. I prefer the city for work, but I want a quiet place later.
p3.a7: Cities offer jobs, schools and entertainment but are crowded and polluted, whereas the countryside is peaceful and fresh with fewer services. I prefer the city for now, because of my career.

p3.q: Is it good for older people to live in big cities? Who benefits more from cities?
p3.a6: Not really. The city is noisy and polluted, and life is fast and expensive. But hospitals are good. Young people benefit more because there are more jobs and entertainment.
p3.a7: Not ideal: noise, pollution and a fast pace, although healthcare is better. Young people benefit more thanks to jobs and entertainment.

p3.q: Will the entire population move to cities? Will people live in the countryside in the future?
p3.a6: No. We still need farmers and food, and some people like the quiet life. With the internet, some people can work from the countryside, so more people may even return.
p3.a7: No, as we'll always need agriculture, and remote work may even lead some people back to rural areas.

p3.q: Are people in the countryside friendlier?
p3.a6: Generally yes, because everyone knows each other and they help each other. In big cities, people are busy and often don't know their neighbours.
p3.a7: Generally, yes, since communities are tight-knit, whereas city dwellers are busy and often don't know their neighbours.

p3.q: What should the government do to improve citizens' safety?
p3.a6: More police, more cameras and street lights, and better laws. It should also improve traffic safety and teach people about safety.
p3.a7: Deploy more police, install cameras and street lighting, enforce traffic laws and run safety education.

p3.q: What changes usually happen in cities? Any changes in your city?
p3.a6: New roads, buildings and shops appear. In Hanoi, there are metro lines, new apartment buildings and more traffic. Many old houses are replaced.
p3.a7: New roads, buildings and shops. In Hanoi, metro lines and apartment towers have appeared, though traffic has worsened and old houses are disappearing.

p3.q: Why do tourists choose certain cities? Modern or historical? Are tourist cities good for living?
p3.a6: They choose cities for culture, food, scenery or shopping. Historical cities are more special, but modern cities are fun too. Tourist cities are not always good to live in, because they are crowded and expensive.
p3.a7: For culture, food, scenery or shopping. Historic cities are more distinctive, though modern ones are fun. Tourist hotspots aren't necessarily good to live in, being crowded and costly.

p3.q: Why do many people choose to live in cities?
p3.a6: For jobs, higher salary, better education and healthcare, and more entertainment.
p3.a7: For jobs, higher salaries, better education and healthcare, and a livelier social scene.

p3.q: Do cities lose their individual character as they grow?
p3.a6: I agree. When cities grow, they build similar modern buildings and malls, and old streets disappear. Many cities start to look the same.
p3.a7: I agree to some extent. As cities expand, similar malls and towers replace old streets, so many start to look alike.

cards.title: Describe a music event that you didn't enjoy
points: when and where it was held
and explain why you didn't enjoy it
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: đêm nhạc EDM/ rock ngoài trời quá ồn, bạn bè rủ đi.

notes.v: last autumn, a park in Hanoi
too loud, crowded, not my style, long queue, hot

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about an outdoor music festival that I went to last autumn.

It took place in a big park in Hanoi, on Saturday night. I went there with three friends, because they love EDM music and invited me.

I didn't enjoy it for several reasons. First, the music was too loud, and my ears hurt. I couldn't talk to my friends at all. Second, it was very crowded. There were a lot of people jumping and pushing, and I felt uncomfortable. Third, EDM is not my style. I prefer slow and soft songs like ballads. We also waited in a long line for food and drinks, and it was hot.

I felt tired and a little regretful, because I paid for an expensive ticket. After about one hour, I told my friends I had a headache and I went home.

I learned that I should choose events that match my taste.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about an outdoor music festival I attended last autumn, which I really didn't enjoy.

It was held in a large park in Hanoi on a Saturday night, and I went along with three friends who are crazy about EDM and had persuaded me to join.

There were several reasons it wasn't for me. Firstly, the music was deafening, my ears were ringing and I couldn't hold a conversation with my friends. Secondly, it was packed, with people jumping and shoving, which made me feel claustrophobic. Thirdly, EDM simply isn't my cup of tea; I'm more of a ballad person. On top of that, we queued for ages for food and drinks, in the heat.

I felt drained and rather regretful, especially as I'd paid a hefty ticket price. After an hour, I made an excuse about a headache and went home.

It taught me to choose events that suit my taste instead of just following the crowd.

My friends were a little disappointed that I left early, but they understood, and we met up for a quiet drink the next weekend. Now I always check the music style and the crowd size before buying tickets.

p3.q: What kind of music events do people like today?
p3.a6: Young people like music festivals, live concerts and EDM parties. Many people also like live shows of famous Vietnamese and Korean singers.
p3.a7: Music festivals, live concerts and EDM nights are popular with the young, and shows by Vietnamese and K-pop stars sell out fast.

p3.q: What do people enjoy about large music events?
p3.a6: They can see their idols in person, feel the atmosphere and sing together with thousands of people. It's also a chance to go out with friends.
p3.a7: Seeing idols in person, the electric atmosphere, singing along with thousands of others, and a fun outing with friends.

p3.q: Why might younger and older people not enjoy the same events?
p3.a6: They have different tastes. Young people like loud and fast music, while older people prefer calm, traditional music. Older people also don't like crowds and noise.
p3.a7: Their tastes differ: the young like loud, fast music, while older people prefer calmer, traditional styles and dislike crowds and noise.

p3.q: Should children have music lessons at school?
p3.a6: Yes, music helps them to relax, develop their brain and express themselves. They can also find their talent.
p3.a7: Yes, music aids brain development, self-expression and relaxation, and may reveal hidden talents.

p3.q: Why is music often played during physical exercise?
p3.a6: Music gives energy and keeps people motivated. A fast rhythm helps them keep the pace and forget they're tired.
p3.a7: It energises and motivates people, and a fast rhythm helps them keep pace and take their minds off fatigue.

p3.q: Is playing music in shops an effective way to sell more?
p3.a6: I agree. Nice music makes customers feel relaxed, so they stay longer and buy more. Different music can also suit different shops, like fast music in a clothes shop for young people.
p3.a7: I agree. Pleasant music relaxes shoppers so they linger and spend more, and the style can be matched to the clientele.

cards.title: Describe one of your friends who learned something new, not from a teacher
points: and explain how you feel about it
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: bạn Hung, tự học guitar/ làm bánh. Bài này: tự học chơi guitar qua YouTube.

notes.v: wanted to play for girlfriend's birthday / relax

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my close friend, Hung. He is a very funny person, and we've known each other for many years.

Last year, he learned to play the guitar by himself. He never took any class and he didn't have a teacher.

He learned from YouTube videos and a guitar app. Every evening, he practised for about thirty minutes, even when he was tired. At first, his fingers hurt, and the sound was terrible. But he didn't give up. When he had a problem, he asked friends who can play.

He wanted to learn it because he wanted to play a song at his friend's birthday party. He also thought that the guitar helped him relax after work.

After six months, he could play several songs well, and he really played at that party. Everyone was surprised and happy.

I admire Hung a lot. He showed me that we can learn anything by ourselves if we are patient. He also motivates me to study English every day.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my close friend Hung, who's hilarious and whom I've known for many years.

Last year, he taught himself the guitar, without any classes or a teacher.

He relied on YouTube tutorials and a guitar app. Every evening, he practised for about thirty minutes, even when he was exhausted. At first, his fingertips were sore and everything sounded awful, but he persevered. Whenever he got stuck, he asked friends who play for tips.

His motivation was to perform a song at a friend's birthday party, and also because he found playing a great way to unwind after work.

Six months later, he could play several songs fluently, and he performed at the party as planned. Everyone was blown away.

I really admire him. He proved that with patience, you can master almost anything on your own, and he inspires me to keep up my daily English practice.

He recently uploaded a short video of himself playing on social media, and it got hundreds of likes. Seeing how far he has come without any formal lessons makes me believe that curiosity and discipline are the best teachers.

p3.q: Is it necessary to keep learning after graduating? Is it important to learn new skills all life long?
p3.a6: Yes, very. Technology changes fast, so if we stop learning, we are left behind. Learning also keeps our brain active.
p3.a7: Yes. Technology evolves rapidly, so those who stop learning fall behind, and learning keeps the mind sharp.

p3.q: Should teachers make learning fun? Does a good teacher make learning more interesting?
p3.a6: Yes. Students remember better and have more motivation when lessons are fun. A good teacher uses games, examples and stories.
p3.a7: Yes, fun lessons boost motivation and retention, and a good teacher brings them alive through games, examples and stories.

p3.q: Are there too many subjects for students?
p3.a6: In Vietnam, I think yes. Students are under pressure with many subjects and exams, so they have little time for hobbies. Some subjects are not very useful.
p3.a7: In Vietnam, arguably yes. Students juggle too many subjects and exams, leaving little time for hobbies, and some content isn't practical.

p3.q: Focus on a few subjects or learn many? Is learning many subjects good for work?
p3.a6: It's better to focus on a few subjects at one time to learn deeply. But knowing many subjects helps in work, because I can solve problems in more ways. For example, IT and English help me together.
p3.a7: Focusing on a few at a time gives depth, but broad knowledge is valuable at work, as it lets you approach problems from several angles; for me, IT and English complement each other.

p3.q: Should enterprises provide training for employees?
p3.a6: Yes. It improves employees' skills and productivity, and makes them loyal. It's good for both sides.
p3.a7: Yes. It upgrades skills, boosts productivity and increases loyalty, which benefits both sides.

p3.q: Is it good for older adults and retired people to continue learning?
p3.a6: Yes. It keeps their brain healthy, gives them a hobby and keeps them from being lonely. Retired people can even go back to school if they want.
p3.a7: Yes, it keeps their minds healthy, gives them purpose and social contact, and returning to education can be fulfilling for retirees.

p3.q: What can children learn from parents?
p3.a6: They learn behaviour, manners, honesty and life skills like cooking and managing money.
p3.a7: Manners, honesty and values, plus practical skills such as cooking and handling money.

p3.q: What subjects do children often enjoy?
p3.a6: They like art, music, PE and English because they are creative and fun, and they like science experiments.
p3.a7: Art, music, PE and English, which are creative and active, and hands-on science experiments.

p3.q: Are some children well-behaved because of their parents?
p3.a6: Yes. Children copy their parents. If parents are polite and responsible, children will be the same.
p3.a7: Yes, children imitate their parents, so polite, responsible parents tend to raise well-behaved kids.

p3.q: Benefits for adults of returning to study?
p3.a6: They can get new skills, a better job and a higher salary. They are also more confident and have a clear goal.
p3.a7: New skills, better job prospects and higher pay, plus more confidence and a clearer purpose.

cards.title: Describe a person who solved a problem in a smart way
points: and explain why you think it was a smart way
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: anh đồng nghiệp xử lý lỗi hệ thống bằng cách viết script tự động (hợp nghề IT).

notes.v: repeated manual tests, 2 days each release, many errors
wrote automation script, ran at night, report in the morning

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about Mr Duc, a senior colleague in my company. He is a tester and a developer.

Last year, our team had a big problem. For every new version of the software, we had to test the same functions by hand. It took two days, and people often made mistakes because they were tired. The team was always stressed.

Mr Duc solved this problem in a smart way. He wrote a small automation program that tested the main functions by itself. He set it to run at night, and in the morning, everyone got a report with the results. He did it in just one week, and used free tools.

I think the solution was smart because it saved a lot of time and money. It also made fewer mistakes and the team could focus on more important tasks.

I really admire him. I feel lucky to work with him, and I want to learn how to write automation scripts like him.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Mr Duc, a senior colleague of mine who works as both a tester and developer.

Last year, our team faced a persistent problem. For every release, we had to manually re-test the same functions, which took two days, and fatigue led to frequent mistakes. Everyone was permanently stressed.

Mr Duc came up with a really clever solution. He wrote a lightweight automation program that tested the core functions on its own. He scheduled it to run overnight, so that every morning we'd find a detailed report waiting. He built it within a week using free tools.

I consider it smart because it saved enormous amounts of time and money, and it eliminated human error. It also freed the team to concentrate on more valuable tasks, such as exploring new scenarios.

I really admire his creativity and I feel fortunate to work with him. He's inspired me to learn automation scripting myself.

What impressed me most was that he shared his script with the whole team and patiently explained how it worked. That generosity, together with his clever thinking, is exactly the kind of colleague I'd like to become.

p3.q: Are children born smart or do they learn? Why are some children more intelligent?
p3.a6: I think it's both. Some children are born with a good brain, but nutrition, family and learning environment are also very important. Children who read a lot and are encouraged by parents often become smarter.
p3.a7: A bit of both. Genes matter, but nutrition, family support and learning environment are just as influential; children who are encouraged and read a lot often thrive.

p3.q: How do children become smart at school? How important are schools?
p3.a6: At school, they learn knowledge, how to think and how to work in a group. Good teachers and activities like debates and experiments help them. School is important, but family and self-study are also necessary.
p3.a7: Schools teach knowledge, critical thinking and teamwork through debates and experiments, and good teachers make a big difference, though family and self-study matter too.

p3.q: Why are some people well-rounded and others good at only one thing?
p3.a6: Some people have many interests and chances to try different things. Others focus only on one area, because they like it or have talent. A person may be very good at maths but poor at communication.
p3.a7: Some have varied interests and opportunities, while others devote themselves to one passion or talent; someone brilliant at maths may struggle with communication.

p3.q: Why does society need people with different types of intelligence?
p3.a6: Because society needs many jobs: doctors, engineers, artists and farmers. Each type of intelligence is useful, and together they make society develop.
p3.a7: Because society needs doctors, engineers, artists and farmers alike, and diverse talents together drive progress.

p3.q: Are very clever children usually happy?
p3.a6: Not always. They may feel pressure from high expectations, or find it hard to make friends. Some also feel lonely.
p3.a7: Not necessarily. They may feel pressured by high expectations or isolated from peers.

p3.q: Can people become good at anything if they try hard enough?
p3.a6: To some extent, yes. Practice can improve most skills. But talent also matters, and nobody can be perfect at everything.
p3.a7: To a large extent, since practice improves most skills, but natural aptitude counts too, and no one can excel at everything.

cards.title: Describe a person who often helps others
points: and explain why you think he/she often helps others
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: bà Lan, hàng xóm (nhân vật đã dùng ở các file trước).

notes.v: live next door, since I was a child
free rice/meals for poor, looks after kids, takes old people to hospital, donates
she was poor, wants to share, feels happy

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about Mrs Lan, who often helps other people. She's about sixty years old.

I know her because she is my neighbour. She has lived next door for more than twenty years, since I was a child.

She helps people in many ways. Every month, she cooks free meals for poor people and sells almost nothing in her small shop for them. When parents are busy, she looks after the neighbours' children after school. She also takes old neighbours to the hospital when they are sick. When there is a flood or a storm in the countryside, she collects clothes and money to send there.

She likes helping people because she had a difficult life when she was young, so she understands the feelings of the poor. She says helping others makes her happy.

I respect her very much. She is a good example for me, and I try to be kind to the people around me.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Mrs Lan, a neighbour of mine in her sixties who's always helping others.

I've known her since I was a child, as she's lived next door for over twenty years.

She helps in all sorts of ways. Every month, she cooks free meals for people in need. When neighbours are at work, she kindly looks after their children after school, and she takes elderly neighbours to hospital when they're unwell. Whenever floods or storms hit the countryside, she collects clothes and donations to send there.

The reason she's so generous is that she had a hard life when she was young, so she empathises deeply with people who are struggling. She says that helping others is what gives her the greatest happiness.

I hold her in the highest regard. She's a role model for me, and I try to follow her example by being kind to those around me.

When my father was ill a few years ago, she brought us soup every day without being asked. I'll never forget that, and I hope that one day I can help others with the same sincerity.

p3.q: How can children help their parents? Should parents teach children to help with housework?
p3.a6: Children can wash dishes, clean the house, cook simple meals and take care of younger siblings. Parents should teach them, because it helps them be independent and responsible, and everyone in the family should share the work.
p3.a7: By washing dishes, tidying up, cooking simple meals and minding younger siblings. Parents should teach this early, as it builds independence and responsibility, and housework should be shared by everyone.

p3.q: Should children be taught to help others? What makes them help each other at school?
p3.a6: Yes, it teaches kindness and teamwork. At school, children help each other because they're friends, teachers encourage them, or they want praise.
p3.a7: Yes, it cultivates kindness and teamwork. At school, they help one another out of friendship, teacher encouragement or a desire for praise.

p3.q: Should students do community service? Do they volunteer? Why do people volunteer?
p3.a6: Yes. They learn responsibility and skills, and they also help society. In Vietnam, many students join the "Green Summer" volunteer campaign. People volunteer because they want to help others and feel meaningful.
p3.a7: Yes, it builds responsibility and skills while benefiting society. Many Vietnamese students join the "Green Summer" campaign. People volunteer to help others and find purpose.

p3.q: What help do people need when looking for a new job? Who should they ask: colleagues or family?
p3.a6: They need advice for their CV, interview tips and job information. They can ask both. Family gives emotional support, and colleagues know about the work and can introduce jobs.
p3.a7: Advice on CVs and interviews and information about openings. Both: family gives emotional support, while colleagues offer industry insight and referrals.

p3.q: What machines help people at home?
p3.a6: Washing machines, rice cookers, vacuum cleaners, dishwashers, air fryers and robot vacuum cleaners.
p3.a7: Washing machines, rice cookers, vacuum cleaners, dishwashers, air fryers and robot vacuums.

p3.q: Is it necessary for employees to ask their manager for help?
p3.a6: Yes, when they have a problem they can't solve. Asking early saves time and avoids bigger mistakes. A good manager is happy to help.
p3.a7: Yes, when stuck. Asking early saves time and prevents bigger mistakes, and good managers welcome it.

p3.q: Will many people lose their jobs because of AI?
p3.a6: I think some people will, especially in simple and repeated jobs. But new jobs will also appear. We need to learn new skills to work with AI.
p3.a7: Some will, particularly in routine jobs, but new roles will emerge, so we must upskill and learn to work alongside AI.

cards.title: Describe a time you needed to use your imagination
points: why you needed to use your imagination
and explain how you felt about it
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: kể truyện cho em họ nhỏ nghe/ trang trí phòng. Bài này: bịa chuyện kể cho em họ 5 tuổi không chịu ngủ.

notes.v: a rabbit astronaut who flies to the moon to find carrots
acted voices, drew pictures on phone

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a time I needed to use my imagination. It was last Tet at my grandmother's house.

My little cousin is five years old, and one night she couldn't sleep. She asked me to tell her a story, but I didn't have any story book. I only had my phone, and the internet was slow in the village.

So I had to make up a story by myself. I imagined a small rabbit who wanted to be an astronaut. He flew to the moon in a carrot-shaped rocket to find the biggest carrot in the universe. On the moon, he met a friendly robot and they became friends.

I changed my voice for each character and showed some pictures on my phone. She laughed a lot, and she listened until she fell asleep.

I felt happy and a bit surprised, because I didn't know I could be so creative. It was a very nice moment, and now she asks for a new story each time I visit.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a time I had to draw on my imagination, which was last Tet at my grandmother's house.

My five-year-old cousin couldn't sleep one night and begged me to tell her a story. The trouble was that I had no storybook, and the village internet was too slow to look anything up.

So I had to improvise a story on the spot. I dreamed up a little rabbit who longed to be an astronaut. He blasted off to the moon in a carrot-shaped rocket in search of the biggest carrot in the universe, and on the moon, he befriended a kind-hearted robot.

I did different voices for each character and showed a few pictures on my phone. She giggled throughout and eventually drifted off.

I felt delighted, and a little surprised at how inventive I could be. It was a magical moment, and these days she demands a new story every time I visit.

I realised that I rarely use my imagination at work, where everything has to be precise and logical. That night reminded me how refreshing it is to be playful, and I now try to draw or write a little story whenever I can.

p3.q: Is imagination important to children? Should teachers encourage it?
p3.a6: Yes, very. Imagination helps children to be creative, solve problems and learn more easily. Teachers should encourage them by asking open questions, letting them draw and tell stories.
p3.a7: Very. It fosters creativity and problem-solving and makes learning easier. Teachers can encourage it with open-ended questions, drawing and storytelling.

p3.q: What subjects help imagination?
p3.a6: Art, music, literature and even science, because scientists need to imagine new ideas. Creative writing is also helpful.
p3.a7: Art, music, literature and creative writing, and science too, since discoveries start with imagining possibilities.

p3.q: What jobs require imagination?
p3.a6: Designers, writers, film directors, architects, game developers and advertisers. Even testers need it to think of unusual situations.
p3.a7: Designers, writers, directors, architects, game developers and advertisers, and even testers, who must imagine unusual scenarios that could break a system.

p3.q: Is imagination essential for scientists?
p3.a6: Yes. Scientists must imagine something that doesn't exist yet and then test it. Many great discoveries began with imagination, like Einstein's thought experiments.
p3.a7: Absolutely. Scientists must first imagine what doesn't yet exist; Einstein's thought experiments are a famous example.

p3.q: Which requires more imagination: reading or watching cartoons?
p3.a6: Reading. When we read, we must create the pictures in our mind. In cartoons, everything is already shown.
p3.a7: Reading, as we must picture the scenes ourselves, whereas cartoons present everything ready-made.

p3.q: What games require or develop imagination?
p3.a6: Role-play games like playing doctor, building with Lego, drawing, puzzles and story-telling games. Some video games with open worlds also help.
p3.a7: Role-play, building with Lego, drawing, puzzles and storytelling games, plus open-world video games.

p3.q: How can teachers encourage imagination?
p3.a6: They can give creative projects, let students make their own stories and not punish "wrong" answers. They should praise new ideas.
p3.a7: Through creative projects, letting students write their own stories, not penalising unusual answers and praising original ideas.

p3.q: What's the relationship between creativity and imagination?
p3.a6: Imagination is thinking of new ideas in the mind, and creativity is using these ideas to make something real. Imagination is the beginning of creativity.
p3.a7: Imagination is conceiving new ideas; creativity is turning them into something tangible, so imagination is the seed of creativity.

p3.q: Can adults have lots of imagination?
p3.a6: Yes, of course. Many writers, artists and engineers are adults. But adults are often busy and practical, so they use imagination less.
p3.a7: Of course; writers, artists and engineers prove it, although adults often become too practical and use it less.

cards.title: Describe a movie you watched and enjoyed recently
points: when and where you watched it
who you watched it with and what it was about
and explain why you enjoyed it
cards.note: Phim giả định (không dùng tên thật): một phim Việt về gia đình, xem ở rạp cùng em trai. Bạn thay bằng phim thật.

notes.v: two weeks ago, cinema in Hanoi
family reunion at Tet, misunderstanding, love

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a Vietnamese family movie that I watched two weeks ago.

I watched it at a cinema in Hanoi, on Saturday evening, with my younger brother. We bought a big popcorn and had a good time.

The movie is about a big family who gather together at Tet. At first, there are many small problems among the family members, because they don't understand each other. The grandmother is ill, and the children are too busy. Then, because of one special event, everyone starts to talk and listen, and they understand how much they love each other.

I enjoyed it for several reasons. It was funny, and I laughed a lot. But it was also touching, and at the end I almost cried. The story is very familiar to me because it is like my own family. The actors also did very well.

After the movie, my brother and I called our grandmother and said we would visit her soon.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a Vietnamese family film I watched two weeks ago and thoroughly enjoyed.

I saw it at a cinema in Hanoi on Saturday evening with my younger brother, and we shared a large bucket of popcorn.

The film revolves around a big family reunion at Tet. Initially, there are lots of small tensions because the members don't really understand each other: the grandmother is unwell and her children are too busy to notice. But a pivotal event brings everyone together, and they finally start to talk and listen, realising how much they care for one another.

I loved it for several reasons. It was genuinely funny, but also deeply moving, and I nearly cried at the end. The story felt so relatable, rather like my own family. And the cast delivered convincing performances.

Afterwards, my brother and I phoned our grandmother and promised to visit her soon, which shows how powerful the film was.

I'd recommend it to anyone who wants to laugh and cry in the same two hours, preferably with their family. It's a good reminder that even busy people should make time to sit down together.

p3.q: What kinds of movies are successful? What factors make a successful movie?
p3.a6: Comedy, family dramas and action movies are successful in Vietnam. A good movie needs a good story, good actors, nice pictures and music, and good marketing.
p3.a7: Comedies, family dramas and action films do well in Vietnam. Success depends on a strong story, good acting, visuals, music and effective marketing.

p3.q: Do Vietnamese prefer domestic or foreign movies?
p3.a6: Both. Young people like Hollywood and Korean movies. But Vietnamese movies are getting better and some became big hits, especially at Tet.
p3.a7: Both. Young people like Hollywood and Korean films, but Vietnamese productions are improving, with some huge hits at Tet.

p3.q: Do only famous directors/actors make good movies? Are famous actors more likely to make a film successful?
p3.a6: No, not only them. Famous names attract audiences, but a weak story can still fail. There are many good movies with new directors and unknown actors.
p3.a7: Not exclusively. Big names draw crowds, but a weak story still flops, and plenty of excellent films come from new directors and unknown actors.

p3.q: Why do people prefer the cinema? Do people still go? Where do they watch? Home or cinema?
p3.a6: The cinema has a big screen, great sound and a special atmosphere. Many young people still go on dates or with friends. But more and more people watch at home on Netflix or phones, because it's cheaper and convenient.
p3.a7: Cinemas offer a big screen, immersive sound and atmosphere, and still attract couples and friends. But streaming at home is cheaper and more convenient, so it's growing.

p3.q: Why don't some people enjoy watching movies?
p3.a6: They find them boring or too long, they prefer other hobbies, or they don't have time. Some don't like sitting in silence for two hours.
p3.a7: They find them boring or too long, prefer other hobbies or lack time.

p3.q: What qualities do actors need? Which is more important: acting skills or appearance?
p3.a6: They need imagination, confidence, a good memory and hard work. I think acting skills are more important. Appearance can attract people at first, but only skills keep them.
p3.a7: Imagination, confidence, a good memory and dedication. Acting skills matter more; looks may attract attention, but only talent sustains a career.

p3.q: Is being an actor a difficult job?
p3.a6: Yes, I agree. They work long hours, repeat scenes many times and have no private life when famous. It's also an unstable job.
p3.a7: I agree. They endure long hours, repeated takes, little privacy when famous and an unstable career.

cards.title: Describe a programme you like to watch
points: what it is about and how often you watch it
and explain why you like watching it
cards.note: Chương trình giả định: kênh YouTube/ chương trình về công nghệ và du lịch ẩm thực. Bài này: chương trình tài liệu về du lịch/ẩm thực.

notes.v: YouTube / Netflix on phone, at home
host travels, local food, culture, people

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a travel and food documentary series that I like to watch.

I usually watch it at home, on my phone or my laptop. I find it on YouTube and Netflix. I often watch it in the evening, after dinner, or before bed.

The programme is about a host who travels to different countries. In each episode, he visits a city, eats local food and talks with local people. We can see the markets, the street food and the daily life there. He also explains the history of the dishes.

I watch about two or three episodes a week.

I like it for several reasons. First, it's relaxing after a long day at work. Second, I can learn about different cultures without travelling. Third, the pictures are beautiful, and it has English subtitles, so I can improve my English at the same time. It also gives me ideas for my future trips.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a travel and food documentary series that I'm addicted to.

I usually watch it at home on my phone or laptop, via YouTube or Netflix, typically in the evening after dinner or just before bed.

The show follows a host who travels around the world. In each episode, he explores a different city, tries the local cuisine and chats with the locals. We get to see bustling markets, street food stalls and everyday life, and he explains the history behind each dish.

I watch roughly two or three episodes a week.

I love it for several reasons. For one thing, it's a wonderful way to unwind after a long day. For another, I learn about different cultures without leaving my sofa. And the cinematography is gorgeous, while the English subtitles help me practise at the same time. It's also a great source of inspiration for future trips.

Sometimes I pause an episode to note down a useful English phrase, so the show doubles as a listening lesson. It's a small habit, but it makes my evenings feel both relaxing and productive.

p3.q: What programmes are popular in your country?
p3.a6: Game shows, talent shows, reality shows, dramas, football matches and news are popular on TV. Online, short videos, vlogs, music videos and livestreams are very popular.
p3.a7: On TV, game shows, talent shows, dramas, football and news. Online, short videos, vlogs, music videos and livestreams dominate.

p3.q: Do people like foreign TV programmes?
p3.a6: Yes, especially Korean dramas, Hollywood films and Chinese series. They are fun and have high quality. With Vietsub, it's easy to understand.
p3.a7: Yes, particularly Korean dramas, Hollywood films and Chinese series, which are high quality and come with Vietnamese subtitles.

p3.q: Benefit of kids watching animal videos instead of visiting zoos?
p3.a6: It's cheaper and more convenient, and animals aren't kept in cages. Children can also see wild animals in nature that they can't see in a zoo. But visiting a zoo gives a real experience.
p3.a7: It's cheaper, convenient and shows animals in the wild rather than in cages, though a zoo visit offers a real-life experience.

p3.q: Do teachers play videos in class?
p3.a6: Yes, nowadays many teachers do, especially in English and science lessons. Videos make lessons more interesting and easier to understand.
p3.a7: Yes, increasingly, especially in English and science, as videos make lessons livelier and easier to grasp.

p3.q: Are talk shows a waste of time? Can we acquire knowledge from TV?
p3.a6: Not always. Some talk shows are only gossip, but others have useful topics. We can learn a lot from documentaries, news and educational programmes.
p3.a7: Not necessarily; some are mere gossip, while others cover useful topics. Documentaries, news and educational shows can teach us a great deal.

p3.q: What do old and young people watch? Do they enjoy similar shows?
p3.a6: Old people like news, traditional opera and old films. Young people like short videos, music shows and series. Some family shows are enjoyed by both.
p3.a7: Older people prefer news, traditional opera and classic films; young people go for short videos, music shows and series. Family shows are a rare meeting point.

p3.q: What other programmes do you like?
p3.a6: I also like English learning channels and technology reviews on YouTube.
p3.a7: English learning channels and tech reviews on YouTube.

p3.q: Why do some people spend so much time on shows? Are there too many shows?
p3.a6: Because they are entertaining and easy to access. Algorithms suggest videos, so people can't stop. Yes, there are too many, and sometimes people spend a long time choosing.
p3.a7: They're entertaining and easy to access, and algorithms keep feeding more. There are indeed too many, so people waste time choosing.

p3.q: Should parents choose what their children watch?
p3.a6: Yes, especially for young children. Parents should choose safe and educational programmes and watch with their children. For teenagers, parents can discuss more than control.
p3.a7: Yes for young children, to ensure safe, educational content; with teenagers, discussion works better than control.

cards.title: Describe an item on which you spent more than expected
points: when and where you bought it
how much you expected to pay
and explain why you spent more than expected
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: mua một chiếc ghế công thái học (ergonomic chair) cho bàn làm việc/ học tiếng Anh tại nhà. (Khác Topic 26 là sửa điện thoại.)

notes.v: better quality chair, delivery & assembly fee, back pain, upgrade

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about an office chair that I bought six months ago.

I bought it at a furniture store in Hanoi after I saw it on a website. I work at a computer for many hours every day, and my back often hurt, so I wanted a better chair for my desk at home, where I also study English.

I planned to pay about 1.5 million dong for a simple chair. But when I went to the store, the staff told me that cheap chairs are not good for the back. They showed me a chair with a support for the back and the neck. It cost 3 million dong. There was also a delivery fee and an assembly fee, so I paid 3.4 million in total.

At first, I felt worried because it was twice my budget. But after using it for a few weeks, my back pain was much better and I could study longer. So now I feel satisfied. I think it was worth the money.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about an ergonomic chair that I bought six months ago and ended up spending far more on than planned.

I bought it from a furniture store in Hanoi, having first spotted it on their website. I sit at a computer for hours every day and my back had started to ache, so I wanted a proper chair for my desk at home, where I also study English.

I'd budgeted around 1.5 million dong for a basic one. At the store, however, the sales assistant explained that cheap chairs don't offer adequate support, and he showed me a model with lumbar and neck support priced at three million. With delivery and assembly fees, I paid 3.4 million in total.

I was uneasy at first, as it was more than double my budget. But after a few weeks, my back pain had eased noticeably and I could study for longer stretches. Now I feel it was money well spent, as health is worth investing in.

Looking back, I don't regret the purchase, because I use it every single day, but it taught me to compare prices and read reviews before paying. Now I set a budget first and stick to it, which has saved me a lot of money.

p3.q: Do you often buy more than you expected?
p3.a6: Sometimes. When I go shopping for one thing, I often see other nice things and buy them. Sales and online shopping also make me spend more.
p3.a7: Occasionally. I go out for one item and end up adding others, and sales and online shopping make it worse.

p3.q: What do young people spend most of their money on?
p3.a6: Clothes, phones, eating out, coffee, travel, entertainment and beauty products.
p3.a7: Fashion, gadgets, eating out, coffee, travel, entertainment and beauty products.

p3.q: Is it important to save money? Why?
p3.a6: Yes. We need money for emergencies, like illness, and for big plans such as buying a house or studying. Saving also gives peace of mind.
p3.a7: Yes. It cushions us against emergencies such as illness, funds big goals like a house or education and gives peace of mind.

p3.q: Do people buy things they don't need?
p3.a6: Yes, a lot. Advertising, discounts and social media make people want to buy more, and they follow trends.
p3.a7: Very often. Advertising, discounts and social media fuel the urge to buy, and trends add to it.

p3.q: Is it good to teach children to save money?
p3.a6: Often yes. Good items last longer and are better for our health, like my chair. But we should not pay for only the brand name.
p3.a7: Often. Quality items last longer and may benefit health, as with my chair, though we shouldn't pay merely for a brand name.

cards.title: Describe a shopping place you often go to
points: how often you go there and who you go with
and explain why you often go there
cards.note: Nơi giả định: chợ/ siêu thị gần nhà ở ngoại thành, và Shopee (không dùng lại Aeon của Topic 36). Bài này: siêu thị WinMart gần nhà.

notes.v: near, clean, fair prices, wide choice, open late

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a supermarket near my house, called WinMart.

It's about five minutes by walking from my house, in my neighbourhood in the outskirts of Hanoi.

I usually buy vegetables, fruit, meat, milk and snacks there. I also buy some household things like soap and tissue, and skincare products.

I go there two or three times a week, usually after work on my way home from the bus stop. Sometimes I go with my mother at the weekend, and we buy food for the whole week.

I often go there for several reasons. First, it's near my house and it's very convenient. Second, it's clean and the food is fresh, and there are many things to choose from. Third, the prices are reasonable and there are often promotions. It's also open until ten at night, so I can go even when I come home late.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a WinMart supermarket just around the corner from my home.

It's roughly a five-minute walk from my house on the outskirts of Hanoi.

I usually pick up vegetables, fruit, meat, milk and snacks there, as well as household essentials like soap and tissues, and the occasional skincare product.

I go two or three times a week, normally after work on my way back from the bus stop. At weekends, I sometimes go with my mother to stock up on groceries for the week.

There are several reasons I'm a regular. First and foremost, it's so close that it couldn't be more convenient. Secondly, it's clean, the produce is fresh and there's a wide selection. Thirdly, the prices are reasonable, with frequent promotions. And since it's open until 10 p.m., I can still shop after a late day at the office.

The staff there know me by now and often recommend new products that suit my skin and my budget. That friendly, personal service is the main reason I keep coming back instead of ordering online.

p3.q: Do people go to shopping malls frequently? What places do people like to shop?
p3.a6: In big cities, many people go to malls at weekends, because there are food, cinemas and shops. People also like supermarkets, street markets and online shops like Shopee and TikTok Shop.
p3.a7: In big cities, malls are popular at weekends for the mix of shopping, food and cinemas, alongside supermarkets, traditional markets and online platforms like Shopee and TikTok Shop.

p3.q: How have shopping habits changed in recent decades?
p3.a6: Before, people mostly went to markets and small shops and paid in cash. Now they shop online, pay by phone and watch livestream sales.
p3.a7: Previously, people relied on markets and small shops and paid cash; now they shop online, pay by phone and buy through livestreams.

p3.q: Will shops and malls disappear?
p3.a6: I don't think so. Some small shops may close because of online shopping. But people still like to touch and try things, and malls are also a place for entertainment.
p3.a7: Unlikely. Some small shops will close, but people still like to touch and try goods, and malls double as entertainment venues.

p3.q: Differences between street markets and big shopping malls?
p3.a6: Markets are cheaper, you can bargain and the food is fresh, but they're hot and crowded. Malls are clean and air-conditioned, but more expensive and with fixed prices.
p3.a7: Markets are cheaper, allow haggling and have fresh produce, but they're hot and crowded; malls are clean and air-conditioned but pricier with fixed prices.

p3.q: Differences between age groups?
p3.a6: Young people like online shopping and fashion. Middle-aged people compare prices and buy for their family. Old people prefer to buy at markets and small shops because they trust them.
p3.a7: Young people favour online shopping and fashion; middle-aged people compare prices and shop for the family; older people prefer markets and familiar shops.

p3.q: Has shopping become a hobby? Does buying things make people happy?
p3.a6: For many people, yes, especially young women. Shopping makes people happy for a short time, but it's not real, long-term happiness. Sometimes people feel regret later.
p3.a7: For many, yes, especially young women. The happiness is fleeting, though, and regret often follows.

p3.q: Do people waste too much time shopping? Do they buy unnecessary things?
p3.a6: I agree. Some people spend hours scrolling shopping apps, and they buy things they don't need because of sales and advertisements.
p3.a7: I agree. Many spend hours scrolling shopping apps and buy unnecessary things lured by sales and advertisements.

p3.q: How much influence does advertising have?
p3.a6: A lot. Advertising makes products look attractive and creates a need. Famous people and social media ads are especially strong for young people.
p3.a7: A great deal. Advertising makes products desirable and even creates needs, especially via celebrities and social media.

cards.title: Describe a time when you encouraged someone to do something that he or she didn't want to do
points: what you encouraged him/her to do
why he/she didn't want to do it
and explain how you encouraged him/her and what happened
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: động viên bạn Nam đi thi chứng chỉ ISTQB/ hoặc em trai đi khám răng. Ở đây: động viên bạn Nam đi thi chứng chỉ.

notes.v: afraid of failing, English exam, lazy, expensive
studied together, shared notes, mock tests, promised lunch

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about the time I encouraged my friend, Nam, to take an exam.

Nam is my colleague, and we're also close friends. I encouraged him to take the ISTQB Foundation exam, which is a testing certificate.

He didn't want to do it for a few reasons. He was afraid of failing, because the exam is in English. He also felt lazy after work and thought the exam fee was expensive.

I tried to encourage him in several ways. First, I told him that I was also afraid, so we could study together. We studied for one hour every evening in a café. I shared my notes and found some practice tests. I also promised to treat him to lunch if he passed.

The result was great. Nam passed the exam with a good score, and later, he got a better position at work. He was very happy and thanked me. I was also very proud and happy.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the time I persuaded my friend Nam to sit an exam he was reluctant to take.

Nam is both a colleague and a close friend, and I urged him to take the ISTQB Foundation exam, a well-known software testing certificate.

He was hesitant for several reasons. He was scared of failing, particularly as the exam is in English. He also felt too drained after work to study, and thought the fee was steep.

I tried a few approaches. First, I admitted that I was nervous too, and suggested we prepare together. We studied for an hour every evening at a café, I shared my notes and found some mock tests. And I promised him lunch if he passed.

The outcome was fantastic. Nam passed with a good score, and a few months later he was promoted. He was over the moon and thanked me sincerely, and I felt really proud and happy that my encouragement had paid off.

A few weeks later, he sent me a message saying he had passed and thanked me for believing in him. Those few words made my whole week, and I learned that a little encouragement can change someone's confidence.

p3.q: How could employers motivate staff? Is money the most important? Praise or money?
p3.a6: Employers can give bonuses, promotions, training and praise. Money is important, but not the most. Praise and a good environment also keep people motivated, especially for long-term.
p3.a7: Through bonuses, promotions, training and recognition. Money matters, but it isn't everything; praise and a positive environment sustain motivation in the long run.

p3.q: Is the role of a leader important? How should leaders encourage? Should they discuss decisions? Is encouragement the boss's most important role?
p3.a6: Yes, very. A leader gives direction and keeps the team together. Leaders should listen, praise good work and discuss important decisions with the team. Encouragement is important, but a boss must also plan and make decisions.
p3.a7: Very. Leaders give direction and unity, should listen, praise good work and consult the team on key decisions. Encouragement is vital, though not the only part of a boss's role.

p3.q: Is it good that a leader likes taking risks?
p3.a6: A little risk can bring new chances, but too much risk is dangerous for the team. A good leader should think carefully.
p3.a7: Calculated risks can open opportunities, but reckless ones endanger the team.

p3.q: Will more women become world leaders?
p3.a6: I think so. Women have more education and chances now, and many countries have female leaders. But change may be slow because of traditional views.
p3.a7: Probably, as women gain education and opportunities, although traditional attitudes may slow the change.

p3.q: Why do many people want to be leaders? Why are some afraid?
p3.a6: They want higher salaries, power and respect. Some are afraid because of heavy responsibility and pressure, and fear of making mistakes.
p3.a7: Pay, status and influence appeal to many; others fear responsibility, pressure and making mistakes.

p3.q: How do people become leaders? Can everyone? Qualities of a good leader?
p3.a6: They become leaders by experience, skills and good results. I think not everyone can, because it needs communication and decision skills, but many can learn. A good leader is honest, fair, and has a clear vision, and listens.
p3.a7: Through experience, skills and results. Not everyone is suited, but many can learn. Good leaders are honest, fair, visionary and good listeners.

p3.q: When should parents encourage children? Should they reward them? What kind of encouragement?
p3.a6: When children try hard, even if they fail. Rewards for helping others are fine, but small ones like praise or hugs are better than money. Parents should encourage with kind words and attention.
p3.a7: When children make an effort, even if they fail. Small rewards such as praise are better than money, and parents should encourage with kind words and attention.

p3.q: Are some people better at persuading? Why do children often not want to do what parents ask?
p3.a6: Yes, some people are better because they communicate well and understand others' feelings. Children don't want to do it when they are tired or want freedom, or they don't understand the reason.
p3.a7: Yes, good communicators with empathy persuade more effectively. Children resist when tired, wanting independence or not understanding the reason.

cards.title: Describe a piece of technology, not a phone, that you would like to own
points: what this piece of technology is
what you would use it for
and explain why you would like to own it
cards.note: Thiết bị giả định: máy tính bảng/ máy đọc sách? Bài này: robot hút bụi thông minh (robot vacuum).

notes.v: cleans floor automatically, mop, schedule, app control
busy, tired after work, help mother, clean, dust allergy
easy: app, a bit hard at first

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a smart robot vacuum cleaner that I would like to own.

It's a small round machine that cleans the floor by itself. Some models can also mop the floor. We can control it with an app on the phone and set the time for cleaning.

I would like to have it for several reasons. I'm busy with work and I'm often tired after coming home, so I don't have time to clean the house. My mother always does it, and I want to help her. Also, I have a little problem with dust, so a clean floor is good for me.

It would help me in many ways. It could clean every day when I'm at work, so the house would always be clean. I would have more free time on the weekend to rest or study.

I think it would be easy to use because I only need to press a button or use the app. But maybe it's a little difficult at the beginning to connect it to Wi-Fi.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a smart robot vacuum cleaner that's high on my wish list.

It's a compact, disc-shaped device that cleans floors autonomously, and some models even mop. You can control it via a phone app and schedule cleaning sessions.

I'd love to own one for several reasons. I'm swamped at work and usually exhausted when I get home, so I rarely have time for housework, and my mother ends up doing most of it, which I feel bad about. I'm also mildly allergic to dust, so a spotless floor would benefit my health.

It would help in a number of ways. It could clean while I'm at work, so the house would be spotless when I return, and I'd gain precious free time at weekends for resting or studying.

I imagine it would be quite easy to use, as it only takes a button press or a tap on the app. Connecting it to Wi-Fi might be a little fiddly at first, but I'm tech-savvy enough to manage.

I've been watching reviews and saving a little each month, so I can afford it without feeling guilty. When I finally get it, I'm sure it will make both my work and my free time more enjoyable.

p3.q: Differences between the technology of the past and today?
p3.a6: In the past, technology was big, slow and expensive, like old computers and telephones. Today, it's smaller, faster, smart and connected to the internet, and we can do many things with one device.
p3.a7: Past technology was bulky, slow and costly, whereas today's is compact, fast, smart and connected, with one device doing many jobs.

p3.q: What technology do young people like and currently use?
p3.a6: They like smartphones, laptops, smartwatches, wireless earphones, games consoles and social media apps. Nowadays, many also use AI tools like ChatGPT.
p3.a7: Smartphones, laptops, smartwatches, wireless earbuds, game consoles and social apps, plus AI tools like ChatGPT.

p3.q: Differences between online and face-to-face communication?
p3.a6: Online is fast, cheap and we can talk to anyone anywhere, but we can't see body language, so misunderstanding is easier. Face-to-face is warmer and more honest, but needs time and travelling.
p3.a7: Online is fast, cheap and borderless but lacks body language, so misunderstandings are likelier. Face-to-face is warmer and more genuine but takes time and travel.

p3.q: Has technology changed the way people communicate?
p3.a6: Yes, a lot. We send messages, voice notes and videos instead of letters or even calls. We communicate faster, but the messages are shorter.
p3.a7: Enormously. Messages, voice notes and video calls have replaced letters, and communication is faster though more concise.

p3.q: Negative effects on relationships?
p3.a6: People look at their phones instead of talking to each other, even in family meals. Online conflicts and jealousy on social media can also hurt relationships.
p3.a7: People often look at phones instead of each other, even at family meals, and social media can fuel jealousy and conflict.

p3.q: Differences between making friends in real life and online?
p3.a6: Online, it's easier to meet people with similar interests, but we are not sure if they are honest. In real life, friendships build more slowly but are deeper and more reliable.
p3.a7: Online, it's easier to find like-minded people, but you can't be sure of their honesty; real-life friendships form more slowly but run deeper.

p3.q: Is technology positive for young people? Is it healthy to spend lots of time online?
p3.a6: Mostly positive, because it helps learning and entertainment. But spending too much time online is not healthy. It hurts eyes and sleep, and can cause stress and addiction.
p3.a7: Largely positive for learning and entertainment, but excessive online time harms eyesight, sleep and mental health and can lead to addiction.

cards.title: Describe a child you know who likes drawing very much
points: what he/she likes to draw and when
and explain why you think he/she likes drawing so much
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: em họ Mai, 7 tuổi.

notes.v: my uncle's daughter, visit at weekends
creative, imaginative, relaxing, praise from family

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my cousin, Mai. She's seven years old and she loves drawing very much.

She's my uncle's daughter. I see her almost every weekend when we have family meals at my grandmother's house.

She likes drawing animals, especially cats, and flowers and princesses. She also draws our family, and she makes my face very funny! She uses many bright colours, like pink, yellow and blue.

She usually draws after school, before dinner, and also on weekends, when she doesn't have homework. She can sit for one or two hours with her colour pencils and not get bored.

I think she likes drawing so much for several reasons. She has a lot of imagination, and she can create her own world on paper. Drawing also makes her feel relaxed and happy. Also, her family always praises her pictures and puts them on the wall, so she feels proud and wants to draw more.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my cousin Mai, a seven-year-old who's absolutely crazy about drawing.

She's my uncle's daughter, and I see her almost every weekend at family meals at my grandmother's.

Her favourite subjects are animals, especially cats, as well as flowers and princesses. She also draws our family, and she portrays me in a hilarious way! She uses plenty of bright colours like pink, yellow and blue.

She usually draws after school, before dinner and at weekends when there's no homework. She can happily sit for an hour or two with her coloured pencils without getting bored.

I think there are a few reasons she loves it so much. She has a vivid imagination and can build her own world on paper. Drawing is also calming and makes her happy. On top of that, her family always praises her pictures and sticks them on the wall, which makes her proud and eager to draw even more.

Her parents have stuck some of her drawings on the fridge, and she beams with pride whenever visitors compliment them. I hope she keeps this hobby, because it clearly makes her happy and confident.

p3.q: What's the right age for children to learn drawing? At what age do they start?
p3.a6: Children usually start to draw at two or three years old, with simple lines. They can learn basic skills from five or six, when they can hold the pencil well.
p3.a7: Children start scribbling around two or three, and formal learning suits ages five or six, once they can control a pencil.

p3.q: Why do children draw more than adults?
p3.a6: Children have a lot of imagination and are not afraid of making mistakes. Adults are busy, and some think they can't draw well.
p3.a7: Children are imaginative and uninhibited, while adults are busy and often self-conscious about their skills.

p3.q: Why do people visit galleries and museums instead of viewing art online?
p3.a6: In real life, you can see the real size, colours and details. You also feel the atmosphere, and you can go with friends. Online pictures can't give that feeling.
p3.a7: In person, you appreciate the true scale, colours and texture, and soak up the atmosphere, which a screen can't replicate.

p3.q: Should galleries and museums be free?
p3.a6: I think they should be free or cheap for students and children. This helps everyone to learn. But they also need money to keep the place, so a small fee is fair for others.
p3.a7: Ideally free or discounted for children and students, so everyone can learn, though a modest fee for others helps maintain them.

p3.q: How do artworks inspire people? Can people learn about life from art?
p3.a6: Art gives people new ideas and feelings. By looking at art, people can learn about history, culture and how people lived in the past. I agree with this idea.
p3.a7: Art stirs ideas and emotions and offers glimpses of history, culture and how people lived, so I agree it teaches us a lot about life.

p3.q: Differences between reading a book and visiting a museum?
p3.a6: A book gives detailed information and we can read anywhere. A museum gives real experience: we can see and sometimes touch things, so it's more interesting and easier to remember.
p3.a7: Books provide detailed information anywhere, whereas museums offer immersive, memorable first-hand experience.

p3.q: Should children have art lessons at school?
p3.a6: Yes. Art lessons develop creativity, patience and observation skills. They also help children relax after academic subjects.
p3.a7: Yes, they build creativity, patience and observation and give children a break from academic subjects.

cards.title: Describe a person who makes plans a lot
points: what kind of plans he/she makes
and explain how you feel about this habit
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: bạn Trang (người giỏi ngôn ngữ ở Topic 11) hoặc chị gái họ. Bài này: bạn Trang, bạn đại học. Khác Topic 27 (quản lý giỏi lên kế hoạch).

notes.v: study plan, monthly budget, weekend, trips, career for 5 years
organised, anxious, likes control, saves time

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my friend, Trang. She makes plans for almost everything.

I know her from university, where we were in the same class. We have been friends for about eight years.

She makes many kinds of plans. She has a study plan for every week, a budget plan for every month, and a plan for every weekend. She also plans her trips carefully, with a list of places, hotels and prices. She even has a five-year plan for her career.

I think she likes making plans because she's an organised person. She also feels anxious when she doesn't know what will happen, so a plan makes her feel safe. She says a plan saves her time and money.

I admire her habit because she always has a clear goal and she isn't late for anything. But sometimes it is a bit tiring for friends, because she wants us to follow the plan exactly. I also learn from her and now I make a weekly study plan.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my friend Trang, who plans virtually everything in her life.

We met at university, where we were in the same class, and we've been friends for around eight years.

She makes all sorts of plans: a weekly study timetable, a monthly budget and a schedule for every weekend. Her trips are meticulously researched, with lists of sights, hotels and costs, and she even has a five-year career plan.

I think the reason is that she's naturally organised. She also tends to feel anxious when things are uncertain, so planning gives her a sense of security. She maintains that it saves her both time and money.

I admire her habit, as she always has clear goals and is never late. That said, it can be a bit exhausting for her friends, since she expects everyone to stick rigidly to the plan. Nevertheless, I've learned from her and I now draw up a weekly study plan of my own.

Sometimes I tease her for being too organised, but I have to admit her plans rarely go wrong. Spending time with her has encouraged me to write a simple to-do list every morning, and it really helps.

p3.q: Is it important to plan ahead? Is planning important in general?
p3.a6: Yes, very. A plan saves time, reduces stress and helps us reach goals. Without a plan, we may waste time. But we should also be flexible.
p3.a7: Yes. Planning saves time, reduces stress and helps us achieve goals, though we need flexibility too.

p3.q: Should children plan their future careers? Is a college major related to a future career?
