p3.a6: They don't need to decide exactly, but they should think about their interests. The major is often related to the job, such as medicine or IT. But many people change their career later.
p3.a7: They needn't decide precisely, but should explore their interests. A major often links to a career, as in medicine or IT, although many people switch later.

p3.q: Should children ask teachers or parents for advice when making plans?
p3.a6: Yes, because adults have experience. But the final decision should be theirs.
p3.a7: Yes, adults bring experience, but the final decision should remain theirs.

p3.q: What activities do we need to plan ahead?
p3.a6: Trips, weddings, big events, studying for exams, moving house and financial plans like saving for a house.
p3.a7: Trips, weddings, big events, exam preparation, moving house and financial goals like saving for a home.

p3.q: Is making study plans popular among young people?
p3.a6: Yes, many students do, especially before exams. They use apps or notes to plan. But some don't follow their plan.
p3.a7: Yes, particularly before exams, using apps or notebooks, although not all stick to them.

p3.q: Does everyone in your country make everyday plans?
p3.a6: No. Some people, like office workers, make daily plans. Others live more freely and decide at the moment. It depends on personality and job.
p3.a7: Not everyone. Office workers often plan daily, while others live spontaneously; it depends on personality and occupation.

cards.title: Describe something that you can't live without (not a computer or phone)
points: and explain why you can't live without it
cards.note: Món đồ giả định: tai nghe không dây (earphones).

notes.v: music, English listening, block noise, calls
bored, noisy, stressed, hard to study

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my wireless earphones, which I can't live without.

I use them every day. I wear them on the bus to work, at the office when I need to focus and in the evening when I do exercise or study.

They are important to me for several reasons. First, I listen to music with them, and it makes me relax. Second, I use them to learn English, for example listening to podcasts and IELTS tests. Third, the bus is noisy and crowded, and with earphones I can block the noise. I can also take calls without using my hands.

If I didn't have them, my life would be more difficult. My bus trip, which takes more than one hour, would feel boring and stressful. I would also find it harder to study English.

That's why I feel I can't live without them. They help me relax and study every day.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my wireless earphones, something I genuinely can't live without.

I use them daily: on the bus to work, at the office when I need to concentrate and in the evenings when I exercise or study.

They matter to me for several reasons. Firstly, music helps me unwind. Secondly, they're a vital study tool, as I listen to English podcasts and IELTS recordings with them. Thirdly, my bus is noisy and packed, and the earphones block out the chaos. They also let me take calls hands-free.

Without them, life would be much tougher. My bus journey, which takes over an hour, would be tedious and stressful, and studying English would be far harder, as I'd have fewer opportunities to practise listening.

That's why I feel so dependent on them: they're my daily source of relaxation and learning, and they make my commute bearable.

When I forgot it at home once, I felt strangely lost the whole day, which proves how dependent I've become. Still, I wouldn't change it, because it makes my daily life so much easier and more enjoyable.

p3.q: Why are children attracted to new things such as electronics?
p3.a6: They are curious and like colourful and fun things. Electronics have games and videos, so they are exciting. Children also copy their friends and parents.
p3.a7: They're curious and drawn to colourful, entertaining gadgets with games and videos, and they imitate friends and parents.

p3.q: Why do grown-ups hate to throw out old things?
p3.a6: Old things hold memories. Some grown-ups also think they may need them later, or they feel it's a waste. Older people lived in a poorer time, so they keep everything.
p3.a7: Old items carry memories, and some think they might be useful later or consider discarding wasteful; older generations grew up in poorer times, so they hoard.

p3.q: How are the way people buy things and shopping habits affected? What influences people to buy? How do shops attract customers?
p3.a6: People now buy online, pay by phone and compare prices easily. They are influenced by advertisements, friends, social media, sales and trends. Shops attract customers with promotions, nice displays, free samples, loyalty cards and friendly staff.
p3.a7: People now shop online, pay by phone and compare prices instantly. Ads, social media, friends, sales and trends influence them, while shops lure customers with promotions, attractive displays, free samples, loyalty cards and friendly service.

p3.q: Why do all children like toys?
p3.a6: Toys are fun, and they help children play and imagine. Toys also make them feel safe and happy.
p3.a7: Toys are fun, spark imagination and give children comfort and security.

p3.q: Is it good for a child to take their favourite toy everywhere?
p3.a6: It's OK for small children because it gives them security, especially in new places. But it's not good if the child can't be without it when they grow older, or they may lose it.
p3.a7: It's fine for young children, as it provides security in unfamiliar places, but becomes a concern if they can't function without it as they grow older.

cards.title: Describe a traditional product made in your country which you like
points: and explain why you like it
cards.note: Sản phẩm giả định: nón lá (conical hat) – làng nón Chuông, Hà Nội (gần nhà bạn ở ngoại thành).

notes.v: Chuong village, Thanh Oai, Hanoi (and Hue)
palm leaves dried, ironed, bamboo frame, sewn with thread
hundreds of years, farmers, Ao dai symbol
light, cool, beautiful, symbol of Vietnam

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about the non la, which is the Vietnamese conical hat.

It's made in many places, but a famous one is Chuong village in Thanh Oai district, in Hanoi, not far from my house. Hue is also famous for it.

It's made by hand. First, people pick palm leaves, dry them in the sun and iron them flat. Then they make a frame from thin bamboo. After that, they put the leaves on the frame and sew them with thin thread. It takes a lot of time and care. In Hue, people even put thin pictures between the layers.

It's traditional because Vietnamese people have made and used it for hundreds of years. Farmers wore it to protect from sun and rain. It's also part of the traditional dress, ao dai.

I like it because it's light, cool and beautiful. When I see a girl in ao dai with a non la, I think it shows the gentle beauty of Vietnam. It's also a nice gift for foreign friends.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the non la, Vietnam's iconic conical hat.

It's produced in many areas, but one famous place is Chuong village in Thanh Oai district of Hanoi, not far from my home. Hue is renowned for it too.

It's entirely handmade. Artisans first gather palm leaves, dry them in the sun and iron them flat. Then they shape a delicate bamboo frame, layer the leaves on top and stitch everything together with fine thread. It requires great patience and skill. In Hue, craftspeople even insert thin pictures or poems between the layers.

It's traditional because Vietnamese people have been making and wearing it for centuries. Farmers used it as protection from sun and rain, and it has become inseparable from the ao dai, our national costume.

I like it because it's light, cool and elegant. A girl in an ao dai and a non la perfectly captures the gentle beauty of Vietnam. It also makes a wonderful gift for foreign friends.

Buying it also supports the local craftspeople who keep the tradition alive, which makes me feel good about my purchase. I think such products deserve more attention, especially from young people like me.

p3.q: Why are traditional products important?
p3.a6: They show the history and culture of a country. They also create jobs for local people, such as in craft villages, and attract tourists.
p3.a7: They embody a nation's history and culture, provide livelihoods in craft villages and attract tourists.

p3.q: Are traditions important for a country? Should people be proud of their culture?
p3.a6: Yes. Traditions create national identity and bring people together. People should be proud of their culture, because if we aren't, nobody will keep it. But we should also be open to learn from others.
p3.a7: Yes, traditions form national identity and unite people. We should be proud of our culture, or nobody will preserve it, while remaining open to other cultures.

p3.q: What are some traditional Vietnamese products?
p3.a6: Non la, ao dai, Bat Trang pottery, silk from Van Phuc, lacquer paintings, Dong Ho paintings, bamboo products and fish sauce.
p3.a7: Non la, ao dai, Bat Trang ceramics, Van Phuc silk, lacquerware, Dong Ho folk paintings, bamboo goods and fish sauce.

p3.q: Why is it important for children to learn about traditional products?
p3.a6: So they know their roots and keep the traditions. Children who understand the work of craftspeople respect their efforts more and may continue the craft.
p3.a7: So they know their roots and carry traditions forward; understanding craftspeople's effort fosters respect and may inspire them to continue the craft.

p3.q: Where should children learn about culture: at school or at home?
p3.a6: Both. At home, family stories and festivals give them real feeling. At school, teachers give organised knowledge and field trips to craft villages.
p3.a7: Both: home provides lived experience through family stories and festivals, school provides structured knowledge and visits to craft villages.

cards.title: Describe a place which is far away that you would like to visit in the future
points: what you would like to do there and who you would go with
and explain why you would like to visit it
cards.note: Địa điểm giả định: Thụy Sĩ (Alps) hoặc Nhật Bản (đã dùng ở Topic 35). Bài này: Thụy Sĩ.

notes.v: trains through Alps, snow, lakes, cheese, chocolate, photos

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about Switzerland, a country in Europe that's very far from Vietnam.

I know about it from films and from YouTube videos. A colleague of mine also visited Switzerland last year and showed me many beautiful photos.

If I go there, I would like to travel by train through the Alps, because the views are said to be amazing. I would visit the lakes and small villages and take a lot of photos. I would also see the snow in winter, try skiing a little and eat cheese and chocolate.

I would like to go with my family, especially my parents, because they have never travelled abroad. If it is not possible, I will go with close friends.

I want to go there in the future because the scenery is like a picture. It is very clean and peaceful. I think it'd be a dream trip, and it would be a great reward for my hard work after I save enough money.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Switzerland, a faraway European country I'd love to visit one day.

I know about it through films and YouTube, and a colleague who went last year showed me stunning photos.

If I went, I'd take scenic train rides through the Alps, which are famous for their breathtaking views. I'd explore the lakes and charming villages, take heaps of photos, see snow in winter, have a go at skiing, and of course indulge in Swiss cheese and chocolate.

I'd like to go with my family, especially my parents, who've never travelled abroad. Failing that, I'd go with close friends.

I want to visit in the future because the scenery looks like a postcard, and the country is spotlessly clean and tranquil. It would be a dream trip, and a fitting reward for my hard work once I've saved enough. It also motivates me to keep studying English, as I'll need it to travel independently.

I imagine myself walking along quiet streets, trying local food and taking hundreds of photos. Even if I can't go soon, dreaming about it keeps me motivated to work hard and save money.

p3.q: Where do people usually travel on holidays?
p3.a6: They go to the beach, mountains and famous cities. Families also like resorts and theme parks. Some go back to their hometown.
p3.a7: Beaches, mountains and famous cities, with families favouring resorts and theme parks, and some returning to their hometown.

p3.q: Why do some people think staying at home on holidays is enjoyable?
p3.a6: It's cheap, relaxing and there are no crowds or traffic jams. They can sleep late, watch films and eat home-made food.
p3.a7: It's cheap and relaxing, with no crowds or traffic, and they can sleep in, watch films and enjoy home cooking.

p3.q: How do students who take a gap year differ from other students?
p3.a6: They are often more mature, independent and clear about their goals, because they have travelled, worked or volunteered. But some may find it hard to go back to study.
p3.a7: They tend to be more mature, independent and focused, having travelled or worked, though some struggle to readjust to study.

p3.q: Do teenagers travel with friends or alone?
p3.a6: Mostly with friends or family, because it's safer and cheaper. A few teenagers travel alone, but parents usually worry.
p3.a7: Mostly with friends or family, for safety and cost; solo travel is rare as parents worry.

p3.q: What's the most desirable place to visit during the holiday?
p3.a6: I think the beach, because people can relax and have fun. Nature places like mountains and islands are also desirable for people who want to escape the city.
p3.a7: Beaches, as they combine relaxation and fun, along with mountains and islands for those escaping the city.

p3.q: What does tourism have to do with cultural exchange?
p3.a6: When tourists visit a place, they learn the local food, language and customs, and locals learn about tourists' cultures too. It helps people understand and respect each other.
p3.a7: Tourists absorb local food, language and customs while locals learn about visitors' cultures, which promotes mutual understanding and respect.

cards.title: Describe an occasion when the electricity suddenly went off
points: what you were doing at that time
what you did after the electricity went off
and explain how you felt about it
cards.note: Lưu ý đánh số: PDF đánh số lại từ Topic 54 ở phần cuối, nên mình đánh số tuần tự 56–66 để không bị trùng.

notes.v: candle, phone flashlight, went outside, talked with neighbours, fan

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about an occasion when the electricity suddenly went off. It happened last summer on a very hot evening.

I was at home, in my bedroom, around eight o'clock. I was doing an online English class on my laptop, and the lesson was only half-way.

Suddenly, everything went dark. The fan stopped, the internet stopped and my laptop only had a little battery. At first, I was annoyed because it was hot and I couldn't finish my class.

Then I used my phone as a flashlight and found some candles. My mother and my brother went out in front of the house, because it was cooler there. Many neighbours were also outside. We sat together, talked and shared fruit. The children played games under the moon.

The electricity came back after two hours. After the first anger, I felt quite relaxed. I realised that we sometimes spend too much time with technology and forget to talk to each other. It was a nice evening.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the evening when the electricity suddenly went off, which happened last summer during a heatwave.

I was in my bedroom at about eight o'clock, halfway through an online English lesson on my laptop.

All of a sudden, the room went pitch-black. The fan stopped, the Wi-Fi died and my laptop was nearly out of battery. I was irritated, as it was stiflingly hot and I couldn't finish my lesson.

I used my phone's torch to find some candles. Then my mother and brother suggested going outside, where it was cooler, and we found plenty of neighbours already there. We sat together chatting and sharing fruit while the children played games under the moonlight.

The power returned after about two hours. After my initial frustration, I felt surprisingly relaxed. It made me realise that we spend so much time with technology that we forget to talk to the people around us. It ended up being a lovely evening.

Strangely, I enjoyed the evening more than I expected, because for once nobody was staring at a screen. It reminded me how valuable simple conversation is, and I try to switch off my phone for an hour now and then.

p3.q: Which is better, electric bicycles or ordinary bicycles?
p3.a6: Electric bicycles are better for long distances and hills, and for older people. But ordinary bicycles are cheaper, healthier and don't need charging.
p3.a7: E-bikes suit long distances, hills and older riders, whereas ordinary bikes are cheaper, give exercise and need no charging.

p3.q: Will electric bicycles replace ordinary bicycles?
p3.a6: I don't think completely. Some people still like to exercise on normal bicycles. But electric ones will be more popular because of technology and lower prices.
p3.a7: Not entirely. Many cyclists prefer the exercise, though e-bikes will keep gaining ground as prices fall.

p3.q: Which is better, electric cars or petrol cars?
p3.a6: Electric cars are better for the environment and cheaper to run. Petrol cars are still better for long trips because of charging problems. But I think electric cars are the future.
p3.a7: Electric cars are cleaner and cheaper to run, while petrol cars remain more practical for long trips due to charging limits; still, electric is the future.

p3.q: How did people live without electricity in the ancient world?
p3.a6: Turn off lights and devices when not using them, use LED lights and energy-saving air conditioners, and use solar power.
p3.a7: Switch off unused devices, use LED lights and energy-efficient appliances, and adopt solar power.

cards.title: Describe an occasion when you were not allowed to use your mobile phone
points: why you were not allowed to use your phone
what you did without it and for how long
and explain how you felt about it
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: thi chứng chỉ ISTQB ở phòng thi, không được dùng điện thoại 2 tiếng (hoặc buổi họp/ chuyến bay).

notes.v: last year, ISTQB exam room, test centre
rule: prevent cheating, phone locked in bag at the front
focused on the exam, looked at clock, thought
anxious at first, then focused, relaxed after

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about an occasion when I wasn't allowed to use my phone. It happened last year, when I took my ISTQB exam at a testing centre in Hanoi.

The rule of the exam was that candidates must put all phones and bags in a locker, because the exam centre wanted to prevent cheating. We could not take our phones in the room.

I couldn't use my phone for about two and a half hours, including waiting time and the exam time.

Without my phone, I did nothing but concentrate on the questions. I also looked at the clock sometimes, to check the time. Before the exam, I just sat and read my notes, because I couldn't scroll on social media.

At the beginning, I felt a bit anxious, because I was used to checking my phone all the time. But then I felt calm and focused. After the exam, I realised that I could live without my phone for two hours, and it was good for my mind.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the time I wasn't allowed to use my phone, which was when I sat my ISTQB exam at a testing centre in Hanoi last year.

The rule was that all candidates had to leave their phones and bags in a locker, to prevent cheating. Phones were strictly banned from the exam room.

In total, I was without my phone for around two and a half hours, including waiting time and the exam itself.

With no phone to turn to, I had nothing to do but focus on the questions. I occasionally glanced at the wall clock to manage my time. Beforehand, I just sat and went over my notes, since I couldn't scroll through social media.

Initially, I felt a bit uneasy, as I'm used to checking my phone constantly. But soon, I felt calm and absorbed. Afterwards, it struck me that I can survive without my phone for a couple of hours, and that it was actually good for my mind.

At first I felt restless, but after a while I noticed more details around me and listened more carefully. That experience made me realise I don't always need my phone, and I now try to put it away during meals.

p3.q: How do young and old people use phones differently? Why?
p3.a6: Young people use phones for social media, games, videos and shopping. Older people use them for calls, messages and news, and some are slow with apps. The reasons are different habits and different levels of technology skill.
p3.a7: Young people use phones for social media, games, videos and shopping, while older people mainly call, text and read news, due to different habits and tech skills.

p3.q: Positive and negative impact on friendship?
p3.a6: Positive: we can keep in touch with friends easily. Negative: people look at the phone rather than talk when they meet, and misunderstandings happen in messages.
p3.a7: Positive: it keeps friends connected. Negative: people ignore each other in person, and text messages cause misunderstandings.

p3.q: Is it a waste of time to take pictures with phones?
p3.a6: Not always. Photos keep memories. But if people spend too much time taking photos, they don't enjoy the moment.
p3.a7: Not necessarily, as photos preserve memories, but excessive photo-taking stops people enjoying the moment.

p3.q: Is it necessary to have laws or new rules on phone use?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. For example, it's dangerous to use phones while driving, so we need laws and fines. Schools also need rules to stop students from using phones in class.
p3.a7: Yes. Using phones while driving is dangerous, so laws and fines are needed, and schools need rules to keep phones out of lessons.

p3.q: Examples of how phones can be annoying?
p3.a6: Loud ringtones in the cinema, people talking loudly on the bus, constant notifications and people checking phones during meetings.
p3.a7: Loud ringtones in cinemas, people talking loudly on buses, constant notifications and phones at meetings.

p3.q: Which places don't allow phones?
p3.a6: Exam rooms, hospitals, petrol stations, some classrooms, courtrooms and during flights, usually in "flight mode".
p3.a7: Exam rooms, hospitals, petrol stations, many classrooms, courtrooms, and phones must be in flight mode on planes.

p3.q: When should parents allow children to have phones?
p3.a6: I think around 12 or 13, when they go to secondary school and need to contact parents. Parents should still control the time and content.
p3.a7: Around 12 or 13, when they start secondary school and need to contact parents, with parental limits on time and content.

p3.q: Were social rules stricter in the past?
p3.a6: I agree. In the past, children had to respect elders strictly, and families had many rules. Now society is more open and free, but sometimes it's too relaxed.
p3.a7: I agree. Rules, especially respect for elders, were stricter; today's society is more liberal, sometimes perhaps too relaxed.

p3.q: Is it prevalent that people are addicted to phones?
p3.a6: Yes, very. Many people can't be without their phones, even at night. They feel anxious when they have no signal. Young people are the most addicted.
p3.a7: Very. Many can't put theirs down, even at night, and feel anxious without signal, particularly young people.

cards.title: Describe a time when you felt proud of a family member
points: and explain why you felt proud of him/her
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: em trai (17 tuổi, mơ làm bác sĩ ở Topic 1) đạt giải học sinh giỏi cấp thành phố môn Hóa.

notes.v: studied hard every night, nervous but brave, humble
closer, I support him, he asks me for advice

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about the time I felt proud of my younger brother, Khoi.

He's seventeen years old. Last March, he won the second prize in the chemistry contest for high school students of Hanoi city.

I felt proud for several reasons. First, he studied very hard for the contest. For three months, he studied every night until midnight, and he even gave up playing games. Second, he is quite shy, and he was very nervous before the contest. But he was brave and did his best. Third, after he won, he was humble. He didn't boast to his friends and said thank you to his teachers and our parents.

When the result was announced, my whole family was happy. My mother cried, and we had a special dinner to celebrate.

This experience made our relationship closer. Before, I often teased him. Now I respect him more. I support his dream of being a doctor, and he sometimes asks me for advice.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the time I felt incredibly proud of my younger brother, Khoi.

He's seventeen, and last March he won second prize in Hanoi's chemistry contest for high-school students.

There were several reasons I was so proud. Firstly, he'd worked extremely hard for it. For three months, he studied until midnight every night and even gave up gaming. Secondly, he's rather shy and was very nervous beforehand, yet he stayed courageous and gave it his all. Thirdly, he handled his success with humility. He didn't boast to his classmates, and he thanked his teachers and our parents.

When the result came out, the whole family was overjoyed. My mother even shed a few tears, and we held a special dinner to celebrate.

It definitely brought us closer. I used to tease him a lot, but now I have a lot more respect for him. I'm fully behind his dream of becoming a doctor, and he occasionally turns to me for advice, which I find really touching.

Our whole family celebrated with a big dinner, and my parents couldn't stop smiling. Seeing how hard he worked inspires me to stay disciplined with my own goals, including my English.

p3.q: When do parents feel proud of children? What do children do to make parents proud?
p3.a6: When children get good marks, win prizes, behave well or help others. Also when they get a good job or become independent.
p3.a7: When children achieve good results, win awards, behave well, help others, or land a good job and become independent.

p3.q: Should parents reward children? Too often? Do rewards help? Reward for homework or housework?
p3.a6: Yes, rewards motivate children, but small ones like praise, a favourite meal or a short trip. If parents reward too often, children only work for rewards. For housework, I think parents shouldn't pay money, because children should help the family.
p3.a7: Yes, modest rewards like praise or a treat motivate children, but too frequent rewards make them work only for gifts. For housework, paying money isn't ideal, as helping the family should come naturally.

p3.q: On what occasions would adults be proud of themselves? When did you last feel proud of yourself?
p3.a6: When they finish a difficult project, get promoted or help someone. Recently, I felt proud when I completed the first month of my English study plan without skipping any day.
p3.a7: On finishing a difficult project, getting promoted or helping someone. Most recently, I felt proud completing a full month of my English study plan without missing a day.

p3.q: Children working hard just for grades?
p3.a6: It's not very good. Grades are important, but if children only study for grades, they feel pressure and they don't love learning. Understanding is more important.
p3.a7: Not ideal. Grades matter, but studying solely for them creates pressure and kills the love of learning; understanding matters more.

p3.q: What did you do to make parents proud? What advantages of yours make you proud?
p3.a6: I studied hard and got into university and then found a job. I'm proud that I'm patient and don't give up easily.
p3.a7: I studied hard, got into university and found a job. I'm proud of being patient and persistent.

p3.q: Does any job bring a sense of pride?
p3.a6: Yes, jobs that help others, such as doctors, teachers and firefighters. Also jobs that build things, like engineers.
p3.a7: Yes, those that serve others, like doctors, teachers and firefighters, or create something, like engineers.

p3.q: Have things people are proud of changed compared to the past?
p3.a6: Yes. In the past, people were proud of having a stable government job or a big family. Now many people are proud of being independent, having a successful business or being famous online.
p3.a7: Yes. Previously, a stable state job or a large family were sources of pride; now it's independence, a successful business or online influence.

cards.title: Describe your favourite place in your house where you can relax
points: what you do there and when
and explain why you find it relaxing
cards.note: Nơi giả định: phòng ngủ/ góc cửa sổ của bạn (ở nhà bố mẹ, ngoại thành).

notes.v: my bedroom, corner by the window
small, bean bag/ armchair, bookshelf, plants, warm light
listen music, skincare, read, study English, look outside
quiet, private, comfortable, my own space

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my favourite place to relax in my house: the corner by the window in my bedroom.

My bedroom is on the second floor. It's quite small, but I like the corner by the window the most. In this corner, I have a soft chair, a small table and a bookshelf. I also have some small plants, and I use a warm yellow light, so it feels cosy. From the window, I can see the trees and the neighbours' roofs.

I usually sit there to listen to music, read books, do my skincare or study English. Sometimes I just sit and look outside and do nothing.

I usually spend time there in the evening, after dinner, and on weekend mornings.

This place helps me relax because it's quiet and private, and I can be alone. Everything in it is what I like, and nobody tells me what to do there. It's my own small world after a stressful day.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my favourite spot for relaxing at home: the window corner of my bedroom.

My room is on the second floor and it's fairly small, but that corner is my favourite part. I've set up a soft armchair, a small table and a bookshelf, along with a few little plants and a warm yellow lamp, which makes it incredibly cosy. Through the window, I can see treetops and neighbouring rooftops.

I usually sit there to listen to music, read, do my skincare routine or study English. Sometimes I simply gaze outside and do absolutely nothing.

I spend time there mostly in the evenings after dinner, and on weekend mornings.

It helps me relax because it's quiet and private, so I can be alone with my thoughts. Everything in that corner reflects my taste, and no one disturbs me. After a stressful day, it's my own little sanctuary where I can recharge.

I've arranged a few plants and soft lights there, so it feels cosy and calm after a long day. It's my little escape, and I honestly think everyone needs a corner like this at home.

p3.q: Why is it difficult for some people to relax?
p3.a6: They have too much work or worry about the future. Some people are always on their phones, so their minds can't stop. Others feel guilty if they rest.
p3.a7: Heavy workloads and worries about the future, constant phone use that keeps the mind busy, and guilt about resting.

p3.q: What are the benefits of doing exercise?
p3.a6: Exercise makes us healthy and strong. It also reduces stress, improves sleep and makes us feel happier.
p3.a7: It strengthens the body, reduces stress, improves sleep and lifts mood.

p3.q: Do people in your country exercise after work?
p3.a6: Some do. Many people walk or run in parks in the evening, play badminton or football, or go to the gym. But many others are too tired, so they exercise in the early morning or only on weekends.
p3.a7: Some do: walking and jogging in parks, badminton, football or the gym. Many are too tired and prefer early mornings or weekends.

p3.q: Where do people spend most of their time at home?
p3.a6: In the living room, because the family watches TV and eats there. Young people stay in their bedroom with computers or phones. In the kitchen, mothers spend a lot of time cooking.
p3.a7: The living room, where families watch TV and eat together, though young people stay in their bedrooms and mothers spend much time in the kitchen.

p3.q: Should there be classes to train young people and children how to relax?
p3.a6: I think it could be helpful. Many students are stressed because of exams. Simple classes for breathing, yoga or meditation can help them manage stress.
p3.a7: It could help, as exam stress is common; simple classes in breathing, yoga or meditation would teach them to manage it.

p3.q: Which is more important: mental or physical relaxation?
p3.a6: I think both are important, but mental relaxation is more important today because many people have stress and anxiety. Mental relaxation also helps the body relax.
p3.a7: Both matter, but mental relaxation arguably matters more today, given widespread stress and anxiety, and it helps the body unwind too.

cards.title: Describe your perfect job
points: what skills or qualifications you would need
where you would like to work
and explain why it would be the perfect job for you
cards.note: Nghề giả định: QA Automation Lead/ Test Manager tại công ty công nghệ quốc tế (khớp với mục tiêu ở Topic 28). Bạn có thể chọn công việc mơ ước khác.

notes.v: QA Automation Lead at an international tech company
detail-oriented, enjoy IT, like helping team

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my perfect job: a QA automation lead in an international technology company.

For this job, I'd need several skills and qualifications. First, I need strong skills in automation testing and programming. I also need certificates like ISTQB. Second, I must have good English, because I would work with foreign colleagues and clients. Third, I would need leadership and communication skills, to guide my team.

I would like to work in a modern office in Hanoi, and I want flexible hours, so I can work at home sometimes.

This job would be suitable for me because I like IT, and I'm careful with details, which is important for testing. I also like helping other people to improve.

I think it's my perfect job because it has a good salary, many chances to learn and a good work-life balance. It would give me a stable life and let me support my family.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my idea of a perfect job: being a QA automation lead at an international tech company.

It would demand a particular skill set. Firstly, strong automation testing and programming abilities, backed up by certifications such as ISTQB. Secondly, good English, since I'd be working with foreign colleagues and clients. Thirdly, leadership and communication skills to guide a team effectively.

I'd like to work in a modern office in Hanoi, with flexible hours that allow me to work from home occasionally.

It would suit me because I'm passionate about IT and have a keen eye for detail, which is crucial in testing. I also enjoy coaching others and watching them progress.

I'd call it perfect because it offers a competitive salary, constant opportunities to learn and a healthy work-life balance. It would give me financial security, and the means to look after my parents, while still leaving time for my own interests.

I know such a job is hard to find, so I'm improving my English and technical skills step by step. If I keep going, I believe I'll get closer to it, and that thought motivates me every day.

vocab.m: cân bằng công việc – cuộc sống

p3.q: What jobs do children want? What are dream jobs in your country?
p3.a6: Children often want to be doctors, teachers, police officers, pilots or YouTubers. In Vietnam, many adults dream of jobs in IT, banking, medicine or being a civil servant, because they are stable and well paid.
p3.a7: Children dream of being doctors, teachers, police officers, pilots or YouTubers. Vietnamese adults aspire to IT, banking, medicine or civil service for stability and good pay.

p3.q: What should people consider when choosing jobs?
p3.a6: Their interests, skills, salary, working hours, the location and the chances to grow. They should also think about the company's culture.
p3.a7: Interests, skills, salary, hours, location, career growth and company culture.

p3.q: Is salary the main reason? Salary or interest?
p3.a6: Salary is important because everyone needs money, but it isn't the only reason. I think interest is more important in the long run, because if you don't like the job, you'll feel tired and unhappy, even with a high salary.
p3.a7: Salary matters, but not exclusively. Long term, genuine interest is more important, as even a high salary can't compensate for a job you dislike.

p3.q: What kind of job can be called a "dream job"?
p3.a6: A job that matches your passion, has a good salary, nice colleagues and time for life outside work. It makes you feel excited to go to work.
p3.a7: One that matches your passion, pays well, has good colleagues and leaves time for life outside work, so you look forward to Monday.

p3.q: Do ideal jobs change as people grow up?
p3.a6: Yes, a lot. When we are young, we think about exciting jobs. When we grow up, we think about stability, salary and family.
p3.a7: Very much. Children are drawn to exciting jobs, while adults prioritise stability, income and family.

p3.q: How can people find a perfect job?
p3.a6: They should understand themselves, try different jobs, learn skills and get advice from experienced people. They also need patience.
p3.a7: By knowing themselves, trying different roles, building skills, seeking advice and being patient.

p3.q: Why do some jobs attract more people? Why do people choose their dream job?
p3.a6: Jobs with high pay, high status or an easy and stable life attract more people. People also choose a dream job because of their passion, family influence or because they want to help others.
p3.a7: Jobs offering high pay, status or stability attract more people, and people choose dream jobs out of passion, family influence or a wish to help others.

cards.title: Describe an occasion when many people were smiling
points: and explain how you felt about it
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: tiệc cưới của người bạn/ buổi họp lớp. Bài này: đám cưới của anh họ.

notes.v: last November, cousin's wedding, a restaurant in Hanoi
happy couple, funny speech, music, photos

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my cousin's wedding, where many people were smiling.

It happened last November, at a restaurant in Hanoi, on a sunny Sunday.

There were about two hundred guests: our relatives, the friends of the bride and groom, and neighbours. My parents and my grandmother were also there.

There were many reasons to smile. The bride and groom looked very happy and beautiful. The MC told funny stories about them, and everyone laughed. A band played a beautiful song, and the guests sang along. Then we took a lot of photos and said, "Cheese!" together.

I took many photos of the family, said congratulations to the couple and gave them a gift. I also sang a short song with my cousins.

When I saw so many smiling faces, I felt very happy and warm. A smile is contagious, so I couldn't stop smiling too. My cheeks hurt at the end of the day.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my cousin's wedding, an occasion where everyone seemed to be beaming.

It took place last November at a restaurant in Hanoi on a bright, sunny Sunday.

There were around two hundred guests, including relatives, friends of the newlyweds and neighbours, as well as my parents and grandmother.

There was no shortage of reasons to smile. The bride and groom looked radiant and blissfully happy. The MC told amusing anecdotes about them that had the whole room in stitches. A live band played a lovely song and the guests sang along. Then we gathered for group photos and said "cheese" in unison.

I took lots of family photos, congratulated the couple, gave them our gift and even sang a short song with my cousins.

Seeing so many smiling faces filled me with warmth and joy. Smiles are contagious, so I couldn't stop grinning either. By the end of the day, my cheeks were actually aching.

I couldn't help smiling too, and the mood stayed with me for the rest of the day. It showed me how contagious happiness is, and how a small, joyful moment can brighten a whole crowd.

p3.q: Do people who like to smile seem friendlier?
p3.a6: Yes, usually. A smile shows a positive attitude, so people feel comfortable to talk to them. But a smile is not always real, so we can't judge only by it.
p3.a7: Usually, yes, as a smile signals warmth and approachability, though it isn't always genuine, so we shouldn't judge by it alone.

p3.q: Why do most people smile in photographs?
p3.a6: Because they want to look happy and good in the photo, and also keep a happy memory. The photographer often asks them to smile.
p3.a7: To look happy and attractive and to capture a pleasant memory, often at the photographer's prompting.

p3.q: Do women smile more than men?
p3.a6: I think so, in many cultures. Women are often taught to be gentle and friendly, and men to look serious. But it depends on the person.
p3.a7: In many cultures, yes, as women are often expected to appear warm while men are expected to look serious, but it varies individually.

p3.q: Do people smile more when younger or older?
p3.a6: Younger people, especially children, smile more, because they have fewer worries. Older people smile less, but their smiles can be more meaningful.
p3.a7: The young, especially children, smile more freely with fewer worries, while older people smile less often but perhaps more meaningfully.

p3.q: Why do people smile?
p3.a6: Because they are happy, they want to be polite or to show friendliness. Sometimes people smile to hide nervousness.
p3.a7: Out of happiness, politeness or friendliness, and sometimes to mask nervousness.

p3.q: Do elderly people have better control of feelings? When should people not show emotions?
p3.a6: Yes, usually, because of their experience. Young people are more emotional. People should not show emotions in formal meetings, interviews or when talking with an angry customer, or in sad situations like funerals.
p3.a7: Generally, as experience brings emotional control. Showing emotions is best avoided in formal meetings, interviews, difficult customer interactions and solemn occasions.

p3.q: Are people motivated more by emotions than logic? Is it good to be driven by emotions?
p3.a6: In daily life, I think emotions are strong, for example in shopping or relationships. Emotions give us passion, but big decisions need logic. A balance is best.
p3.a7: In daily life, emotions often drive us, such as when shopping or in relationships. Emotions give passion, but important decisions need logic, so a balance is best.

cards.title: Describe a program or app on your computer or phone
points: what the program or app is
and explain why it is useful to you
cards.note: App giả định: Google Calendar/ Notion hoặc app học tiếng Anh. Bài này: ứng dụng ghi chú Notion/ Notes – dùng lên kế hoạch học tiếng Anh. Mình chọn "Notion".

notes.v: notes, to-do list, study plan, vocabulary, work tasks
two years ago, a colleague recommended

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about an app that I use on my phone and my computer. It's called Notion.

I use it every day, usually in the morning to make my to-do list, and in the evening to review my day.

I use it for several things. I write my work notes and my test plans. I keep my English study plan and my vocabulary lists in it. I also write my weekly budget.

I started using it about two years ago. One of my colleagues recommended it to me, and showed me how to use it.

I think it's very useful for a few reasons. First, it helps me stay organised, so I don't forget important things. Second, it's free for personal use. Third, it syncs between my phone and my laptop, so I can use it on the bus or at the office. I think it's one of the most important apps in my life.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Notion, an app I use on both my phone and computer.

I use it every single day, typically in the morning to set up my to-do list and in the evening to review how the day went.

It serves several purposes. I keep my work notes and test plans there, along with my English study schedule and vocabulary lists. I also track my weekly budget with it.

I started using it roughly two years ago, when a colleague recommended it and showed me the basics.

I find it extremely useful for several reasons. Firstly, it keeps me organised, so nothing important slips through the cracks. Secondly, the free version is more than enough for personal use. Thirdly, it syncs seamlessly between my phone and laptop, so I can update it on the bus or at the office. Honestly, it's one of the most indispensable apps in my daily life.

It has simple tools, a clean design and rarely crashes, so I can rely on it every day. As a tester, I appreciate well-built software, and this app is a great example of it.

p3.q: Differences between old and young people when using apps?
p3.a6: Young people learn new apps quickly and use many apps for entertainment and social media. Older people use fewer apps, for calls, messages and news, and sometimes need help.
p3.a7: Young people pick up new apps quickly and use many for entertainment and socialising, while older people use fewer, mainly for calls and messages, and often need help.

p3.q: Why do some people not like using apps?
p3.a6: They find apps complicated, or worry about security and privacy. Some feel apps waste time or prefer to do things face-to-face.
p3.a7: They find them complicated, worry about privacy and security, or prefer face-to-face methods.

p3.q: Which apps are popular or not popular? What apps do you have?
p3.a6: Zalo, Facebook, TikTok, YouTube, Shopee and Grab are popular, because they are useful in daily life. Less popular are special apps for professionals. On my phone, I have Zalo, Notion, Grab, a banking app and English learning apps.
p3.a7: Zalo, Facebook, TikTok, YouTube, Shopee and Grab are hugely popular for their everyday usefulness, while niche professional apps are less so. On my phone I have Zalo, Notion, Grab, a banking app and English-learning apps.

p3.q: Should parents limit their children's use of computer programs and games?
p3.a6: Yes. Children can get addicted and it hurts their eyes and studies. Parents can set time limits, like one hour a day, use parental control apps and play with the children.
p3.a7: Yes, since children can become addicted, harming their eyesight and studies. Parents can set daily limits, use parental controls and join in.

p3.q: Are young people more reliant on apps?
p3.a6: Yes. They use apps to order food, take a taxi, study, pay and even make friends. Without apps, many of them would feel lost.
p3.a7: Yes. They rely on apps for food, rides, study, payments and even friendships, and would feel lost without them.

p3.q: Drawbacks of too many apps?
p3.a6: They take up phone memory and battery, and send many notifications, which distract us. They also collect our personal data, so there is a risk to privacy.
p3.a7: They eat up storage and battery, bombard us with distracting notifications and collect personal data, which poses privacy risks.

p3.q: Benefits of apps as a tool for education?
p3.a6: Students can learn anywhere, at their own speed. Apps use games, videos and quizzes, so they make learning more fun. They also give instant feedback.
p3.a7: Learning anywhere at one's own pace, with games, videos and quizzes that make it engaging, plus instant feedback.

cards.title: Describe a famous person you would like to meet
points: and explain why you would like to meet him/her
cards.note: Nhân vật giả định: một doanh nhân công nghệ nổi tiếng của Việt Nam. Mình để chung là "a famous Vietnamese tech entrepreneur" để bạn thay bằng tên người bạn thật sự muốn gặp.

notes.v: a famous Vietnamese tech entrepreneur (bạn thay tên thật)
news, YouTube interviews, books, social media
founding a successful technology company, from nothing
learn how to succeed, overcome failure, career
ask about failures, advice for young engineers, thank

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a famous Vietnamese technology entrepreneur whom I would like to meet. (You can replace this with a real name.)

I know about him from the news, from YouTube interviews and also from a book about his life, which a colleague lent me.

He's famous for starting a successful technology company in Vietnam, which now has many employees and customers. He started with very little money, and he met many difficulties, but he didn't give up.

I would like to meet him because I want to learn how he became successful. I'm working in IT, so I'm very interested in his experience. I also want to learn how he faced failure.

If I met him, I would first say thank you for inspiring young people. Then I would ask him about the most difficult time in his career and how he overcame it. I would also ask what advice he had for a young engineer like me who wants to grow in his career.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a famous Vietnamese tech entrepreneur I'd love to meet. (Replace with a real name when you practise.)

I know about him through news reports, YouTube interviews and a book about his life that a colleague lent me.

He's famous for building a successful technology company from scratch, which now employs a great many people and serves millions of customers. He started with very little capital and faced numerous setbacks, but he never gave up.

I'd love to meet him because I want to understand how he achieved such success. As someone working in IT, his experience resonates with me, and I'm particularly curious about how he dealt with failure.

If I met him, I'd first thank him for inspiring so many young people. Then I'd ask him about the toughest period of his career and how he overcame it, and what advice he'd give to a young engineer like me who aspires to grow professionally.

I'd love to hear how he handled failure and kept going, because that's something I struggle with. Even a short conversation could give me ideas and energy that I would carry for years.

p3.q: Advantages and disadvantages of being a famous child?
p3.a6: Advantages: they earn money, get good chances and become confident. Disadvantages: they lose privacy and childhood, have a lot of pressure, and may be criticised online.
p3.a7: Upsides: money, opportunities and confidence. Downsides: loss of privacy and childhood, heavy pressure and online criticism.

p3.q: What can children do to become famous? What can they do with fame? Why do they want to?
p3.a6: They can become famous through talent shows, sports, music or social media like TikTok and YouTube. With fame, they can earn money, help charities or spread positive messages. Children want to be famous because they see idols and want money, attention and an exciting life.
p3.a7: Via talent shows, sports, music, TikTok or YouTube. Fame can be used to earn money, support charities and spread positive messages. Children want it for the money, attention and glamorous image they see in idols.

p3.q: Do people become famous because of talent? Can they without talent?
p3.a6: Many do, such as singers and athletes. But some become famous because of luck, looks, a scandal or a viral video, even without talent. But fame without talent usually doesn't last long.
p3.a7: Many do, but some achieve fame through luck, looks, scandal or viral videos, though fame without talent rarely lasts.

p3.q: What kinds of famous people are in the news? Are there more celebrities now? Does everyone enjoy celebrity news?
p3.a6: Singers, actors, footballers and influencers. Yes, there are more because of social media. Not everyone enjoys it. Some people think it's useless gossip, but many people, especially young people, like to follow it.
p3.a7: Singers, actors, footballers and influencers, and there are more now thanks to social media. Not everyone enjoys it; some dismiss it as gossip, though many young people love following it.

p3.q: Do people like packaged celebrities or those with genuine talent?
p3.a6: Short-term, many people like packaged celebrities because they look good and are promoted heavily. But in the long term, people respect those with real talent.
p3.a7: Packaged celebrities may win short-term attention through heavy promotion, but people ultimately respect genuine talent.

p3.q: Would people still want fame if they knew what they'd face?
p3.a6: Some would still want it, because of the money and attention. But others would change their mind because of the loss of privacy, pressure and online hate.
p3.a7: Some would, for the money and attention, but others would reconsider given the lost privacy, pressure and online hate.

cards.title: Describe a time when you gave advice to others
points: and explain whether the advice was helpful
cards.note: Câu chuyện giả định: khuyên em trai/ bạn Nam chọn ngành học (hoặc cách học tiếng Anh). Bài này: khuyên đồng nghiệp mới cách học tiếng Anh/ test.

notes.v: how to learn software testing and manage time / not to quit
stressed, many bugs, thinking about leaving

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a time that I gave advice to a new colleague, Hanh.

She joined my company three months ago as a junior tester. She was a fresh graduate. After two months, she felt very stressed, because there were so many things to learn and she made some mistakes. She told me she was thinking about leaving the job.

I gave her some advice. First, I told her that everyone makes mistakes at the beginning, and it's normal. Second, I advised her to write down what she learned every day and to ask questions to the seniors. Third, I suggested she learn only one new thing each week, not everything at once.

She listened carefully and said thank you. She started to follow my advice. After about one month, she became more confident and made fewer mistakes.

I think my advice was helpful, because she's still working with us and she looks happier. I also felt happy that I could help someone.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about the time I advised a new colleague named Hanh.

She joined my company three months ago as a junior tester straight out of university. After two months, she was feeling overwhelmed by how much there was to learn, and she'd made a few mistakes. She confided in me that she was considering quitting.

I offered her several pieces of advice. First, I reassured her that everyone makes mistakes at the start, and that it's perfectly normal. Second, I suggested keeping a daily learning log and not hesitating to ask senior colleagues questions. Third, I recommended tackling just one new topic a week rather than trying to master everything at once.

She listened attentively, thanked me and began putting it into practice. Within a month, she seemed much more confident and was making fewer errors.

I believe my advice was valuable, as she's still with us and appears much happier. It also gave me a real sense of satisfaction to have helped someone.

Later, he told me the advice had helped him calm down and make a clearer decision. I felt happy to have helped, and it reminded me to listen carefully before giving opinions.

p3.q: Is it good to ask strangers online for advice? Problems of asking too many people?
p3.a6: It can be useful for simple things like technology or travel. But strangers may give wrong or biased advice, so we should check. If we ask too many people, we get different opinions and become more confused. We also may lose our own opinion.
p3.a7: Useful for simple matters like tech or travel, but strangers may be inaccurate or biased, so verify. Asking too many people brings conflicting opinions and confusion, and we may lose confidence in our own judgment.

p3.q: What personalities do advice-givers need? Who is most suitable? Qualities?
p3.a6: They should be patient, honest, kind and good listeners. They also need experience and knowledge, and should not judge people.
p3.a7: Patient, honest, empathetic good listeners with relevant experience, and non-judgmental.

p3.q: Should parents, teachers and friends give advice? Is it necessary to listen to friends?
p3.a6: Yes. Parents and teachers have experience, so their advice helps young people avoid mistakes. Friends understand our situation, so it's good to listen too. But finally, we should decide by ourselves.
p3.a7: Yes. Parents and teachers have experience that helps young people avoid mistakes, and friends understand our situation. But the final decision is ours.

p3.q: How to give young people and old people advice?
p3.a6: For young people, we should be gentle, give examples and respect their opinions. For older people, we should be very polite and respectful, and suggest rather than tell.
p3.a7: With young people, be gentle, use examples and respect their views; with older people, be especially respectful and suggest rather than instruct.

p3.q: In which areas are people more or less willing to accept advice?
p3.a6: People accept advice more on health, technology and money. They accept less on personal choices like marriage, appearance or religion.
p3.a7: More receptive on health, technology and finance, less on personal matters like marriage, appearance or religion.

p3.q: Have you received advice from professionals?
p3.a6: Yes, a doctor told me to sleep earlier and reduce screen time. It was useful. I also got advice from my university teacher about my career.
p3.a7: Yes. A doctor told me to sleep earlier and cut screen time, which was useful, and a university lecturer advised me on my career.

p3.q: Should people prepare before giving advice? When should they think carefully?
p3.a6: Yes. They should understand the situation and not give advice quickly. It's important to think carefully when the advice is about big matters like health, money or marriage, because it could affect someone's life.
p3.a7: Yes, they should understand the situation first. Careful thought matters most with major issues like health, money or marriage, as the advice could change someone's life.

p3.q: Why do some people ask others for advice on almost everything?
p3.a6: They lack confidence or are afraid of making mistakes. Some depend on others, and some just want to feel supported.
p3.a7: They lack confidence, fear mistakes, depend on others or simply want reassurance.

p3.q: When is it better to ask friends than family? Why do older people ask younger people for advice?
p3.a6: Friends are better for topics like technology, fashion or relationships, because they are the same age and don't judge. Older people ask the young about new technology and trends, which they don't understand.
p3.a7: Friends suit topics like technology, fashion or relationships, as they're peers and less judgmental. Older people consult the young about new technology and trends.

p3.q: Can anyone learn to give advice effectively?
p3.a6: I agree. With practice, anyone can learn to listen, ask good questions and speak kindly. Experience also helps.
p3.a7: I agree; with practice, anyone can learn to listen, ask good questions and speak tactfully.

cards.title: Describe a movie you watched recently that you felt disappointed about
points: when and where you watched it
and explain why you felt disappointed about it
cards.note: Phim giả định (không nêu tên thật): một bộ phim hành động/ viễn tưởng nổi tiếng nhưng cốt truyện yếu. Bạn thay bằng phim thật.

notes.v: weak story, boring, too long, bad ending, high expectations from trailer
no, or only if you like effects

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a science fiction action movie that I watched last month and felt disappointed about. (Replace with a real film.)

I watched it at a cinema in Hanoi on Saturday evening with three of my friends. We were very excited because the trailer looked amazing, and the first movie was very good.

I was disappointed for several reasons. First, the story was weak and hard to understand. There were too many characters, and I couldn't follow what was happening. Second, the movie was too long, nearly three hours, and some scenes were boring. Third, the ending was not satisfying and didn't make sense. The special effects were good, but they were not enough to save the movie.

I think my expectations were too high, so I felt more disappointed. I wasted two hours and some money.

I wouldn't recommend it to other people, unless they love special effects and don't care about the story. They should watch the first movie instead.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a sci-fi action sequel I saw last month and found really disappointing. (Replace with a real film.)

I watched it at a cinema in Hanoi on a Saturday evening with three friends. We were all buzzing, as the trailer looked spectacular and the first instalment had been excellent.

There were several reasons it let me down. First, the plot was weak and convoluted, with so many characters that I lost track of what was going on. Second, it dragged on for almost three hours, with several tedious scenes. Third, the ending was unsatisfying and made little sense. The special effects were impressive, but they couldn't compensate for the lack of a decent story.

My expectations were perhaps too high, which made it worse. I felt I'd wasted both time and money.

I wouldn't recommend it, except to those who care only about visual effects. I'd tell everyone else to rewatch the original instead.

Afterwards, my friends and I laughed about how bad it was, so the evening wasn't a total waste. Now I always read a few reviews before choosing a film, which saves both money and time.

p3.q: Do you believe movie reviews?
p3.a6: Partly. Reviews can help me to choose, but I don't trust them completely, because people have different tastes, and some reviews are paid. I usually read several reviews and watch the trailer.
p3.a7: Partly. They help me choose, but tastes differ and some reviews are paid, so I read several and watch the trailer.

p3.q: What types of films are there and popular in your country?
p3.a6: Comedy, family dramas, horror, action, romance, animation and historical films. Comedy and family movies at Tet are the most popular, and also Hollywood superhero movies.
p3.a7: Comedies, family dramas, horror, action, romance, animation and historical films. Comedies and family films at Tet are most popular, along with Hollywood superhero movies.

p3.q: Are historical films popular in your country? Why?
p3.a6: Some are, but not as much as comedy or action. They need a big budget and good stories. But when they are good, people like to learn about history and feel proud.
p3.a7: Moderately, less than comedy or action, as they need big budgets and strong stories; when well made, they spark pride and interest in history.

p3.q: Are films with famous actors more likely to succeed?
p3.a6: They attract more audiences at the beginning, but a bad film with a famous star can still fail, like the one that I watched.
p3.a7: They draw bigger opening audiences, but a poor film with a star still flops, as my example shows.

p3.q: Why are Japanese animated films so popular?
p3.a6: They have beautiful pictures, creative stories and deep emotions, so they are good for both children and adults. Japanese culture is also popular around the world.
p3.a7: Their beautiful artwork, imaginative stories and emotional depth appeal to both children and adults, and Japanese culture is globally popular.

p3.q: Should directors pay a lot to famous actors? Should actors be paid more?
p3.a6: If actors bring many viewers, a high salary is reasonable. But it's not good if the production spends most of the budget on actors and little on the script. I think the crew should also be paid fairly.
p3.a7: If stars draw big audiences, high pay is justified, but overspending on actors at the expense of the script is unwise, and the crew deserve fair pay too.

cards.title: Describe an important old thing that your family has kept for a long time
points: how long your family has kept it
and explain why it is important to your family
cards.note: Đồ vật giả định: chiếc đồng hồ cổ / bộ ấm chén/ bàn thờ... Bài này: chiếc radio cũ của ông nội.

notes.v: memories, grandfather, news, music, history, still works

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about an old radio that belonged to my grandfather. My family has kept it for more than fifty years.

My grandfather bought it when he was a young man, and he used it to listen to the news and traditional music. After he passed away, my grandmother kept it. Now it stays on a wooden shelf in the living room of my grandmother's house. She cleans it every week.

My family has kept it for so long because it has many memories of my grandfather. He loved it very much, and when I was a child, I often sat with him to listen to old songs and stories on the radio. It still works, although the sound is a bit noisy.

This old thing is important to my family because it connects us with our past. When we look at it, we remember my grandfather, and it reminds us to love and respect our family. We will keep it for the next generation.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about an old radio that once belonged to my grandfather, which my family has kept for over fifty years.

He bought it as a young man and used it to listen to the news and traditional music. After he passed away, my grandmother took care of it. It now sits on a wooden shelf in the living room of her house, and she dusts it every week.

The reason we've held onto it for so long is the memories attached to it. My grandfather cherished it, and as a child, I often sat beside him listening to old songs and stories on it. Remarkably, it still works, although the sound is slightly crackly.

It's important to my family because it's a tangible link to our past. Whenever we look at it, we remember my grandfather, and it reminds us to value family bonds. It's more than an object; it's a piece of our family history, and we intend to pass it on to the next generation.

I keep it carefully in my room and show it to visitors with pride. I hope to pass it on to my children one day, so that our family story continues through it.

p3.q: What old things do people keep and why? Why do grown-ups hate throwing old things away? What do families keep?
p3.a6: People keep photos, letters, jewellery, old clothes and furniture. They keep them because of memories and emotions. Grown-ups often think "maybe I need it later", or they feel it's a waste. In my family, they keep photos, old radio, ancestor altars and jewellery.
p3.a7: Photos, letters, jewellery, old clothes and furniture, kept for their sentimental value. Grown-ups hate discarding things, thinking they may be useful later or that it's wasteful. Families often keep photos, heirlooms and ancestral altars.

p3.q: Differences between the things old and young people keep? Things valued in the past and today?
p3.a6: Old people keep traditional things like old coins, letters and furniture. Young people keep things like game cards, concert tickets or digital photos. In the past, people valued gold and land. Today, people value experiences, technology and digital things.
p3.a7: Older people keep traditional items like coins, letters and furniture; younger people keep game cards, concert tickets and digital photos. Past generations valued gold and land, whereas today people value experiences and technology.

p3.q: Differences between the things people keep today and in the past?
p3.a6: In the past, people kept physical things. Now many things are digital, like photos on the phone or the cloud, so people keep fewer physical objects.
p3.a7: In the past, memories were physical objects; now they're digital, such as phone photos and cloud storage, so people keep fewer tangible items.

p3.q: Is keeping old things a great way to connect with the past?
p3.a6: Yes. Old things tell stories and help us imagine the life of our ancestors. They bring generations closer.
p3.a7: Yes, they tell stories and help us picture our ancestors' lives, bringing generations closer.

p3.q: Other things kept for a long time? What do people pass down?
p3.a6: Besides photos, families keep family recipes, wedding rings, gold jewellery, land, old books and family trees. In Vietnam, people also pass down ancestor altars, family names and traditions.
p3.a7: Besides photos, recipes, wedding rings, gold jewellery, land, books and family trees; in Vietnam, ancestral altars, family traditions and genealogies are also handed down.

p3.q: What things are kept in museums?
p3.a6: Old tools, clothes, paintings, documents, weapons, coins and things of famous people. They show how people lived in the past.
p3.a7: Ancient tools, clothing, paintings, documents, weapons, coins and belongings of famous figures, showing how people used to live.

p3.q: Influence of technology on museums? Benefits of technology for learning history?
p3.a6: Museums now have online tours, QR codes and virtual reality, so visitors can see more. Technology makes history more vivid and interesting, and we can learn from home through videos and 3D models.
p3.a7: Museums offer virtual tours, QR codes and VR, widening access, and technology brings history to life through videos and 3D models that can be explored from home.

p3.q: Why do people visit museums?
p3.a6: To learn about history and culture, to enjoy art, to spend time with family, or as a tourist activity. Students also visit for school projects.
p3.a7: To learn about history and culture, enjoy art, spend time with family, as tourists or for school projects.
